S01: Understanding AI agents

What Does the Course Cover

The AI Agents Bootcamp is a structured curriculum that progresses from agent fundamentals through architecture patterns (LangChain, LangGraph) to full end-to-end agent projects.

The course follows a deliberate pedagogical arc: foundational concepts first (what agents are, their types, essential components), then design patterns (augmented LLMs, prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, ReAct, ReWoo, reflection, multi-agent systems), then practical frameworks (LangChain for LLM integration, LangGraph for stateful workflows with nodes, edges, and control flow), and finally three capstone projects that consolidate theory into working systems. Each section builds on prior material, making sequential completion essential. The course includes downloadable resources (notes, exercise files, notebooks) that serve as both practice and supplementary learning material.

  • The curriculum follows four phases: fundamentals, design patterns, framework programming (LangChain + LangGraph), and capstone projects.
  • LangGraph enables stateful agent workflows through defined nodes, edges, and control flow, with built-in error handling and memory management.
  • Sequential completion is critical because each section builds directly on prior concepts.
  • Exercise files are not optional practice; they contain additional insights beyond what lectures cover.
📌
Course Arc

Fundamentals to architecture to frameworks to three real-world capstone projects.

1

Fundamentals (S01-S09)

Agent types, components, learning mechanisms, architecture patterns, implementation, n8n hands-on, infrastructure, business context

2

Agentic workflows, prompting strategies, all five workflow patterns, planning, memory, governance, evaluation

3

4

LangGraph (S30-S35)

States, nodes, edges, conditional routing, message management, thread persistence

5

Capstone Projects (S36-S40)

ReAct job helper, ReWoo job helper, multi-agent parallelized business evaluator

Takeaways

  • Follow the course sequentially; skipping sections creates knowledge gaps that compound later.
  • Complete every exercise; they contain learning material not covered in lectures.

What Is an AI agent?

An AI agent is a software system that goes beyond assisting humans to autonomously managing tasks, reasoning through problems, and executing multi-step workflows with minimal human intervention.

The evolution from LLMs to AI agents represents a fundamental shift in how AI is deployed. LLMs proved that machines could dramatically boost productivity (writing emails in 5 minutes instead of 30, researching topics in hours instead of days). But LLMs still require a human operator. AI agents take the next step: they reason, plan, and act autonomously. An AI agent combines an LLM's reasoning capability with the ability to perceive its environment, make decisions, and execute actions in a loop. Where an LLM answers questions, an agent completes objectives. This distinction (tool vs. autonomous worker) is the defining line between current AI usage and the emerging agentic paradigm.

  • LLMs are powerful reasoning engines but require human prompting for each step; agents operate autonomously toward objectives.
  • An AI agent perceives its environment, reasons about what to do, acts, and then evaluates the outcome in a continuous loop.
  • The shift from LLM-as-tool to agent-as-worker mirrors how businesses evolved from using calculators to deploying autonomous systems.
  • Agentic AI enables systems that manage tasks independently rather than merely assisting human operators.
📌
LLM vs Agent

LLM writes an email when prompted; agent monitors inbox, drafts replies, schedules follow-ups autonomously.

💡
LLM vs Agent: Calculator vs Autonomous Employee

An LLM is like a brilliant calculator: you press buttons (prompts) and get answers, but it never picks up a task on its own. An AI agent is like an autonomous employee: (1) it perceives its work environment (inbox, databases, schedules), (2) it reasons about priorities without being told each step, (3) it takes multi-step actions (drafts emails, sends them, monitors responses), and (4) it evaluates outcomes and refines its approach. The calculator amplifies YOUR throughput; the employee creates independent throughput.

Quick Check

1. What is the key difference between an LLM and an AI agent?

An LLM uses neural networks while an agent uses rule-based systems
An agent operates autonomously toward objectives while an LLM requires human prompting for each step
An LLM can only process text while an agent can process images
An agent is always more accurate than an LLM

Takeaways

  • An AI agent is defined by its autonomy loop: perceive, reason, act, evaluate, repeat.
  • The business value of agents comes from replacing human-in-the-loop with human-on-the-loop.

Why AI Agents Are Believed to Be the Next Big Thing?

AI agents represent a generational technology shift comparable to the internet, with industry surveys showing near-universal adoption efforts and forecasts predicting automation of up to 70% of office work within a decade.

The momentum behind AI agents is driven by convergence of capability and economic incentive. Every major tech company has flagship agent projects. An IBM/Morning Consult survey of 1,000 enterprise AI developers found 99% were actively exploring or building AI agents. Industry forecasts predict agents could automate up to 70% of office work within ten years. This creates a dual workforce impact: employees gain more time for high-value work (improving product quality), while some businesses will opt to operate with fewer, highly-skilled people who manage agentic workflows. The emerging role of 'manager of AI agents' (overseeing agent workflows and ensuring smooth operations) is described as the job of the future. Current agents are primitive compared to what is coming, much like early mobile apps were to modern ones. The strategic imperative is to learn now, while the technology is still in its infancy.

  • 99% of surveyed enterprise AI developers are actively exploring or building AI agents (IBM/Morning Consult, n=1000).
  • Industry forecasts predict AI agents could automate up to 70% of office work within the next decade.
  • The 'manager of AI agents' is emerging as a new career role: a person who orchestrates agent workflows and ensures operational quality.
  • Today's agents are analogous to early mobile apps; rapid iteration will produce dramatically more capable versions.
  • The internet analogy applies: once AI moves past infancy, it will reshape communication, work, shopping, learning, and entertainment.
📌
Early Mobile Apps vs Now

Today's agents will look primitive compared to next-generation versions, just as early apps evolved rapidly.

📌
Workforce Bifurcation

Some firms empower employees with agents; others replace headcount with fewer agent-managing specialists.

Takeaways

  • Learn agent development now; early expertise in a generational shift compounds over time.
  • The strategic question is not whether agents will transform work, but how fast and how to position for it.
Code Lab 
from openai import OpenAI  # OpenAI SDK import
import os
import docx
import pdfplumber
import subprocess

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.tools import tool  # LangChain framework imports
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode  # LangGraph framework imports
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4.1")  # Initialize chat model
@tool  # Create a LangChain tool
def job_posting_tool(job_link: str) -> str:
    """Extracts structured information from a job posting at the provided URL.

    Args:
        job_link (str): The URL of the job posting.

    Returns:
        str: A structured summary of the job posting's key details.
    """
    completion = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-search-preview",
        web_search_options={"search_context_size": "medium"},
        messages=[
            {
            "role": "user",
            "content": """
            You are a helpful tool that visits the following job posting and carefully read its contents.  
            Summarize the key details in a clear and concise format, including:
            Visit the provided job posting link, read it thoroughly, and extract and summarize all key information. Include:
            - Job title
            - Company name
            - Location
            - Employment type (full-time, part-time, contract, etc.)
            - Salary or compensation (if available)
            - Required qualifications/skills
            - Primary responsibilities
            - Benefits offered
            - Application instructions
            - Posting date (if available)

            Format
            - Respond with a clear, structured bullet-point list.
            - Use exact factual information from the posting, no rewording beyond making it concise.
            - If the posting is missing, inaccessible, or contains no job details, respond with:
            "Job posting unavailable or contains no job details."

            Do's 
            - Ensure all extracted details are accurate and directly taken from the posting.
            - Keep descriptions short, professional, and easy to scan.
            - Use consistent formatting for all fields (e.g., “Job Title: …”).  
            Don'ts
            - Do not include filler language, speculation, or personal opinions.
            - Do not rewrite or interpret details—only report factual information from the posting.
            """
        },
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": f"Visit this job posting and extract details:\n{job_link}"
        }
    ],
    )
    return completion.choices[0].message.content
@tool  # Create a LangChain tool
def extract_cv_text(file_path: str) -> str:
    """Extracts the text content from a CV file in PDF, DOCX, or DOC format. The CV should be inside the same folder that this notebook is in.

    Args:
        file_path (str): The local file path to the CV document. 

    Returns:
        str: The extracted plain text from the CV, or an error message if the format is unsupported or cannot be read.
    """
    
    ext = os.path.splitext(file_path)[-1].lower()
    
    if ".docx" in ext:
        try:
            doc = docx.Document(file_path)
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .docx file: {e}"
        
    elif ".pdf" in ext:
        try:
            text = []
            with pdfplumber.open(file_path) as pdf:
                for page in pdf.pages:
                    page_text = page.extract_text()
                    if page_text:
                        text.append(page_text)
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .pdf file: {e}"
    
    elif ".doc" in ext:
        try:
            temp_docx = file_path + ".temp.docx"
            subprocess.run(['soffice', '--headless', '--convert-to', 'docx', '--outdir', os.path.dirname(file_path), file_path], check=True)
            
            doc = docx.Document(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            
            os.remove(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading .doc file: {e}"
    
    else:
        return "Unsupported file format. Please use .pdf, .docx, or .doc."
tools = [job_posting_tool, extract_cv_text]
tool_node = ToolNode(tools=tools)  # Pre-built tool executor node
llm_with_tools = llm.bind_tools(tools)
from langgraph.graph import MessagesState  # LangGraph framework imports
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, SystemMessage  # LangChain framework imports

sys_msg = SystemMessage(content="""  # System prompt message
You are an expert career assistant that helps the user with questions related to jobs, careers, and applications.

Your key capabilities:
- You have access to the user's CV and can read its contents using the `extract_cv_text` tool.
- You can look up and extract details from job postings using the `job_posting_tool`.
- You can compare the user's CV against one or more job postings to determine suitability and provide tailored advice.
- You can suggest improvements to the CV for better alignment with target roles.

When answering:
1. First, think step-by-step about the user's request.
2. If the task requires reading the CV, call the CV extraction tool before answering.
3. If the task involves evaluating job postings, call the job posting tool to gather accurate information before answering.
4. Compare and reason about the information before providing your final response.

Response format:
- Be clear, concise, and structured with bullet points or numbered lists.
- Use section headers when possible (e.g., "Strengths", "Weaknesses", "Recommendations").
- Support your statements with evidence from the CV or job postings.
- Avoid vague language—be specific and factual.

Constraints:
- Do not invent or guess details about the user's experience or job postings.
- Only use information available in the CV, job postings, or provided context.
- Keep your tone professional, friendly, and supportive.


""")
def assistant(state: MessagesState):  # Pre-built messages state
   return {"messages": [llm_with_tools.invoke([sys_msg] + state["messages"])]}  # Execute the graph
from langgraph.graph import START, StateGraph  # LangGraph framework imports
from langgraph.prebuilt import tools_condition  # LangGraph framework imports
from IPython.display import Image, display

builder = StateGraph(MessagesState)  # Create state graph

builder.add_node("assistant", assistant)  # Register node in graph
builder.add_node("tools", ToolNode(tools))  # Register node in graph

builder.add_edge(START, "assistant")  # Connect nodes
builder.add_conditional_edges("assistant", tools_condition)  # Add conditional routing

builder.add_edge("tools", "assistant")  # Connect nodes
react_graph = builder.compile()  # Compile the graph
display(Image(react_graph.get_graph(xray=True).draw_mermaid_png()))
messages = [HumanMessage(content="""  # User message type
        Can you take a look at my CV ath the location 'cv-template2.pdf'  and these 3 job applications and tell me whichone is the most suitable for my expiriance: 
        
        'https://www.indeed.com/viewjob?jk=247e94f9a28c544f&tk=1isdf5na1h72t810&from=serp&vjs=3',
        'https://www.indeed.com/viewjob?jk=744686732444f370&tk=1isns1midj72r8b4&from=serp&vjs=3',
        'https://www.indeed.com/viewjob?jk=01e2f371f220e42a&tk=1isns1midj72r8b4&from=serp&vjs=3'
        
        """)]
result = react_graph.invoke({"messages": messages})  # Execute the graph
for m in result['messages']:
    m.pretty_print()

from langgraph.prebuilt import tools_condition  # LangGraph framework imports
from IPython.display import Image, display

config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}}

from openai import OpenAI  # OpenAI SDK import
import os
import docx
import pdfplumber
import subprocess

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.tools import tool  # LangChain framework imports
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode  # LangGraph framework imports

from langsmith import traceable
os.environ["LANGSMITH_TRACING"] = "true"
os.environ["LANGSMITH_API_KEY"] = "YOUR_LANGSMITH_API_KEY"
os.environ["LANGSMITH_PROJECT"] = "Agents Course"
os.environ["LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT"] = "https://api.smith.langchain.com"
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4.1")  # Initialize chat model
@tool  # Create a LangChain tool
def job_posting_tool(job_link: str) -> str:
    """Extracts structured information from a job posting at the provided URL.

    Args:
        job_link (str): The URL of the job posting.

    Returns:
        str: A structured summary of the job posting's key details.
    """
    completion = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-search-preview",
        web_search_options={"search_context_size": "medium"},
        messages=[
            {
            "role": "user",
            "content": """
            You are a helpful tool that visits the following job posting and carefully read its contents.  
            Summarize the key details in a clear and concise format, including:
            Visit the provided job posting link, read it thoroughly, and extract and summarize all key information. Include:
            - Job title
            - Company name
            - Location
            - Employment type (full-time, part-time, contract, etc.)
            - Salary or compensation (if available)
            - Required qualifications/skills
            - Primary responsibilities
            - Benefits offered
            - Application instructions
            - Posting date (if available)

            Format
            - Respond with a clear, structured bullet-point list.
            - Use exact factual information from the posting, no rewording beyond making it concise.
            - If the posting is missing, inaccessible, or contains no job details, respond with:
            "Job posting unavailable or contains no job details."

            Do's 
            - Ensure all extracted details are accurate and directly taken from the posting.
            - Keep descriptions short, professional, and easy to scan.
            - Use consistent formatting for all fields (e.g., “Job Title: …”).  
            Don'ts
            - Do not include filler language, speculation, or personal opinions.
            - Do not rewrite or interpret details—only report factual information from the posting.
            """
        },
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": f"Visit this job posting and extract details:\n{job_link}"
        }
    ],
    )
    return completion.choices[0].message.content
@tool  # Create a LangChain tool
def extract_cv_text(file_path: str) -> str:
    """Extracts the text content from a CV file in PDF, DOCX, or DOC format. The CV should be inside the same folder that this notebook is in.

    Args:
        file_path (str): The local file path to the CV document. 

    Returns:
        str: The extracted plain text from the CV, or an error message if the format is unsupported or cannot be read.
    """
    
    ext = os.path.splitext(file_path)[-1].lower()
    
    if ".docx" in ext:
        try:
            doc = docx.Document(file_path)
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .docx file: {e}"
        
    elif ".pdf" in ext:
        try:
            text = []
            with pdfplumber.open(file_path) as pdf:
                for page in pdf.pages:
                    page_text = page.extract_text()
                    if page_text:
                        text.append(page_text)
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .pdf file: {e}"
    
    elif ".doc" in ext:
        try:
            temp_docx = file_path + ".temp.docx"
            subprocess.run(['soffice', '--headless', '--convert-to', 'docx', '--outdir', os.path.dirname(file_path), file_path], check=True)
            
            doc = docx.Document(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            
            os.remove(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading .doc file: {e}"
    
    else:
        return "Unsupported file format. Please use .pdf, .docx, or .doc."
tools = [job_posting_tool, extract_cv_text]
tool_node = ToolNode(tools=tools)  # Pre-built tool executor node
llm_with_tools = llm.bind_tools(tools)
from langgraph.graph import MessagesState  # LangGraph framework imports
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, SystemMessage  # LangChain framework imports

sys_msg = SystemMessage(content="""  # System prompt message
You are an expert career assistant that helps the user with questions related to jobs, careers, and applications.

Your key capabilities:
- You have access to the user's CV and can read its contents using the `extract_cv_text` tool.
- You can look up and extract details from job postings using the `job_posting_tool`.
- You can compare the user's CV against one or more job postings to determine suitability and provide tailored advice.
- You can suggest improvements to the CV for better alignment with target roles.

When answering:
1. First, think step-by-step about the user's request.
2. If the task requires reading the CV, call the CV extraction tool before answering.
3. If the task involves evaluating job postings, call the job posting tool to gather accurate information before answering.
4. Compare and reason about the information before providing your final response.

Response format:
- Be clear, concise, and structured with bullet points or numbered lists.
- Use section headers when possible (e.g., "Strengths", "Weaknesses", "Recommendations").
- Support your statements with evidence from the CV or job postings.
- Avoid vague language—be specific and factual.

Constraints:
- Do not invent or guess details about the user's experience or job postings.
- Only use information available in the CV, job postings, or provided context.
- Keep your tone professional, friendly, and supportive.


""")
@traceable(name="Job Posting Tool")
def assistant(state: MessagesState):  # Pre-built messages state
   return {"messages": [llm_with_tools.invoke([sys_msg] + state["messages"])]}  # Execute the graph
from langgraph.graph import START, StateGraph  # LangGraph framework imports
from langgraph.prebuilt import tools_condition  # LangGraph framework imports
from IPython.display import Image, display

builder = StateGraph(MessagesState)  # Create state graph

builder.add_node("assistant", assistant)  # Register node in graph
builder.add_node("tools", ToolNode(tools))  # Register node in graph

builder.add_edge(START, "assistant")  # Connect nodes
builder.add_conditional_edges("assistant", tools_condition)  # Add conditional routing

builder.add_edge("tools", "assistant")  # Connect nodes
react_graph = builder.compile()  # Compile the graph
display(Image(react_graph.get_graph(xray=True).draw_mermaid_png()))
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver  # LangGraph framework imports
memory = MemorySaver()  # In-memory persistence
react_graph_memory = builder.compile(checkpointer=memory)  # Compile the graph
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}}
messages = [HumanMessage(content="""  # User message type
        Can you take a look at my CV ath the location 'cv-template2.pdf'  and these 3 job applications and tell me whichone is the most suitable for my expiriance: 
        
        'https://www.indeed.com/viewjob?jk=247e94f9a28c544f&tk=1isdf5na1h72t810&from=serp&vjs=3',
        'https://www.indeed.com/viewjob?jk=744686732444f370&tk=1isns1midj72r8b4&from=serp&vjs=3',
        'https://www.indeed.com/viewjob?jk=01e2f371f220e42a&tk=1isns1midj72r8b4&from=serp&vjs=3'
        
        """)]
result = react_graph_memory.invoke({"messages": messages}, config)  # Execute the graph
for m in result['messages']:
    m.pretty_print()
messages = [HumanMessage(content="""  # User message type
        I’ve attached my CV (cv-template2.pdf). I’m targeting entry-level data-analysis roles. Please review the document and provide:
1. A bullet-point list of my key strengths and accomplishments that align with data-analysis positions.
2. A bullet-point list of weaknesses or areas for improvement, grouped by content, formatting, and wording.
3. Three actionable suggestions to make the CV more compelling for hiring managers and ATS systems.
Please keep the total response under 300 words.
        
        """)]
result = react_graph_memory.invoke({"messages": messages},config)  # Execute the graph

for m in result['messages']:
    m.pretty_print()

from openai import OpenAI  # OpenAI SDK import
import os
import docx
import pdfplumber
import subprocess

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.tools import tool  # LangChain framework imports
from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode  # LangGraph framework imports

from langsmith import traceable

#ReWOO imports
from typing import List   # Type hints
from typing_extensions import TypedDict, Dict, Any  # Type hints
import re
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate  # LangChain framework imports
os.environ["LANGSMITH_TRACING"] = "true"
os.environ["LANGSMITH_API_KEY"] = "YOUR_LANGSMITH_API_KEY"
os.environ["LANGSMITH_PROJECT"] = "Agents Course"
os.environ["LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT"] = "https://api.smith.langchain.com"
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4.1")  # Initialize chat model
class ReWOO(TypedDict):
    task:str
    plan_string: str
    steps: List
    results: dict
    result: str
planner_prompt = """For the following task, make plans that can solve the problem step by step. For each plan, indicate \
which external tool together with tool input to retrieve evidence. You can store the evidence into a \
variable #E that can be called by later tools. (Plan, #E1, Plan, #E2, Plan, ...) Use the following format:
Plan: Explain the plan.
#E1 = TOOL[tool-input] 

Plan: Explain the plan for the next step
#E2 = TOOL[tool-input]


Allowed TOOLs:  
1) LLM[input]    – Let the language model reason  
2) CV[input]     – The tool extract_cv_text, input = local path  
3) JobPost[input]– The tool job_posting_tool, input = a job-url  

Do not invent any other tool names.  
Begin!

Task: {task}
"""
task = """
look into my cv called cv-template2.pdf can you evaluate it 
and how would it perform on this posting: https://www.indeed.com/viewjob?jk=247e94f9a28c544f&tk=1isdf5na1h72t810&from=serp&vjs=3
"""

result = llm.invoke(planner_prompt.format(task=task))  # Execute the graph

print(result.content)
plan_regex = r"Plan:\s*(.+?)\s*(#E\d+)\s*=\s*(\w+)\[(.+?)\]"
@traceable(name="Planner Node")
def planner_node(state: ReWOO):
    task = state["task"]
    raw_plan = llm.invoke(planner_prompt.format(task=task)).content  # Execute the graph
    steps = re.findall(plan_regex, raw_plan, flags=re.S)
    return {"plan_string": raw_plan, "steps": steps}
@tool  # Create a LangChain tool
def job_posting_tool(job_link: str) -> str:
    """Extracts structured information from a job posting at the provided URL.

    Args:
        job_link (str): The URL of the job posting.

    Returns:
        str: A structured summary of the job posting's key details.
    """
    completion = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-search-preview",
        web_search_options={"search_context_size": "medium"},
        messages=[
            {
            "role": "user",
            "content": """
            You are a helpful tool that visits the following job posting and carefully read its contents.  
            Summarize the key details in a clear and concise format, including:
            Visit the provided job posting link, read it thoroughly, and extract and summarize all key information. Include:
            - Job title
            - Company name
            - Location
            - Employment type (full-time, part-time, contract, etc.)
            - Salary or compensation (if available)
            - Required qualifications/skills
            - Primary responsibilities
            - Benefits offered
            - Application instructions
            - Posting date (if available)

            Format
            - Respond with a clear, structured bullet-point list.
            - Use exact factual information from the posting, no rewording beyond making it concise.
            - If the posting is missing, inaccessible, or contains no job details, respond with:
            "Job posting unavailable or contains no job details."

            Do's 
            - Ensure all extracted details are accurate and directly taken from the posting.
            - Keep descriptions short, professional, and easy to scan.
            - Use consistent formatting for all fields (e.g., “Job Title: …”).  
            Don'ts
            - Do not include filler language, speculation, or personal opinions.
            - Do not rewrite or interpret details—only report factual information from the posting.
            """
        },
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": f"Visit this job posting and extract details:\n{job_link}"
        }
    ],
    )
    return completion.choices[0].message.content
@tool  # Create a LangChain tool
def extract_cv_text(file_path: str) -> str:
    """Extracts the text content from a CV file in PDF, DOCX, or DOC format. The CV should be inside the same folder that this notebook is in.

    Args:
        file_path (str): The local file path to the CV document. 

    Returns:
        str: The extracted plain text from the CV, or an error message if the format is unsupported or cannot be read.
    """
    
    ext = os.path.splitext(file_path)[-1].lower()
    
    if ".docx" in ext:
        try:
            doc = docx.Document(file_path)
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .docx file: {e}"
        
    elif ".pdf" in ext:
        try:
            text = []
            with pdfplumber.open(file_path) as pdf:
                for page in pdf.pages:
                    page_text = page.extract_text()
                    if page_text:
                        text.append(page_text)
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .pdf file: {e}"
    
    elif ".doc" in ext:
        try:
            temp_docx = file_path + ".temp.docx"
            subprocess.run(['soffice', '--headless', '--convert-to', 'docx', '--outdir', os.path.dirname(file_path), file_path], check=True)
            
            doc = docx.Document(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            
            os.remove(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading .doc file: {e}"
    
    else:
        return "Unsupported file format. Please use .pdf, .docx, or .doc."
tools = [job_posting_tool, extract_cv_text]
tool_node = ToolNode(tools=tools)  # Pre-built tool executor node
llm_with_tools = llm.bind_tools(tools)

@traceable(name="Job Posting Tool")

   return {"messages": [llm_with_tools.invoke([sys_msg] + state["messages"])]}  # Execute the graph

def _current_index(state: ReWOO):
    done = len(state.get("results", {}))
    total = len(state["steps"])
    return None if done >= total else done
@traceable(name="Executor Node")
def executor_node(state: ReWOO):
    idx = _current_index(state)
    if idx is None:
        return {}
    plan_text, step_name, tool_name, tool_input = state["steps"][idx]
    for k, v in state.get("results", {}).items():
           if tool_name == "LLM" and k in tool_input:
               tool_input = tool_input.replace(k, v)

    if tool_name == "LLM":
        out = llm.invoke(tool_input).content  # Execute the graph
    elif tool_name == "CV":
        out = extract_cv_text.invoke(tool_input)  # Execute the graph
    elif tool_name == "JobPost":
        out = job_posting_tool.invoke(tool_input)  # Execute the graph
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown tool {tool_name}")

    results = dict(state.get("results", {}))
    results[step_name] = str(out)
    return {"results": results}

@tool  # Create a LangChain tool
def job_posting_tool(job_link: str) -> str:
    """Extracts structured information from a job posting at the provided URL.

    Args:
        job_link (str): The URL of the job posting.

    Returns:
        str: A structured summary of the job posting's key details.
    """
    completion = client.chat.completions.create(

        web_search_options={"search_context_size": "medium"},
        messages=[
            {
            "role": "user",

            Summarize the key details in a clear and concise format, including:
            Visit the provided job posting link, read it thoroughly, and extract and summarize all key information. Include:
            - Job title
            - Company name
            - Location
            - Employment type (full-time, part-time, contract, etc.)
            - Salary or compensation (if available)
            - Required qualifications/skills
            - Primary responsibilities
            - Benefits offered
            - Application instructions
            - Posting date (if available)

            Format
            - Respond with a clear, structured bullet-point list.
            - Use exact factual information from the posting, no rewording beyond making it concise.
            - If the posting is missing, inaccessible, or contains no job details, respond with:
            "Job posting unavailable or contains no job details."

            Do's 
            - Ensure all extracted details are accurate and directly taken from the posting.
            - Keep descriptions short, professional, and easy to scan.
            - Use consistent formatting for all fields (e.g., “Job Title: …”).  
            Don'ts
            - Do not include filler language, speculation, or personal opinions.
            - Do not rewrite or interpret details—only report factual information from the posting.
            """
        },
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": f"Visit this job posting and extract details:\n{job_link}"
        }
    ],
    )
    return completion.choices[0].message.content
@tool  # Create a LangChain tool
def extract_cv_text(file_path: str) -> str:
    """Extracts the text content from a CV file in PDF, DOCX, or DOC format. The CV should be inside the same folder that this notebook is in.

    Args:
        file_path (str): The local file path to the CV document. 

    Returns:
        str: The extracted plain text from the CV, or an error message if the format is unsupported or cannot be read.
    """
    
    ext = os.path.splitext(file_path)[-1].lower()
    
    if ".docx" in ext:
        try:
            doc = docx.Document(file_path)
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .docx file: {e}"
        
    elif ".pdf" in ext:
        try:
            text = []
            with pdfplumber.open(file_path) as pdf:
                for page in pdf.pages:
                    page_text = page.extract_text()
                    if page_text:
                        text.append(page_text)
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .pdf file: {e}"
    
    elif ".doc" in ext:
        try:
            temp_docx = file_path + ".temp.docx"
            subprocess.run(['soffice', '--headless', '--convert-to', 'docx', '--outdir', os.path.dirname(file_path), file_path], check=True)
            
            doc = docx.Document(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            
            os.remove(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading .doc file: {e}"
    
    else:
        return "Unsupported file format. Please use .pdf, .docx, or .doc."

def _current_index(state: ReWOO):

    total = len(state["steps"])
    return None if done >= total else done
@traceable(name="Executor Node")
def executor_node(state: ReWOO):
    idx = _current_index(state)
    if idx is None:
        return {}
    plan_text, step_name, tool_name, tool_input = state["steps"][idx]
    for k, v in state.get("results", {}).items():
           if tool_name == "LLM" and k in tool_input:
               tool_input = tool_input.replace(k, v)

        out = llm.invoke(tool_input).content  # Execute the graph
    elif tool_name == "CV":
        out = extract_cv_text.invoke(tool_input)  # Execute the graph
    elif tool_name == "JobPost":

    else:

    results = dict(state.get("results", {}))
    results[step_name] = str(out)
    return {"results": results}

Solve the following task or problem. To solve the problem, we have made step-by-step Plan and

@traceable(name="Solver Node")
def solver_node(state: ReWOO):

    return {"result": answer}

import os, operator
from typing import List, Annotated, Dict  # Type hints
from typing_extensions import TypedDict  # Type hints

from openai import OpenAI  # OpenAI SDK import
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.messages import (  # LangChain framework imports
    SystemMessage,  # System prompt message
    HumanMessage,  # User message type
    AIMessage,
    BaseMessage,
)
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages  # LangGraph framework imports
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END  # LangGraph framework imports
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver  # LangGraph framework imports
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

from IPython.display import Image, display, Markdown
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o", temperature=0)  # Initialize chat model
class State(TypedDict):  # Define the graph state schema
    idea: str
    messages: Annotated[List[BaseMessage], add_messages]  # Message list reducer
    advisor_reports: Annotated[Dict[str, str], operator.or_]
    final_report: str
base_system_msg = SystemMessage(  # System prompt message
    content=(
        """
        You are a helpful tool
        Your job: decide whether you have enough information about the start-up idea.
        If not, ask ONE precise follow-up question.
        If yes, say: DONE
        """

    )
)
def decide_node(state: State):
    conversation = [base_system_msg] + state["messages"]
    ai_reply: AIMessage = llm(conversation)
    return {"messages": [ai_reply]}
def route(state: State):
    last_ai_msg: AIMessage = state["messages"][-1]
    if last_ai_msg.content.strip().upper().startswith("DONE"):
        return "fanout"
    return "ask_user_node"
def ask_user_node(state: State):
    question = state["messages"][-1].content
    print(f"\nAssistant: {question}\n")
    human = input("You: ")
    new_messages = state["messages"] + [HumanMessage(content=human)]  # User message type
    
    return {"messages": new_messages,
            "human_advisor_feedback": human,}

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END  # LangGraph framework imports
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver  # LangGraph framework imports
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

from IPython.display import Image, display, Markdown
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o", temperature=0)  # Initialize chat model
class State(TypedDict):  # Define the graph state schema
    idea: str
    messages: Annotated[List[BaseMessage], add_messages]  # Message list reducer
    advisor_reports: Annotated[Dict[str, str], operator.or_]
    final_report: str
base_system_msg = SystemMessage(  # System prompt message
    content=(
        """
        You are a helpful tool
        Your job: decide whether you have enough information about the start-up idea.
        If not, ask ONE precise follow-up question.
        If yes, say: DONE
        """

    )
)
def decide_node(state: State):
    conversation = [base_system_msg] + state["messages"]
    ai_reply: AIMessage = llm(conversation)
    return {"messages": [ai_reply]}
def route(state: State):
    last_ai_msg: AIMessage = state["messages"][-1]
    if last_ai_msg.content.strip().upper().startswith("DONE"):
        return "fanout"
    return "ask_user_node"
def ask_user_node(state: State):
    question = state["messages"][-1].content
    print(f"\nAssistant: {question}\n")
    human = input("You: ")
    new_messages = state["messages"] + [HumanMessage(content=human)]  # User message type
    
    return {"messages": new_messages,
            "human_advisor_feedback": human,}
def market_analyst_advisor(state: State):
    prompt = f"""
    You are a helpfull senior MARKET ANALYST that gets an idea as an input. You need to Evaluate the market potential, competition, target demographics, and trends:
    Conduct market sizing and competitor research
    Identify target customers and segments
    Assess timing, trends, and macroeconomic influences
    Idea:
    {state['messages']}
    """
    report = llm.invoke([SystemMessage(content=prompt)])  # Execute the graph
    return {"advisor_reports": {"Market Analyst": report.content}}
def legal_advisor(state: State):
    prompt = f"""
    You are a helpfull Legal Advisor that gets an idea as an input. You need to:
    Identify IP, licensing, and trademark needs
    Spot compliance issues (e.g., GDPR, financial regulations)
    Evaluate contract and partnership considerations
    Idea:
    {state['messages']}
    """
    report = llm.invoke([SystemMessage(content=prompt)])  # Execute the graph
    return {"advisor_reports": {"Legal Advisor": report.content}}
def technical_advisor(state: State):
    prompt = f"""
    You are a helpfull  Technical/Product Feasibility Expert that gets an idea as an input. You need to:
    Estimate development complexity and time
    Recommend tech stacks or platforms
    Evaluate risk in terms of infrastructure, scalability, and cost
    Idea:
    {state['messages']}
    """
    report = llm.invoke([SystemMessage(content=prompt)])  # Execute the graph
    return {"advisor_reports": {"Technical Advisor": report.content}}
def strategist_advisor(state: State):
    prompt = f"""
    You are a helpfull Strategist Advisor Expert that gets an idea as an input. You need to:
    Define launch milestones
    Select distribution channels and positioning strategies
    Craft early traction tactics (e.g., community, influencers, PR)
    Idea:
    {state['messages']}
    """
    report = llm.invoke([SystemMessage(content=prompt)])  # Execute the graph
    return {"advisor_reports": {"Strategist Advisor": report.content}}

builder.add_edge("technical_advisor", "collect_and_report")  # Connect nodes
builder.add_edge("strategist_advisor", "collect_and_report")  # Connect nodes

S02: Essential ingredients for building AI agents

Intro

AI agents are built from five core components: environment, sensors, model, decision logic, actuators, and feedback mechanisms.

This section introduces the fundamental building blocks of AI agent systems. Each agent requires an environment to operate in, sensors to perceive that environment, a model to interpret perceptions, decision-making logic to select actions, actuators to execute those actions, and feedback mechanisms to evaluate success. Understanding these components provides the foundation for designing any AI agent architecture.

  • Environment defines the space where the agent operates
  • Sensors collect data from the environment
  • The model interprets sensory input and builds understanding
  • Decision logic determines which action to take
  • Actuators execute chosen actions; feedback evaluates outcomes
🌍
Environment
The external world the agent interacts with
📡
Sensors
Data collection from surroundings
🧠
Model
Interprets perceptions into understanding
⚡
Decision Logic
Selects appropriate actions
🔧
Actuators
Executes actions on environment
🔄
Feedback
Evaluates success of actions

Takeaways

  • Every AI agent, regardless of complexity, relies on these five components
  • The feedback loop is what enables agents to improve over time
  • Understanding components helps you design agents for specific use cases

Environment – The External World That the Agent Perceives and Interacts With

The environment is everything external that the agent perceives and acts upon; its characteristics determine the agent design complexity.

An AI agent's environment encompasses all external factors it must perceive and interact with. A self-driving car's environment includes roads, vehicles, weather, pedestrians, and signs. A chatbot's environment is the text conversation. The nature and complexity of the environment directly dictates what sensors, models, and decision logic the agent requires. Dynamic, unpredictable environments demand more sophisticated agent architectures than static, well-defined ones.

  • Environment = all external factors the agent must handle
  • Self-driving car environment: roads, traffic, weather, pedestrians
  • Chatbot environment: text-based conversation interface
  • Environment complexity determines required agent sophistication
  • Agents must adapt to changing environmental conditions in real time
PropertySimple EnvironmentComplex Environment
PredictabilityHigh (static rules)Low (dynamic changes)
Agent Type NeededSimple reflexGoal-based or learning
ExampleThermostat roomAutonomous vehicle road

Takeaways

  • Always define the environment first when designing an agent
  • Match agent complexity to environment complexity
  • Dynamic environments require agents with memory and adaptation

Sensors – How the Agent Collects Data About its Surroundings

Sensors are the agent's input mechanism for gathering environmental data; they determine what the agent can perceive and therefore what it can act on.

Just as humans use senses to perceive the world, AI agents use sensors to collect input from their environment. Sensors can be physical (cameras, microphones, temperature readers) or digital (API calls, database queries, text input). The quality and type of sensory input fundamentally constrains what an agent can know and do. An agent cannot act on information it cannot perceive, making sensor design a critical architectural decision.

  • Sensors are the agent's means of receiving environmental input
  • Physical sensors: cameras, LIDAR, microphones, thermometers
  • Digital sensors: API endpoints, user text input, database queries
  • Sensor limitations directly constrain agent capabilities
  • Multiple sensor types enable richer environmental understanding
📷
Physical Sensors
Cameras, LIDAR, microphones for real-world data
💻
Digital Sensors
APIs, webhooks, database queries for software agents
👁️
Perception Layer
Converts raw sensor data into structured information

Takeaways

  • Design sensors to capture all information needed for decision-making
  • Sensor quality directly impacts agent performance
  • Consider both physical and digital sensor modalities

Model – the Agent’s Way of Making Sense of Information

Every AI agent is built from five core components: environment, sensors, model, decision-making logic, and actuators/actions, connected by feedback mechanisms that enable continuous improvement.

Before constructing any AI agent, one must understand its fundamental building blocks. The environment defines where the agent operates. Sensors allow it to perceive that environment. The model interprets sensor data into understanding. Decision-making logic determines what action to take. Actuators execute those actions. Finally, feedback mechanisms close the loop by allowing the agent to evaluate whether it achieved its intended goals. These components are universal across all agent types, from simple thermostats to autonomous vehicles. The sophistication of each component determines the agent's overall capability level.

  • Five core components: environment, sensors, model, decision-making logic, actuators/actions.
  • Feedback mechanisms are the sixth element that closes the perceive-act loop and enables learning.
  • These building blocks are universal; every agent type uses them at varying levels of sophistication.
  • Understanding components individually is prerequisite to understanding how agent types differ.
📌
Component Stack

Environment feeds sensors, which feed model, which feeds decision logic, which drives actions, which change environment.

💡
Agent Components as a Thermostat (Scaled Up)

A thermostat is the simplest complete agent: (1) Environment = the room temperature, (2) Sensor = the thermometer reading, (3) Model = comparing current temp to target, (4) Decision logic = 'if below target, heat; if above, cool', (5) Actuator = turning heater/AC on, (6) Feedback = re-reading temperature after action. Every AI agent uses these same six elements, just at vastly different sophistication levels.

Takeaways

  • Master each component individually before trying to build a complete agent system.
  • The feedback loop is what separates a static automation from an adaptive agent.

Decision-making Logic – Rules and Objectives that Guide the Agent’s Actions

The environment is everything external to the agent; it defines the problem space, constraints, and possibilities, and must be characterized first because agent design must align with its operational context.

The environment is everything external to the agent. It defines the problem space, constraints, and possibilities.

  • The environment dictates sensors needed and actions possible.
  • Can be physical (roads, weather) or digital (websites, databases).
  • Agent design MUST align with its operational environment.
  • Agents must learn from environments like humans do.
📌
Self-driving Car

Roads, vehicles, pedestrians, weather: complex, dynamic scenarios.

📌
PE: Test Floor

Tester hardware, handlers, temperature chambers, production schedules.

Takeaways

  • Define the environment FIRST before designing the agent.
  • Misalignment between agent and environment guarantees failure.

Actions – How the Agent Shapes the Environment

Sensors are the mechanisms that allow agents to receive input from their surroundings; without them, the agent is blind regardless of how sophisticated its reasoning is.

Mechanisms that allow agents to receive input from surroundings. Sensor choice must match the environment, and sensor fusion (combining multiple sources) gives richer understanding than any single input.

  • No sensors equals a blind agent, regardless of model capability.
  • Sensor fusion (combining multiple sources) produces richer understanding than any single input.
  • Sensor choice must match the environment the agent operates in.
  • Types span physical (cameras, lidar, GPS, IoT), digital (web scrapers, APIs, databases), and hybrid.
📌
Self-driving Car

Cameras + lidar + GPS + traffic APIs fused together.

📌
PE: Test Data

STDF datalogs, SPC systems, equipment APIs, yield databases.

Quick Check

1. Which of the following best describes the role of sensors in an AI agent?

They execute the agent's decisions on the environment
They allow the agent to gather input data from its environment
They store the agent's memory of past interactions
They define the rules the agent must follow

Takeaways

  • An agent without sensors is blind; sensor selection is a design-critical decision.
  • Sensor fusion (multiple sources) always beats relying on a single input.

The Updated Environment

The model is the agent's brain, processing raw sensor data into meaningful understanding across a capability spectrum from simple ML (fast, interpretable) to LLMs (human-like reasoning, multi-step planning).

The agent's brain. Processes sensor data into meaningful understanding. The model determines WHAT to do; tools handle HOW to do it. LLMs serve as the central reasoning engine in modern agentic systems.

  • Model capability spectrum: simple ML (fast, interpretable) to neural networks (powerful, less interpretable) to LLMs (human-like reasoning).
  • More capable models enable more capable agents but at higher cost.
  • Multimodal models unify perception across different data types (text, image, audio).
  • Understanding without action is useless; the model must connect to decision-making and execution.
📌
Capability Spectrum

Decision trees (fast) to neural nets (powerful) to LLMs (most capable, most expensive).

Takeaways

  • Model selection is a trade-off between capability, interpretability, and cost.
  • The model is WHAT to do; tools are HOW to do it.

S03: from simple to complex structures

Intro

AI agent architectures range from simple reflex to learning agents, each adding complexity and capability.

Agent architectures are classified by complexity and functionality. Starting with simple reflex agents that react to immediate input, the spectrum extends through model-based agents (with memory), goal-based agents (with objectives), utility-based agents (with optimization criteria), and learning agents (with self-improvement). Selecting the right architecture depends on the task requirements, environmental complexity, and acceptable cost.

  • Agent types form a spectrum from simple to sophisticated
  • Simple reflex agents react without memory
  • Model-based agents maintain internal state
  • Goal-based and utility-based agents optimize outcomes
  • Learning agents improve from experience over time
1

Simple Reflex

Direct stimulus-response, no memory

2

Model-based Reflex

Internal state representation of the world

3

Goal-based

Plans actions to achieve specific objectives

4

Utility-based

Optimizes across multiple factors simultaneously

5

Learning

Improves performance through experience

Takeaways

  • Start with the simplest agent type that solves your problem
  • More sophisticated agents cost more to build and maintain
  • Understanding the spectrum helps match architecture to requirements

Key Characteristics of AI Agents

Sophisticated AI agents are defined by five key characteristics: profile/persona, memory, reasoning, actions, and learning capabilities.

Beyond basic perception and action, advanced agents exhibit five defining characteristics. Profile and persona define how the agent presents itself and what role it plays. Memory allows persistence of context across interactions. Reasoning enables complex problem-solving and planning. Actions are the agent's ability to affect its environment. Learning capabilities enable continuous improvement. Not all agents require all five; having four or five indicates a sophisticated system.

  • Profile/Persona: defines the agent's role and communication style
  • Memory: maintains context across interactions and sessions
  • Reasoning: enables planning, problem decomposition, and logic
  • Actions: the agent's ability to execute tasks and affect the environment
  • Learning: continuous improvement from feedback and experience
🎭
Profile & Persona
Role definition and communication style
🧠
Memory
Context persistence across interactions
💡
Reasoning
Planning and problem decomposition
⚡
Actions
Task execution and environment modification
📈
Learning
Continuous improvement from feedback

Takeaways

  • Use these five characteristics as a checklist when evaluating agent frameworks
  • Not every use case requires all five; match to requirements
  • Memory and reasoning are what differentiate agents from simple chatbots

Simple Reflex Agent

Simple reflex agents use direct condition-action rules with no memory or model, making them fast but limited to fully observable environments.

The simple reflex agent is the most basic architecture. It maps current percepts directly to actions using predefined rules, without maintaining memory or building internal models. A thermostat exemplifies this: it reads temperature and activates heating if below threshold. These agents are fast, predictable, and easy to implement, but they fail in partially observable or complex environments where history matters.

  • Operates on condition-action rules (if X then do Y)
  • No internal memory or world model
  • Works only in fully observable environments
  • Example: thermostat activates heating when temp drops below 20C
  • Fast and predictable but cannot handle ambiguity or partial information
1

Perceive

Sensor reads current environment state

2

Match Rule

Condition-action lookup against rule set

3

Act

Execute the matched action immediately

Takeaways

  • Use simple reflex agents for well-defined, fully observable problems
  • They are the cheapest to build and easiest to debug
  • Upgrade to model-based when the environment requires memory

Model-based Reflex Agent

Model-based reflex agents maintain an internal representation of the world, enabling them to handle partially observable environments.

Model-based reflex agents extend simple reflex agents by adding memory that tracks environmental state over time. A robot vacuum cleaner builds a map of the room, remembers which areas are cleaned, and avoids obstacles using its internal model. This allows operation in partially observable environments where current sensor data alone is insufficient for good decisions.

  • Maintains an internal model (memory) of the environment
  • Handles partially observable environments
  • Example: robot vacuum builds room map, tracks cleaned areas
  • Uses history to inform current decisions
  • More capable than simple reflex but more complex to implement
FeatureSimple ReflexModel-based Reflex
MemoryNoneInternal state model
EnvironmentFully observable onlyPartially observable OK
ExampleThermostatRobot vacuum cleaner
ComplexityLowMedium

Takeaways

  • Use model-based agents when the environment is only partially observable
  • The internal model must be kept updated as conditions change
  • Memory introduces complexity but unlocks much richer behavior

Goal-based Agent

Goal-based agents plan sequences of actions to achieve specific objectives, enabling navigation of complex problem spaces.

Goal-based agents go beyond reactive behavior by maintaining explicit goals and planning action sequences to achieve them. Navigation apps like Google Maps exemplify this: they compare routes, adapt to real-time traffic changes, and re-plan when conditions shift. The agent's decision logic evaluates whether potential actions move it closer to the goal, enabling purposeful, multi-step behavior in dynamic environments.

  • Maintains explicit goals that drive action selection
  • Plans multi-step action sequences toward objectives
  • Adapts plans when environmental conditions change
  • Example: GPS navigation recalculating route on traffic jam
  • Decision logic evaluates actions by proximity to goal state

Takeaways

  • Goal-based agents suit tasks with clear success criteria
  • They can handle dynamic environments through re-planning
  • Define goals precisely; vague goals produce poor agent behavior

Utility-based Agent

Utility-based agents optimize across multiple factors simultaneously, selecting actions that maximize overall utility rather than just achieving a binary goal.

Utility-based agents rank higher in sophistication than goal-based agents because they evaluate multiple factors to compute a utility score. Rather than asking "does this achieve the goal?" they ask "how good is this outcome across all relevant dimensions?" An investment advisor agent considers not just return rate but also volatility, liquidity, and diversification. This enables nuanced decision-making in complex trade-off scenarios.

  • Evaluates multiple factors to compute a utility function
  • Optimizes trade-offs rather than pursuing binary goals
  • Example: investment agent weighing returns, risk, liquidity, diversification
  • Produces more nuanced decisions in complex scenarios
  • Requires well-defined utility function calibration

  • Defining the utility function is the hardest and most impactful design decision
  • These agents excel at recommendation and optimization tasks

Learning Agent

Learning agents improve performance over time by incorporating new experiences into their knowledge base, enabling adaptation to unfamiliar environments.

Learning agents possess all capabilities of utility-based and goal-based agents but add a learning element that enhances the model through feedback. New experiences augment the initial knowledge base, improving performance in unfamiliar environments. The learning element processes feedback from outcomes, identifies patterns, and updates the agent's decision-making parameters. This creates a continuous improvement loop that makes the agent increasingly effective.

  • Includes a learning element that updates the model over time
  • Feedback from outcomes drives knowledge improvement
  • Can adapt to previously unseen environments
  • Combines all capabilities of simpler agent types
  • Learning loop: act, observe outcome, update model, repeat

  • The feedback mechanism quality determines learning effectiveness

Intro

AI agents learn through three channels: other agents, external information systems, and human feedback.

AI agent learning is a central capability that enables continuous improvement. Agents acquire knowledge from three primary sources: other AI agents (collaborative learning), external systems like the internet and databases (information retrieval), and human feedback (guidance and correction). Understanding these learning channels is essential for designing agents that can grow in capability over their operational lifetime.

  • Three learning sources: other agents, external systems, humans
  • Agent-to-agent learning enables collaborative knowledge sharing
  • External systems provide vast information access (internet, databases)
  • Human feedback guides alignment and corrects behavior
  • Combining all three sources produces the most capable agents

Learning from Humans

AI agents learn from external sources (other agents, internet) through retrieval and collaborative knowledge sharing, expanding beyond their training data.

AI agents acquire knowledge from external sources in two key ways: connecting to other AI agents and accessing information systems. Agent-to-agent learning enables knowledge transfer and collaborative problem-solving. Internet and database connections allow agents to retrieve up-to-date information beyond their static training data. These external learning pathways are what make agents dynamic rather than frozen at their training cutoff.

  • Agents can learn from other agents through knowledge sharing protocols
  • Internet connectivity provides access to current information
  • Database connections enable structured knowledge retrieval
  • External learning overcomes training data limitations
  • Real-time information access enables agents to handle novel situations

Learning from External Systems

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) ensures continuous human involvement in training, monitoring, and refining AI agents throughout their lifecycle.

Despite their autonomous decision-making, AI agents require human-defined goals and rules. The Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) concept emphasizes continuous human involvement across the agent's lifecycle. During development, humans train the initial model. In deployment, humans monitor performance and provide feedback. During refinement, human corrections improve behavior. This ensures agents remain aligned with human intent and can be course-corrected when they drift.

  • HITL = continuous human involvement in AI agent lifecycle
  • Development stage: humans train the initial model and set rules
  • Deployment stage: humans monitor agent performance in production
  • Refinement stage: human corrections improve agent behavior
  • HITL ensures alignment between agent actions and human intent

Intro

AI agent architecture patterns (ReAct, ReWoo, single vs. multi-agent) define how agents reason, plan, and coordinate to solve problems.

This section distinguishes between LLMs, AI workflows, and true AI agents, then introduces the two key reasoning frameworks: ReAct (reasoning with observation) and ReWoo (reasoning without observation). It also covers single-agent vs. multi-agent system design and how chain-of-thought reasoning enhances decision-making transparency.

  • Clear distinction: LLMs vs AI workflows vs AI agents
  • ReAct: reason, act, observe, repeat
  • ReWoo: plan all steps upfront without intermediate observations
  • Single-agent: simpler, easier to maintain and evaluate
  • Multi-agent: specialized agents collaborating on complex tasks
🔄
ReAct
Iterative reason-act-observe loop
📋
ReWoo
Plan all steps upfront, execute sequentially
👤
Single Agent
One agent with multiple tools
👥
Multi-Agent

Takeaways

  • Choose ReAct when intermediate observations affect next steps
  • Choose ReWoo when the full plan can be determined upfront
  • Start with single-agent; add multi-agent only when specialization is required

Distinguishing LLMs vs AI Workflows vs Agents (Agentic vs Non-agentic AI)

LLMs respond to single prompts, AI workflows chain LLM calls with deterministic logic, and AI agents autonomously decide their own actions and tool usage.

The distinction between LLMs, AI workflows, and AI agents is a spectrum of autonomy. An LLM (like ChatGPT) processes a prompt and returns a response with no persistent state or tool access. An AI workflow chains multiple LLM calls with deterministic orchestration logic (predefined steps). An AI agent autonomously decides which tools to use, when to use them, and how to sequence actions based on reasoning, without predefined step ordering.

  • LLM: single prompt in, single response out, no tools or persistence
  • AI Workflow: predetermined sequence of LLM calls with fixed orchestration
  • AI Agent: autonomous decision-making about tools and action sequences
  • Key differentiator: who decides the next step (human-coded vs. agent-decided)
  • Agents have loops; workflows have linear or branching pipelines
LLMAI WorkflowAI Agent
AutonomyNonePartial (coded)Full (self-directed)
Tool UseNoPredefinedDynamic selection
StateStatelessSession-scopedPersistent memory
Decision FlowSingle callPredeterminedAgent-decided loop

Takeaways

  • Most "AI agents" in production are actually AI workflows with fixed orchestration
  • True agents require reasoning loops that decide next actions dynamically
  • Start with workflows; upgrade to agents only when flexibility is needed

How AI Agents Reason and Act (ReAct)

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) alternates between thinking and tool use, allowing agents to adapt their plan based on each observation.

ReAct is a framework where the agent iterates through a reason-act-observe loop. The agent first reasons about what to do, then takes an action (typically a tool call), observes the result, and reasons again about the next step. This interleaving allows the agent to adapt its plan based on real-time feedback. If a tool returns unexpected data, the agent can change course immediately rather than blindly following a predetermined plan.

  • Loop: Reason -> Act -> Observe -> Reason -> Act -> ...
  • Each observation informs the next reasoning step
  • Enables dynamic adaptation to unexpected tool outputs
  • More robust than fixed plans in uncertain environments
  • Trade-off: more LLM calls (cost/latency) but better accuracy
1

Reason

Agent thinks about what to do next

2

Act

Agent calls a tool or takes an action

3

Observe

Agent processes the result

4

Repeat

Loop continues until task is complete

Takeaways

  • Use ReAct when tool outputs are unpredictable or environment is dynamic
  • Each reasoning step should explicitly reference the previous observation
  • ReAct increases token usage; budget accordingly

How AI Agents Reason without Observation (ReWoo)

ReWoo (Reasoning Without Observation) plans all steps upfront before execution, reducing LLM calls but sacrificing mid-plan adaptability.

ReWoo instructs the agent to generate a complete plan of all required steps before executing any of them. Unlike ReAct, the agent does not observe intermediate tool outputs to decide next actions. The full plan is generated in one reasoning pass, then steps are executed sequentially. This reduces the number of LLM calls (cost and latency) but means the agent cannot adapt if an intermediate step produces unexpected results.

  • All planning happens in a single upfront reasoning step
  • Execution follows the plan without re-reasoning between steps
  • Fewer LLM calls = lower cost and latency
  • Cannot adapt to unexpected intermediate results
  • Best suited for well-understood, predictable task sequences
FeatureReActReWoo
PlanningIncremental (step by step)All upfront
AdaptabilityHigh (re-reasons after each step)Low (fixed plan)
LLM CallsMany (one per step)Few (one for plan)
Cost/LatencyHigherLower
Best ForDynamic/uncertain tasksPredictable task sequences

Takeaways

  • Use ReWoo when the task is well-understood and tool outputs are predictable
  • ReWoo is significantly cheaper for multi-step tasks
  • Combine both: ReWoo for planning, ReAct fallback when a step fails unexpectedly

Single Agents

Single-agent systems use one agent with multiple tools, offering simplicity in evaluation and maintenance while still being powerful.

A single-agent system deploys one AI agent equipped with multiple tools to handle tasks. Despite using only one agent, the system can be highly capable since each integrated tool expands functionality. Single-agent architectures are simpler to evaluate, debug, and maintain compared to multi-agent systems. They are the ideal starting point for lean implementations and should be the default choice unless task complexity genuinely demands specialization.

  • One agent handles all tasks using its available tools
  • Each new tool significantly expands agent capabilities
  • Simpler to evaluate, debug, and maintain
  • Ideal starting point for most use cases
  • Powerful enough for many production applications
🔧
Tool Integration
Each tool expands the single agent's capability surface
🔍
Easy Debugging
One agent = one decision chain to trace
📏
Scalability
Add tools, not agents, to increase capability

Takeaways

  • Default to single-agent architecture unless proven insufficient
  • Adding tools is cheaper than adding agents
  • Evaluate whether multi-agent complexity is truly needed before splitting

Multi-agents

Multi-agent systems use specialized agents collaborating on complex tasks, gaining superior results at the cost of orchestration complexity.

Multi-agent systems assign specialized roles to different agents that collaborate on a shared objective. Like a team with a designer, copywriter, and SEO specialist redesigning a website, each agent brings focused expertise. This specialization produces superior results on complex tasks but introduces coordination overhead: communication protocols, conflict resolution, and orchestration logic. The complexity cost is justified only when the task genuinely benefits from role specialization.

  • Each agent specializes in a specific role or domain
  • Collaboration produces results beyond individual agent capability
  • Introduces orchestration complexity (communication, coordination)
  • Examples: research agent + writing agent + review agent
  • Justified only when task complexity demands specialization
AspectSingle AgentMulti-Agent
ComplexityLowHigh (coordination overhead)
SpecializationGeneralistRole-specific experts
DebuggingStraightforwardComplex (inter-agent interactions)
Best ForMost tasksComplex tasks needing diverse expertise

Takeaways

  • Only use multi-agent when single-agent demonstrably cannot handle the task
  • Define clear roles and communication protocols between agents
  • Start with 2-3 agents maximum; add more only with proven need

Intro

Implementing AI agents in practice requires selecting a model, defining tools, crafting system prompts, and configuring guardrails.

Moving from theory to practice, implementing AI agents involves four key decisions: selecting the right LLM model (balancing capability vs. cost), defining which external tools the agent can access, engineering effective system prompts that guide behavior, and establishing guardrails that prevent harmful or off-track actions. Each decision impacts agent performance, cost, and safety.

  • Model selection: balance intelligence, speed, and cost
  • Tool definition: APIs and interfaces the agent can use
  • Prompt engineering: system prompts that guide agent behavior
  • Guardrails: safety constraints preventing harmful actions
  • All four must be configured together for effective agents

Select Model

Choose LLM based on task requirements and budget

2

Define Tools

3

Engineer Prompts

Craft system instructions for optimal behavior

4

Set Guardrails

Configure safety constraints and boundaries

Takeaways

  • These four decisions form the practical foundation of any agent deployment
  • Start with a capable model and constrain with guardrails rather than starting minimal
  • Iterate on prompts; they are the cheapest lever to improve agent performance

How to Implement AI Agents in Your Business

Successful AI agent implementation follows a structured path: define objectives, assess data readiness, start with a pilot, then scale.

Implementing AI agents in a business requires a methodical approach. First, define clear objectives (enhance customer support, reduce costs, automate workflows). Then assess data requirements and availability. Start with a contained pilot project to validate the approach before scaling. Clear success metrics, stakeholder buy-in, and realistic expectations about capabilities and limitations are essential for successful deployment.

  • Define clear objectives: what problem does the agent solve?
  • Assess data requirements and current data readiness
  • Start with a pilot project, not a company-wide rollout
  • Establish measurable success criteria before deployment
  • Plan for iteration; first deployment is never the final version
1

Define Objectives

Clarify what you want the agent to achieve

2

Assess Data
