3

Pilot

Deploy in contained scope to validate approach

4

Measure

Track performance against success criteria

5

Scale

Expand to broader use cases based on results

Takeaways

  • Never deploy agents without clear, measurable objectives
  • Data readiness is usually the biggest bottleneck, not model capability
  • Pilot-first approach reduces risk and builds organizational confidence

Select a Model

Model selection depends on task complexity, speed requirements, and cost; no single model is universally best.

Choosing an LLM for an AI agent involves balancing capability against practical constraints. Powerful models handle complex reasoning but are slower and more expensive. Lighter models are fast and cheap but less capable. The optimal approach often involves testing multiple models on representative tasks and potentially using different models for different subtasks within the same agent system.

  • No single "best" model; the choice depends on requirements
  • Capability vs. cost vs. speed trade-off is fundamental
  • Test multiple models on your actual tasks before committing
  • Consider using different models for different subtasks
  • Model benchmarks help but real-task performance is what matters
FactorLarge Models (GPT-4, Claude)Small Models (GPT-4o-mini, Haiku)
ReasoningExcellentGood for simple tasks
SpeedSlowerFast
CostHighLow
Best ForComplex reasoning, planningRoutine tasks, high volume

Takeaways

  • Match model capability to task difficulty; do not over-provision
  • Use smaller models for high-volume routine tasks to control costs
  • Benchmark on YOUR tasks, not generic leaderboards

External Tools the Agent Can Use

Tools are the bridge between an agent's intelligence and real-world action; they divide into data tools (retrieval) and action tools (execution).

Agents interact with external software primarily through APIs, which provide structured, reliable interfaces. When APIs are unavailable, agents can interact with software as a human would (browser automation), though this is less reliable. Tools divide into two categories: data tools that help agents gather information (search, database queries, file reads) and action tools that execute changes (sending emails, creating records, deploying code).

  • APIs are the preferred bridge between agents and external systems
  • Fallback: agents can use software as humans do (less reliable)
  • Data tools: gather information (search, read, query)
  • Action tools: execute changes (write, send, deploy)
  • Structured API data is far more reliable than UI scraping
Data ToolsAction Tools
PurposeGather informationExecute changes
ExamplesSearch, DB query, file readSend email, create record, deploy
Risk LevelLow (read-only)Higher (modifies state)
Guardrails NeededMinimalEssential

Takeaways

  • Always prefer API-based tool integration over UI automation
  • Separate data tools from action tools in your architecture for safety
  • Action tools need stronger guardrails since they modify external state

Configuring Instructions and Prompt Engineering Best Practices

A well-crafted system prompt is the most cost-effective lever for improving agent performance, reducing ambiguity and errors in execution.

Prompt engineering for AI agents follows the same principles as for LLMs but with higher stakes, since agents take autonomous actions. Clear, specific system prompts reduce ambiguity, improve decision quality, and minimize errors in multi-step workflows. The system prompt defines the agent's role, constraints, available tools, output format, and escalation rules. Investing time in prompt refinement pays compound returns across every agent interaction.

  • System prompts define role, constraints, tools, and behavior rules
  • Clear prompts reduce errors in autonomous decision-making
  • Prompt refinement is the cheapest way to improve agent performance
  • Include explicit instructions for edge cases and failure modes
  • Iterate on prompts based on observed agent behavior patterns
🎯
Role Definition
Who the agent is and what it does
🚧
Constraints
Boundaries on agent behavior and scope
🔧
Tool Instructions
When and how to use each available tool
📝
Output Format
Expected structure of agent responses

Takeaways

  • Write system prompts as if training a new employee: explicit, complete, no assumptions
  • Include examples of correct behavior for ambiguous scenarios
  • Treat prompts as living documents; iterate based on production behavior

Few-shot Prompting

Few-shot prompting provides example input-output pairs that teach the agent desired behavior patterns without retraining the model.

Prompting techniques range from zero-shot (no examples, relying on pre-trained knowledge) to few-shot (providing several examples of desired behavior). Zero-shot works for simple, well-understood tasks. One-shot provides a single example as a template. Few-shot gives multiple examples covering variations and edge cases. For AI agents, few-shot examples in the system prompt dramatically improve consistency of tool usage, output formatting, and decision-making patterns.

  • Zero-shot: no examples; model uses pre-trained knowledge only
  • One-shot: single example as behavioral template
  • Few-shot: multiple examples showing variations and edge cases
  • More examples = more consistent agent behavior
  • Examples should cover both typical cases and edge cases
1

Zero-shot

No examples; relies on model's training

2

One-shot

Single example establishes the pattern

3

Few-shot

Multiple examples cover variations and edges

Takeaways

  • Use few-shot prompting when you need consistent, specific output patterns
  • Include edge case examples to prevent common failure modes
  • Balance example count; too many waste context window on examples rather than reasoning

Chain of Thought Reasoning

Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting forces models to show reasoning steps, improving accuracy on complex problems and making agent decisions auditable.

Chain-of-thought reasoning asks AI models to explain their intermediate reasoning steps before arriving at a conclusion. This technique improves accuracy on complex problems by preventing the model from jumping to conclusions. For AI agents, CoT makes decision-making transparent and auditable. When an agent explains why it chose a specific tool or action, developers can identify reasoning errors and improve the system prompt accordingly.

  • CoT = showing intermediate reasoning steps before conclusions
  • Improves accuracy on multi-step and complex reasoning tasks
  • Makes agent decisions transparent and debuggable
  • Enables identification of reasoning errors for prompt improvement
  • Trade-off: increases token usage but improves reliability
Without CoTWith CoT
OutputDirect answer onlyReasoning + answer
AccuracyLower on complex tasksHigher (fewer logic jumps)
DebuggabilityOpaqueTransparent reasoning chain
Token CostLowerHigher

Takeaways

  • Enable CoT for any agent making consequential decisions
  • Use CoT output to identify and fix reasoning failures in your prompts
  • CoT is especially valuable during development and debugging phases

Guardrails

Guardrails are layered safety mechanisms that constrain agent behavior, preventing harmful, off-topic, or unauthorized actions.

Like layered road safety mechanisms (guardrails, speed limits, traffic lights, signs), AI agent guardrails use multiple complementary constraints to ensure safe operation. These include input validation (rejecting malicious prompts), output filtering (blocking harmful content), action constraints (limiting which tools can be called and when), scope boundaries (keeping the agent on-topic), and escalation rules (handing off to humans when uncertain).

  • Guardrails use layered mechanisms, not a single safety check
  • Input validation: reject prompt injection and malicious inputs
  • Output filtering: block harmful, biased, or inappropriate content
  • Action constraints: limit tool access and execution permissions
  • Escalation rules: hand off to humans when confidence is low
🛡️
Input Validation
Filter malicious or adversarial inputs
🚦
Action Constraints

📤
Output Filtering

👤

Hand off when agent is uncertain

Takeaways

  • Always implement multiple layers of guardrails, never rely on a single check
  • Action constraints are the most critical guardrail for agents with tools
  • Design guardrails before deployment, not after the first incident

The Importance of Human Intervention

Human oversight during early agent deployment catches edge cases and subtle failures that automated tests miss.

Human intervention is one of the most critical safeguards when deploying AI agents. During initial rollout, human reviewers provide intuition and common sense that automated evaluation cannot replicate. They identify edge cases, subtle inaccuracies, and areas for improvement that only become apparent through real-world interaction. This feedback loop allows teams to refine agent behavior iteratively, building confidence before expanding autonomy.

  • Human oversight is essential during early deployment phases
  • Humans detect subtle failures and edge cases automated tests miss
  • Human feedback creates an iterative improvement loop for agents
  • Common sense and intuition remain uniquely human strengths in evaluation

🔄

⚠️
Edge Cases
Real-world scenarios that test suites never anticipated

Takeaways

  • Always include human-in-the-loop review during initial agent deployment
  • Use human feedback to identify blind spots before scaling autonomy
  • Gradually reduce oversight as agent reliability is empirically confirmed

How to Evaluate AI Agents

A good AI agent must balance multiple criteria simultaneously: accuracy, speed, ethical behavior, and task completion effectiveness.

Evaluating AI agents is more complex than measuring a single metric. Speed without accuracy is useless; politeness without task completion is insufficient. Effective evaluation requires a multi-dimensional framework that considers response quality, task success rate, latency, safety compliance, and user satisfaction together. No single metric captures agent quality.

  • Fast responses are meaningless if they are incorrect
  • Ethical behavior alone does not guarantee task effectiveness
  • Evaluation requires balancing multiple criteria simultaneously
  • A good agent solves its intended task reliably while meeting quality standards
CriterionWhat It MeasuresFailure Mode If Ignored
AccuracyCorrectness of responsesFast but wrong answers
SpeedResponse latencyCorrect but unusably slow
EthicsSafety and complianceEffective but harmful
Task CompletionEnd-to-end successPolite but unhelpful

Takeaways

  • Define evaluation as a multi-metric scorecard, not a single number
  • Weight metrics based on your specific use case priorities

Introduction to n8n

n8n is a no-code workflow automation tool that enables building AI agents through an intuitive drag-and-drop interface in minutes.

n8n (short for 'nodemation') is a workflow automation platform that allows users to create AI workflows and agents with minimal coding. Its drag-and-drop builder provides an intuitive visual interface for connecting nodes into logical workflows. The platform dramatically reduces the barrier to entry for building functional AI agents, enabling rapid prototyping.

  • n8n stands for 'nodemation' (node automation)
  • Drag-and-drop visual builder requires little to no coding
  • Enables creating functional AI agents in minutes
  • Workflows are built by connecting nodes that represent actions

Node Types in n8n

n8n has four node types (triggers, action, logic, AI agent) that combine to define how an automation workflow operates.

The n8n canvas uses nodes as building blocks connected by arrows showing data flow. Four node types exist: triggers (initiate the workflow based on events), action nodes (perform specific tasks), logic nodes (control flow with conditions and branching), and AI agent nodes (enable LLM-powered reasoning). Every workflow begins with a trigger node.

  • Action nodes perform specific tasks (send email, read data)

  • AI agent nodes enable LLM-powered reasoning within the workflow

Defining Your Agent's Personality: The System Prompt

The system prompt defines the agent's role, personality, tone, and behavioral constraints, serving as its foundational instruction set.

Configuring the AI agent node in n8n starts with the system message, which acts as the agent's personality definition. The tools agent type is selected when the agent needs to interact with external tools. The prompt source is set to the chat trigger so input comes directly from user messages. The system message defines who the agent is, how it should behave, its tone, and its limitations.

  • Select 'tools agent' type when the agent needs external tool access
  • Set prompt source to chat trigger for interactive conversations

Adding the Brain: Making Your Workflow Think

Connecting an LLM (like OpenAI's GPT) to the agent node gives it reasoning capability, requiring only an API key and minimal credits.

The AI agent needs an LLM as its reasoning engine. In n8n, this is done by connecting a model node to the agent and providing API credentials. OpenAI's models are a common choice, though any provider works. Setup requires creating API credentials in n8n by pasting your OpenAI API key. The cost is minimal for typical agent usage.

  • The model node connects an LLM to the AI agent
  • API credentials bridge n8n to the LLM provider (e.g., OpenAI)
  • Any LLM provider can be used, not just OpenAI
  • API usage costs are minimal for typical agent workloads

Takeaways

  • Keep API keys secure and monitor usage costs
  • The LLM choice affects agent capability but the workflow pattern remains the same

Implementing Memory in n8n: Building Memory for Your Agent

Without a memory node, agents cannot recall information from earlier in the same conversation, making them unsuitable for multi-turn interactions.

By default, an n8n agent has no memory: it cannot recall information shared earlier in the conversation. This is demonstrated by telling the agent your name and then asking it to recall it, which it fails to do. Adding a memory node (such as window buffer memory) gives the agent short-term conversational memory, enabling coherent multi-turn dialogue essential for personal assistant functionality.

  • Without memory, agents treat each message as independent
  • Window buffer memory stores recent conversation turns
  • Memory is essential for personal assistant use cases
  • Memory nodes connect directly to the AI agent node in n8n
FeatureWithout MemoryWith Memory
Context retentionNone between messagesMaintains conversation history
Multi-turn tasksImpossibleFully supported
User experienceFrustrating repetitionNatural conversation flow

Takeaways

  • Always add memory when building conversational agents
  • Test memory by sharing info and asking the agent to recall it later

Integrating Tools: Google Sheets and Gmail

Tools give agents the ability to act in the real world; connecting Google Sheets (for data lookup) and Gmail (for sending) transforms a chatbot into a functional assistant.

An agent that can only converse is not a personal assistant. Tools enable real-world actions. In this project, two tools are connected: Google Sheets provides access to a contacts database for looking up email addresses, and Gmail enables the agent to send emails. The same pattern applies to more sophisticated databases and communication channels. Tools are what differentiate a chatbot from an agent.

  • Tools transform a conversational agent into an action-capable assistant
  • Google Sheets serves as a simple contacts database
  • Gmail integration enables the agent to send emails
  • The same pattern scales to enterprise databases and APIs
  • Each tool requires its own credential/authentication setup
📊
Google Sheets
Contacts database for email address lookup
📧
Gmail
Email sending capability for the agent
🔑
Credentials
Each tool requires authenticated access

Takeaways

  • Connect tools to give agents real-world action capability
  • Start simple (spreadsheets) and scale to production databases later

Producing the Final Output

An Edit Fields node with manual JSON mapping ensures structured agent output (subject, message) displays correctly in the chat interface.

The final workflow step configures how agent output is displayed. An Edit Fields node with manual mapping and JSON type ensures structured responses (key-value pairs like subject and message) are rendered properly rather than as raw text. This completes the agent loop: trigger receives input, agent reasons and uses tools, and the output node formats and returns results to the user.

  • Edit Fields node controls output formatting
  • Manual mapping gives precise control over displayed fields
  • JSON type preserves structured key-value responses
  • This node is the final step before results appear in chat
  • Completes the full agent workflow: input, reasoning, tools, output

Add Edit Fields Node

Place it as the final node on the canvas

2

Switch to Manual Mapping

3

Add Output Field

4

Connect to Agent

Takeaways

  • Always configure an output node to ensure clean user-facing responses
  • Use JSON type for structured agent outputs with multiple fields

Intro

The AI agent technology stack covers APIs, cloud services, data integration, development frameworks, and deployment, forming the infrastructure foundation for production agents.

This section introduces the technology stack required to build and deploy AI agents in real-world business settings. It covers five key areas: APIs for connecting to LLMs, cloud services for compute, data integration for domain knowledge, development frameworks for building agents, and deployment strategies for serving users at scale.

  • APIs connect agents to external LLM providers
  • Cloud services provide scalable compute infrastructure
  • Data integration gives agents domain-specific knowledge
  • Frameworks (LangChain, etc.) accelerate development
  • Deployment takes agents from prototype to production
1

APIs

Bridge to external LLM models

2

Cloud

Scalable compute infrastructure

3

Data

Domain knowledge and business context

4

Frameworks

Pre-built components for agent features

5

Deployment

Serving agents to end users at scale

Takeaways

  • Understand all five layers of the agent tech stack before building
  • Each layer involves make-vs-buy decisions based on team capabilities

APIs

Most organizations use external LLMs via APIs rather than building their own, making API integration the primary connection pattern between agents and their reasoning engine.

The make-vs-buy decision for LLMs overwhelmingly favors 'buy' for most organizations; few have resources to train their own models. APIs provide the bridge between an AI agent and an external LLM. The API handles sending prompts, receiving responses, and managing the communication protocol. This is the most common integration pattern for production AI agents.

  • Very few organizations can build their own LLM
  • APIs act as bridges between agents and external models
  • API integration is straightforward and well-documented
  • The make-vs-buy decision for LLMs favors external providers for most teams
🌐
API Bridge
Connects your agent to external LLM providers
💰
Cost Model
Pay-per-use instead of massive upfront investment
🔌
Plug & Play
Swap providers without rebuilding the agent

Takeaways

  • Default to external LLM APIs unless you have specific reasons to self-host
  • Design agent architecture to be provider-agnostic for flexibility

Cloud Services

Cloud platforms provide the scalable, on-demand compute infrastructure that AI agents require, avoiding massive upfront hardware investment.

AI agents demand significant computing resources that grow with complexity and usage. Organizations face another make-vs-buy decision: purchase dedicated hardware (GPUs for peak usage) or use cloud services that scale on demand. Cloud solutions offer flexibility, eliminate upfront capital expenditure, and handle variable workloads without over-provisioning.

  • Agent compute demands grow with complexity and user scale
  • On-premise requires buying for peak usage (often wasteful)
  • Cloud provides elastic scaling without upfront investment
  • GPU availability for AI workloads is a key cloud advantage
FactorOn-PremiseCloud
Upfront CostHigh (hardware purchase)Low (pay-as-you-go)
ScalingManual, slowAutomatic, instant
GPU AccessLimited by owned hardwareOn-demand allocation
MaintenanceInternal team requiredManaged by provider

Takeaways

  • Start with cloud for AI agent workloads to avoid premature hardware investment
  • Consider hybrid approaches only after usage patterns stabilize

Data and Knowledge Integration

AI agents are only as effective as the data they can access; connecting them to relevant business databases, knowledge bases, and enterprise systems is essential.

An AI agent without access to relevant data is like a world-class analyst without access to company systems. Agents perform best when connected to databases, ERPs, knowledge bases, and other enterprise data sources. The more relevant context an agent has, the more effective its reasoning and outputs become. Data integration is what transforms a generic LLM into a domain-specific business tool.

  • Agents without data access cannot solve domain-specific tasks
  • Connect agents to databases, ERPs, and knowledge bases
  • More relevant data access equals more effective agent outputs
  • Data integration turns generic LLMs into specialized business tools
🗄️
Databases
Structured business data (SQL, NoSQL)
📚
Knowledge Bases
Documents, wikis, FAQs for RAG
🏢
Enterprise Systems
ERP, CRM, and internal platforms

Takeaways

  • Prioritize data access as the primary differentiator for agent effectiveness
  • Use RAG patterns to give agents access to large document collections

Development Frameworks

LangChain (chains for workflows, agents for autonomous reasoning) and LangGraph (stateful multi-step graphs) are the essential frameworks for building production AI agents.

Modern agent projects use pre-built frameworks rather than starting from scratch. LangChain is the most important library, offering two building blocks: chains (for predefined agentic workflows) and agents (for autonomous tool-calling reasoning). LangGraph extends this with stateful graph-based orchestration for complex multi-step processes. These frameworks handle memory, planning, tool calling, and orchestration out of the box.

  • LangChain is the essential framework to learn first
  • Chains create predefined agentic workflows (fixed steps)
  • Agents enable autonomous LLM-driven tool selection
  • LangGraph adds stateful graph-based orchestration
  • Frameworks provide memory, planning, and tool-calling infrastructure
FrameworkPrimary UseKey Feature
LangChain ChainsAgentic workflowsPredefined step sequences
LangChain AgentsAutonomous agentsLLM decides tools and steps
LangGraphComplex orchestrationStateful multi-step graphs

Takeaways

  • Start with LangChain for both workflow and agent development
  • Use LangGraph when you need stateful, multi-step agent orchestration

Deployment

Deployment moves agents from notebooks to user-facing environments (chat interfaces, backend processes, platform integrations) where they deliver real value.

A working prototype in a Jupyter notebook must be deployed to an environment where users can interact with it. Deployment options include chat interfaces on websites, embedded agents within platforms (e.g., Q&A sections), or backend processes that operate without direct user interaction. The deployment strategy depends on the use case, expected load, and required integration points.

  • Prototypes in notebooks cannot serve real users
  • Chat interfaces are the most common deployment pattern
  • Agents can also run as backend processes without UI
  • Platform embedding places agents where users already work
  • Deployment must account for scaling, monitoring, and reliability
💬
Chat Interface
Web-based conversational UI for end users
🔧
Backend Process
Automated agent running without direct user interaction
📱
Platform Embed
Agent integrated into existing tools and workflows

Takeaways

  • Choose deployment mode based on user interaction patterns
  • Plan for monitoring and observability from day one of deployment

The Key Value Proposition of AI Agents

AI agents represent virtual employees that can perform many human tasks at scale, driving significant cost efficiencies for organizations.

The key value proposition of AI agents is their potential to function as AI employees capable of performing tasks traditionally handled by humans. This translates to substantial cost efficiencies. CNN reports that 41% of companies plan workforce adjustments due to AI capabilities. The economic impact stems from agents' ability to work continuously, scale instantly, and handle repetitive tasks without fatigue.

  • AI agents function as virtual employees for many tasks
  • 41% of companies plan workforce adjustments due to AI (CNN)
  • Cost efficiency is the primary business driver for adoption
  • Agents scale instantly and work continuously without fatigue
💰
Cost Efficiency
Perform tasks at fraction of human labor cost
📈
Scalability
Handle 10 or 10,000 tasks without additional hiring
⏰
24/7 Availability
No breaks, no downtime, continuous operation

Takeaways

  • Position AI agents as force multipliers, not just cost cutters
  • Identify repetitive, high-volume tasks as first automation candidates

AI Agents as Teammates

AI agents will increasingly work alongside humans as virtual teammates, excelling at some tasks while humans maintain edges in others.

AI agents are evolving into workplace teammates across all industries: development, customer service, logistics, and more. They observe human workflows, learn task patterns, and gradually become faster at specific subtasks. However, humans retain advantages in creativity, judgment, and novel problem-solving. Companies must adapt their processes to optimize human-AI collaboration or risk falling behind competitors who do.

  • AI agents will work alongside humans in every industry
  • Agents learn by observing and will surpass humans at specific subtasks
  • Humans maintain advantages in creativity and novel problem-solving
  • Companies that fail to adapt will lose competitive advantage
  • Virtual employees are coming to the job market inevitably
DimensionAI Agent StrengthHuman Strength
SpeedProcesses data instantlyStrategic thinking
ScaleHandles thousands simultaneouslyDeep 1:1 relationships
ConsistencyNever fatigued or distractedCreative improvisation
LearningPattern recognition at scaleTransfer reasoning to novel domains

Takeaways

  • Prepare for AI teammates by identifying which tasks to delegate vs. retain
  • Focus human effort on tasks requiring creativity, empathy, and novel reasoning

First Graph: Defining a State and a Node

Import Relevant Classes and Functions

from langgraph.graph import START, END, StateGraph  # LangGraph framework imports
from typing_extensions import TypedDict  # Type hints
from langchain_openai.chat_models import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, BaseMessage  # LangChain framework imports

Define the State

class State(TypedDict):  # Define the graph state schema
    messages: Sequence[BaseMessage]

state["messages"][0].pretty_print()

Define the Nodes

                  seed = 365, 
                  temperature = 0, 
                  max_completion_tokens = 100)

    response.pretty_print()
    
    return State(messages = [response])
chatbot(state)
Code Lab First Graph: Building the Graph

First Graph: Building the Graph

Set the OpenAI API Key as an Environment Variable

Import Relevant Classes and Functions

from langgraph.graph import START, END, StateGraph  # LangGraph framework imports
from typing_extensions import TypedDict  # Type hints
from langchain_openai.chat_models import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, BaseMessage  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.runnables import Runnable  # LangChain framework imports
from collections.abc import Sequence

Define the State

class State(TypedDict):  # Define the graph state schema
    messages: Sequence[BaseMessage]
state = State(messages = [HumanMessage("Could you tell me a grook by Piet Hein?")])  # User message type
state["messages"][0].pretty_print()

Define the Nodes

chat = ChatOpenAI(model = "gpt-4o",   # Initialize chat model
                  seed = 365, 
                  temperature = 0, 
                  max_completion_tokens = 100)
response = chat.invoke(state["messages"])  # Execute the graph
response.pretty_print()
def chatbot(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING chatbot:")
    
    response = chat.invoke(state["messages"])  # Execute the graph
    response.pretty_print()
    
    return State(messages = [response])
chatbot(state)

Define the Graph

graph = StateGraph(State)  # Create state graph
graph.add_node("chatbot", chatbot)  # Register node in graph

graph.add_edge(START, "chatbot")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("chatbot", END)  # Connect nodes
graph_compiled = graph.compile()  # Compile the graph
isinstance(graph, Runnable)
graph_compiled

Test the Graph

Code Lab Conditional Edges: Defining Nodes and a Routing Function

Conditional Edges: Defining Nodes and a Routing Function

Set the OpenAI API Key as an Environment Variable

Import Relevant Classes and Functions

from langgraph.graph import START, END, StateGraph  # LangGraph framework imports
from typing_extensions import TypedDict  # Type hints
from langchain_openai.chat_models import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, BaseMessage  # LangChain framework imports
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import Literal  # Type hints

Define the State

class State(TypedDict):  # Define the graph state schema
    messages: Sequence[BaseMessage]

Define the Nodes

chat = ChatOpenAI(model = "gpt-4o",   # Initialize chat model
                  seed = 365, 
                  temperature = 0, 
                  max_completion_tokens = 100)
def ask_question(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING ask_question:")
    
    print("What is your question?")
    
    return State(messages = [HumanMessage(input())])  # User message type
ask_question(State(messages = []))
def chatbot(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING chatbot:")
    
    response = chat.invoke(state["messages"])  # Execute the graph
    response.pretty_print()
    
    return State(messages = [response])
def ask_another_question(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING ask_another_question:")
    
    print("Would you like to ask one more question (yes/no)?")
    
    return State(messages = [HumanMessage(input())])  # User message type
ask_another_question(State(messages = []))

Define the Routing Function

def routing_function(state: State) -> str:
    
    if state["messages"].content == "yes":
        return "ask_question"
    else:
        return "__end__"
Code Lab Conditional Edges: Defining Nodes and a Routing Function

Conditional Edges: Defining Nodes and a Routing Function

Set the OpenAI API Key as an Environment Variable

Import Relevant Classes and Functions

from langgraph.graph import START, END, StateGraph  # LangGraph framework imports
from typing_extensions import TypedDict  # Type hints
from langchain_openai.chat_models import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, BaseMessage  # LangChain framework imports
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import Literal  # Type hints

Define the State

class State(TypedDict):  # Define the graph state schema
    messages: Sequence[BaseMessage]

Define the Nodes

chat = ChatOpenAI(model = "gpt-4o",   # Initialize chat model
                  seed = 365, 
                  temperature = 0, 
                  max_completion_tokens = 100)
def ask_question(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING ask_question:")
    
    print("What is your question?")
    
    return State(messages = [HumanMessage(input())])  # User message type
ask_question(State(messages = []))
def chatbot(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING chatbot:")
    
    response = chat.invoke(state["messages"])  # Execute the graph
    response.pretty_print()
    
    return State(messages = [response])
def ask_another_question(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING ask_another_question:")
    
    print("Would you like to ask one more question (yes/no)?")
    
    return State(messages = [HumanMessage(input())])  # User message type
ask_another_question(State(messages = []))

Define the Routing Function

def routing_function(state: State) -> Literal["ask_question", "__end__"]:
    
    if state["messages"][0].content == "yes":
        return "ask_question"
    else:
        return "__end__"

Define the Graph

graph = StateGraph(State)  # Create state graph
graph.add_node("ask_question", ask_question)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("chatbot", chatbot)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("ask_another_question", ask_another_question)  # Register node in graph

graph.add_edge(START, "ask_question")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("ask_question", "chatbot")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("chatbot", "ask_another_question")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_conditional_edges(source = "ask_another_question",   # Add conditional routing
                            path = routing_function)
graph_compiled = graph.compile()  # Compile the graph
graph_compiled
print(graph_compiled.get_graph().draw_ascii())

Test the Graph

graph_compiled.invoke(State(messages = []))  # Execute the graph

Define the Nodes

def ask_another_question(state: MessagesState) -> MessagesState:  # Pre-built messages state
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING ask_another_question:")
    for i in state["messages"]:
        i.pretty_print()
    
    question = "Would you like to ask one more question (yes/no)?"
    print(question)
    
    return MessagesState(messages = [AIMessage(question), HumanMessage(input())])  # Pre-built messages state

Define the Routing Function

def routing_function(state: MessagesState) -> Literal["ask_question", "__end__"]:  # Pre-built messages state
    
    if state["messages"][-1].content == "yes":
        return "ask_question"
    else:
        return "__end__"

Define the Graph

graph = StateGraph(MessagesState)  # Create state graph
graph.add_node("ask_question", ask_question)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("chatbot", chatbot)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("ask_another_question", ask_another_question)  # Register node in graph

graph.add_edge(START, "ask_question")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("ask_question", "chatbot")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("chatbot", "ask_another_question")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_conditional_edges(source = "ask_another_question",   # Add conditional routing
                            path = routing_function)
graph_compiled = graph.compile()  # Compile the graph
graph_compiled

Test the Graph

graph_compiled.invoke(MessagesState(messages = []))  # Execute the graph

Code Lab Summarizing Messages

Summarizing Messages

Set the OpenAI API Key as an Environment Variable

Import Relevant Classes and Functions

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END, MessagesState  # LangGraph framework imports
from langchain_openai.chat_models import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, HumanMessage, SystemMessage, RemoveMessage  # LangChain framework imports
from typing import Literal  # Type hints

Define the State

class State(MessagesState):  # Define the graph state schema
    summary: str
test_state = State()
test_state["summary"]
bool(test_state.get("summary", ""))

Define the Nodes

chat = ChatOpenAI(model = "gpt-4o",   # Initialize chat model
                  seed = 365, 
                  temperature = 0, 
                  max_completion_tokens = 100)
def ask_question(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING ask_question:")
    
    question = "What is your question?"
    print(question)
    
    return State(messages = [AIMessage(question), HumanMessage(input())])  # User message type
def chatbot(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING chatbot:")
    for i in state["messages"]:
        i.pretty_print()
        
    system_message = f'''
    Here's a quick summary of what's been discussed so far:
    {state.get("summary", "")}
    
    Keep this in mind as you answer the next question.
    '''
    
    response = chat.invoke([SystemMessage(system_message)] + state["messages"])  # Execute the graph
    response.pretty_print()
    
    return State(messages = [response])
def ask_another_question(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING ask_another_question:")
    
    question = "Would you like to ask one more question (yes/no)?"
    print(question)
    
    return State(messages = [AIMessage(question), HumanMessage(input())])  # User message type
def summarize_and_delete_messages(state: State) -> State:
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING trim_messages:")
    
    new_conversation = ""
    for i in state["messages"]:
        new_conversation += f"{i.type}: {i.content}\n\n"
        
    summary_instructions = f'''
Update the ongoing summary by incorporating the new lines of conversation below.  
Build upon the previous summary rather than repeating it so that the result  
reflects the most recent context and developments.


Previous Summary:
{state.get("summary", "")}

New Conversation:
{new_conversation}
'''
    
    print(summary_instructions)
    
    summary = chat.invoke([HumanMessage(summary_instructions)])  # Execute the graph
    
    remove_messages = [RemoveMessage(id = i.id) for i in state["messages"][:]]
    
    return State(messages = remove_messages, summary = summary.content)

Define the Routing Function

def routing_function(state: State) -> Literal["summarize_and_delete_messages", "__end__"]:
    
    if state["messages"][-1].content == "yes":
        return "summarize_and_delete_messages"
    else:
        return "__end__"

Define the Graph

graph = StateGraph(State)  # Create state graph
graph.add_node("ask_question", ask_question)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("chatbot", chatbot)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("ask_another_question", ask_another_question)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("summarize_and_delete_messages", summarize_and_delete_messages)  # Register node in graph

graph.add_edge(START, "ask_question")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("ask_question", "chatbot")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("chatbot", "ask_another_question")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_conditional_edges(source = "ask_another_question",   # Add conditional routing
                            path = routing_function)
graph.add_edge("summarize_and_delete_messages", "ask_question")  # Connect nodes
graph_compiled = graph.compile()  # Compile the graph
graph_compiled

Test the Graph

graph_compiled.invoke(State(messages = []))  # Execute the graph
Code Lab First Steps

First Steps

Welcome back to the course everyone! In the previous section, we used the Anaconda Prompt to create a new environment called **langchain_env**. As emphasized, it’s recommended that individual projects be run in separate environments to prevent package conflicts or the accidental removal of important documents. They also offer the flexibility to install different Python versions and maintain unique package sets in each without the risk of interfering with the base setup. We also registered this environment as a Jupyter kernel so that we could use it in our Jupyter notebooks. Finally, we set our OpenAI API key as an environment variable, allowing us to utilize OpenAI’s models and API. I’m now happy to welcome you to this lesson, where we’ll create our first chatbot. We’ll be relying on Python and OpenAI’s API. Note that we won’t be making use of the LangChain framework just yet. This section introduces you to creating chatbots with OpenAI’s API and familiarizes you with its main components. Since OpenAI’s integration in LangChain relies heavily on this API, having a general idea of how it works is valuable. With that said, let’s get to coding! 😊 Load the **dotenv** extension and then apply the **%dotenv** magic command to set your OpenAI API key as an environment variable.

Next, we should configure the OpenAI library to recognize our key. To do so, import the **os** and **openai** libraries.

import os
import openai

Then, set **openai.api_key** to equal **os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY')**, passing the name of the environment variable as an argument.

openai.api_key = os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY')

We’re now ready to experiment with OpenAI’s models. We’ll do so by implementing a helpful chatbot that answers users’ questions. But we’ll also give it a sarcastic twist. 😊 First, create an OpenAI client by utilizing OpenAI’s class of the same name.

client = openai.OpenAI()

Then, define a **completion** variable that will serve as our chatbot object. Set it equal to **client.chat.completions.create**. The first parameter that the **create()** function requires is the model. I’ll opt for GPT-4, but you can experiment with any OpenAI chat model. Just visit their website, pick a language model of your choice, and write the respective name as a string. Keep in mind our discussion about costs—especially if you plan on working on your own projects. Make sure you opt for a cost-sensitive variant. The second required parameter (**messages**) contains the messages we’ll give the model before starting the conversation. These messages will be a way to instruct the model on how to behave. It expects a list of dictionaries, each containing two required key-value pairs.

completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{}, 
                                                        {}])

The key to the first pair is ‘role,’ which can be mapped to one of the following values: ‘system,’ ‘user,’ ‘assistant,’ and ‘tool.’ We’ll work with tools later in the course. For now, let’s focus on the first three. The key to the second pair is ‘content,’ which stores strings with questions, instructions, or other helpful content that will guide the model towards responding suitably. All right! Next, we’ll discuss the difference between system, user, and assistant roles. Catch you in a bit! 😊

Code Lab Creating a Sarcastic Chatbot

Creating a Sarcastic Chatbot

Welcome back, everyone! In this lesson, we’ll resume the implementation of our chat completion in Jupyter Notebook. We’ll start by instructing the chatbot to answer questions sarcastically through a system message and then pass our question as a user-role message. Let’s get into it! For starters, run the first four code cells below.

import os
import openai
openai.api_key = os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY')
client = openai.OpenAI()

Now, the first dictionary in our **messages** list should map the ‘role’ keyword to ‘system’, implying a system message. In addition, set the content to the one already familiar to you: *You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly answers questions with sarcastic responses.* In the second dictionary in the list, we’ll create a user message. I’ll go with the following request: *I’ve recently adopted a dog. Could you suggest some dog names?*

completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'system', 
                                                         'content':''' You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly 
                                                         answers questions with sarcastic responses. '''}, 
                                                        {'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' I've recently adopted a dog. 
                                                         Could you suggest some dog names? '''}])

Run the cell above and inspect the **completion** variable.

completion

We find that **completion** is an instance of the **ChatCompletion** class, with the parameter **choices** storing a list of **Choice** objects that, in turn, keep the responses from the chatbot. By default, the model returns only one response, which is typically the desired setting. This number can be controlled through a parameter called **n**. Of course, more responses result in higher token consumption and, therefore, higher cost. The role assigned to this message is ‘assistant.’ Additionally, information is available on the number of completion, prompt, and total tokens.

Finally, for this lesson, let’s check how the chatbot responded by displaying the output in a more readable form. To do that: <ul> <li>first, retrieve the <strong>choices</strong> list from the <strong>ChatCompletion</strong> object, </li> <li>then select the first and only item in this list, </li> <li>fetch the <strong>messages</strong> parameter from the <strong>Choice</strong> object,</li> <li>and lastly, extract the content from the <strong>ChatCompletionMessage</strong> object.</li> </ul> Make sure you apply the <strong>print</strong>-function to the string to ensure the message is nicely formatted.

print(completion.choices[0].message.content)

Excellent job, everyone. In the upcoming lesson, we’ll discuss additional parameters that can help further control the model’s response. See you in a bit!

Code Lab Temperature, Max Tokens, and Streaming

Temperature, Max Tokens, and Streaming

Welcome back! In this section, we’ve discussed the roles we can employ when passing a message to a model: a system, user, or assistant role. We then used a system message to create a chatbot that adopts a sarcastic persona. In this lesson, we’ll discuss a few more parameters that can affect the model’s response: <ul> <li>Its maximum number of completion tokens,</li> <li>Level of randomness, and </li> <li>The option to stream it.</li> </ul> Let’s begin with the tokens. As discussed earlier, OpenAI sets its model prices based on the number of input tokens (the ones we feed to the model) and the number of completion tokens (those the model generates). Both are capped to prevent users from inputting an excessive number of tokens and to stop the models from generating endless text. Still, it’s essential to have additional control over the amount of text generated. Models often tend to be wordy and provide more information than needed. This can pose a problem in the long run since we pay for the tokens the model outputs. As a side note, this pricing only applies when using OpenAI’s models through the API. In contrast, the ChatGPT platform is subscription-based rather than token-based, and you don’t need to worry about the model generating long texts. It’s time we see the token parameter in action!

import os
import openai
openai.api_key = os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY')
client = openai.OpenAI()

When defining the **completion** variable, keep the system message the same. However, let’s test the model with a different user message. For example: *Could you explain briefly what a black hole is?* Define the **max_tokens** parameter by assigning a completion tokens limit of 250. Run the cell and print out the content.

completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'system', 
                                                         'content':''' You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly 
                                                         answers questions with sarcastic responses. '''}, 
                                                        {'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 250)
completion

As always, our sarcastic chatbot gives an excellent response. 😊

Let’s now see how it performs when we narrow the cap down to 50 tokens.

completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'system', 
                                                         'content':''' You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly 
                                                         answers questions with sarcastic responses. '''}, 
                                                        {'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 50)
completion

This time, we get a much shorter (maybe even incomplete) response. So, we need to be careful not to limit the model too much.

I’ll now revert to 250 completion tokens. Another parameter we’ll use throughout the course is **temperature**. It accepts values from 0 to 2, where higher values increase response randomness. Although it defaults to 1, let's explore its behavior at the extremes. Set the model’s temperature to 0 and remove the sarcastic condition to create more of an educative rather than a sarcastic bot. Let’s again ask it to explain what black holes are.

completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 250, 
                                            temperature = 0)
completion

We obtain an informative response. Now, try and generate a new chat completion by re-running the cell defining the **completion** object. Display the variable. We find the new response is similar to the previous one. Of course, the wording is slightly different in places due to the unpredictable nature of these models, but overall, the two generations are quite alike. Models with lower temperatures can be used when creating a chatbot for educational purposes because the answers must be more academic and informative rather than creative.

Okay, let’s now increase the temperature to maximum and study these results.

completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 250, 
                                            temperature = 2)
completion

Well, we can all agree that this is far from helpful. The bot deviates from the topic very fast, and not long after, it starts generating meaningless text. So, such large temperature values are rarely helpful.

I’ll switch back to a temperature value of zero.

Another parameter that controls determinism is **seed**—like the seeds we’ve fed to machine learning algorithms for reproducibility. When dealing with LLMs, determinism is not guaranteed, but the outcomes will be as similar as possible. (You can experiment with this parameter at home.) From now on, I’ll set the **temperature** parameter to 0 and **seed** to 365 . I suggest you do the same to obtain results like mine.

completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 250, 
                                            temperature = 0, 
                                            seed = 365)

Okay, moving on! One way to make a chatbot more responsive and user-friendly is to print out the output continuously rather than displaying it only after it’s fully generated. The **stream** parameter allows us to achieve precisely that. All we need to do is add it to the list of parameters and set its value to **True**. Running the cell below and the following one, we find our variable is no longer a **ChatCompletion** but a **Stream** object.

completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' Could you explain briefly what a black hole is? '''}], 
                                            max_tokens = 250, 
                                            temperature = 0, 
                                            seed = 365, 
                                            stream = True)
completion

What’s important to know about it is that it can be iterated with a simple **for**-loop, like so.

for i in completion:
    print(i)

Executing the cell, we find a long list of **ChatCompletionChunk** objects. As their name suggests, they contain only a small chunk of the message. Now, within the **for**-loop, let’s print the content of each chunk. Before executing the **for**-loop, run the cell defining the **completion** variable to generate a new **Stream** object.

for i in completion:
    print(i.choices[0].delta.content, end = "")

Look at that! We’ve managed to stream our text on the screen. How cool is that? 😊

This marks the end of our short introduction to the OpenAI API. I’m convinced you now find creating a chatbot with APIs much more fun and rewarding than merely chatting with ChatGPT. It gives you much more control over the responses and allows you to create some exciting chatbots. But wait until you see what LangChain has to offer. 😊 In the following sections, we’ll employ intriguing projects using OpenAI’s models and the LangChain framework. Until then! 😊

Code Lab Short-Term Memory with the InMemorySaver Class

Short-Term Memory with the InMemorySaver Class

Set the OpenAI API Key as an Environment Variable

Import Relevant Classes and Functions

from langgraph.graph import START, END, StateGraph, MessagesState  # LangGraph framework imports
from langchain_openai.chat_models import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, AIMessage, SystemMessage, BaseMessage, RemoveMessage  # LangChain framework imports
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver  # LangGraph framework imports

Define the State

class State(MessagesState):  # Define the graph state schema
    summary: str

Define the Nodes

chat = ChatOpenAI(model = "gpt-4o",   # Initialize chat model
                  seed = 365, 
                  temperature = 0, 
                  max_completion_tokens = 100)
def ask_question(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING ask_question:")
    
    question = "What is your question?"
    print(question)
    
    return State(messages = [AIMessage(question), HumanMessage(input())])  # User message type
def chatbot(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING chatbot:")
        
    system_message = f'''
    Here's a quick summary of what's been discussed so far:
    {state.get("summary", "")}
    
    Keep this in mind as you answer the next question.
    '''
    
    response = chat.invoke([SystemMessage(system_message)] + state["messages"])  # Execute the graph
    response.pretty_print()
    
    return State(messages = [response])
def summarize_messages(state: State) -> State:
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING summarize_messages:")

    new_conversation = ""
    for i in state["messages"]:
        new_conversation += f"{i.type}: {i.content}\n\n"
    
    summary_instructions = f'''
Update the ongoing summary by incorporating the new lines of conversation below. 
Build upon the previous summary rather than repeating it, 
so that the result reflects the most recent context and developments.
Respond only with the summary.

Previous Summary:
{state.get("summary", "")}

New Conversation:
{new_conversation}
'''

    print(summary_instructions)

    summary = chat.invoke([HumanMessage(summary_instructions)])  # Execute the graph
    
    remove_messages = [RemoveMessage(id = i.id) for i in state["messages"][:]]

    return State(messages = remove_messages, summary = summary.content)

Define the Graph

graph = StateGraph(State)  # Create state graph
graph.add_node("ask_question", ask_question)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("chatbot", chatbot)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("summarize_messages", summarize_messages)  # Register node in graph

graph.add_edge(START, "ask_question")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("ask_question", "chatbot")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("chatbot", "summarize_messages")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("summarize_messages", END)  # Connect nodes
checkpointer = InMemorySaver()  # In-memory persistence
graph_compiled = graph.compile(checkpointer)  # Compile the graph
graph_compiled
config1 = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}}

Code Lab The StateSnapshot Class

The StateSnapshot Class

Set the OpenAI API Key as an Environment Variable

Import Relevant Classes and Functions

from langgraph.graph import START, END, StateGraph, MessagesState  # LangGraph framework imports
from langchain_openai.chat_models import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, AIMessage, SystemMessage, BaseMessage, RemoveMessage  # LangChain framework imports
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver  # LangGraph framework imports

Define the State

class State(MessagesState):  # Define the graph state schema
    summary: str

Define the Nodes

chat = ChatOpenAI(model = "gpt-4o",   # Initialize chat model
                  seed = 365, 
                  temperature = 0, 
                  max_completion_tokens = 100)
def ask_question(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING ask_question:")
    
    question = "What is your question?"
    print(question)
    
    return State(messages = [AIMessage(question), HumanMessage(input())])  # User message type
def chatbot(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING chatbot:")
        
    system_message = f'''
    Here's a quick summary of what's been discussed so far:
    {state.get("summary", "")}
    
    Keep this in mind as you answer the next question.
    '''
    
    response = chat.invoke([SystemMessage(system_message)] + state["messages"])  # Execute the graph
    response.pretty_print()
    
    return State(messages = [response])
def summarize_messages(state: State) -> State:
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING summarize_messages:")

    new_conversation = ""
    for i in state["messages"]:
        new_conversation += f"{i.type}: {i.content}\n\n"
    
    summary_instructions = f'''
Update the ongoing summary by incorporating the new lines of conversation below. 
Build upon the previous summary rather than repeating it, 
so that the result reflects the most recent context and developments.
Respond only with the summary.

Previous Summary:
{state.get("summary", "")}

New Conversation:
{new_conversation}
'''

    print(summary_instructions)

    summary = chat.invoke([HumanMessage(summary_instructions)])  # Execute the graph
    
    remove_messages = [RemoveMessage(id = i.id) for i in state["messages"][:]]

    return State(messages = remove_messages, summary = summary.content)

Define the Graph

graph = StateGraph(State)  # Create state graph
graph.add_node("ask_question", ask_question)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("chatbot", chatbot)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("summarize_messages", summarize_messages)  # Register node in graph

graph.add_edge(START, "ask_question")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("ask_question", "chatbot")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("chatbot", "summarize_messages")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("summarize_messages", END)  # Connect nodes
checkpointer = InMemorySaver()  # In-memory persistence
graph_compiled = graph.compile(checkpointer)  # Compile the graph
graph_compiled
config1 = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}}
config2 = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "2"}}
graph_compiled.invoke(State(), config2)  # Execute the graph
graph_states = [i for i in graph_compiled.get_state_history(config1)]
graph_states
for i in graph_states[::-1]:
    print(f'''
Messages: {i.values["messages"]}
Summary: {i.values.get("summary", "")}
Next: {i.next}
Step: {i.metadata["step"]}''')

Define the State

class State(MessagesState):  # Define the graph state schema
    summary: str

Define the Nodes

chat = ChatOpenAI(model = "gpt-4o",   # Initialize chat model
                  seed = 365, 
                  temperature = 0, 
                  max_completion_tokens = 100)
def ask_question(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING ask_question:")
    
    question = "What is your question?"
    print(question)
    
    return State(messages = [AIMessage(question), HumanMessage(input())])  # User message type
def chatbot(state: State) -> State:
    
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING chatbot:")
        
    system_message = f'''
    Here's a quick summary of what's been discussed so far:
    {state.get("summary", "")}
    
    Keep this in mind as you answer the next question.
    '''
    
    response = chat.invoke([SystemMessage(system_message)] + state["messages"])  # Execute the graph
    response.pretty_print()
    
    return State(messages = [response])
def summarize_messages(state: State) -> State:
    print(f"\n-------> ENTERING summarize_messages:")

    new_conversation = ""
    for i in state["messages"]:
        new_conversation += f"{i.type}: {i.content}\n\n"
    
    summary_instructions = f'''
Update the ongoing summary by incorporating the new lines of conversation below. 
Build upon the previous summary rather than repeating it, 
so that the result reflects the most recent context and developments.
Respond only with the summary.

Previous Summary:
{state.get("summary", "")}

New Conversation:
{new_conversation}
'''

    print(summary_instructions)

    summary = chat.invoke([HumanMessage(summary_instructions)])  # Execute the graph
    
    remove_messages = [RemoveMessage(id = i.id) for i in state["messages"][:]]

    return State(messages = remove_messages, summary = summary.content)

Define the Graph

graph = StateGraph(State)  # Create state graph
graph.add_node("ask_question", ask_question)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("chatbot", chatbot)  # Register node in graph
graph.add_node("summarize_messages", summarize_messages)  # Register node in graph

graph.add_edge(START, "ask_question")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("ask_question", "chatbot")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("chatbot", "summarize_messages")  # Connect nodes
graph.add_edge("summarize_messages", END)  # Connect nodes
db_path = "C:/Users/Hristina/Desktop/LangGraph_DB/langgraph.db"
con = sqlite3.connect(database = db_path, check_same_thread = False)
checkpointer = SqliteSaver(con)
graph_compiled = graph.compile(checkpointer)  # Compile the graph
graph_compiled
config1 = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "1"}}
graph_compiled.invoke(State(), config1)  # Execute the graph

Few-Shot Chat Message Prompt Templates

# Run the line of code below to check the version of langchain in the current environment.
# Substitute "langchain" with any other package name to check their version.
pip show langchain
from langchain_openai.chat_models import ChatOpenAI  # LangChain framework imports

from langchain_core.prompts import (ChatPromptTemplate,  # LangChain framework imports
                                    HumanMessagePromptTemplate,   # User message type
                                    AIMessagePromptTemplate, 
                                    FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate)
chat = ChatOpenAI(model_name = 'gpt-4',   # Initialize chat model
                  model_kwargs = {'seed':365},
                  temperature = 0,
                  max_tokens = 100)
TEMPLATE_H = '''I've recently adopted a {pet}. 
Could you suggest some {pet} names?'''
TEMPLATE_AI = '''{response}'''

message_template_h = HumanMessagePromptTemplate.from_template(template = TEMPLATE_H)  # User message type
message_template_ai = AIMessagePromptTemplate.from_template(template = TEMPLATE_AI)
example_template = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([message_template_h, 
                                                     message_template_ai])
examples = [{'pet':'dog', 
             'response':'''Oh, absolutely. Because nothing screams "I'm a responsible pet owner" 
like asking a chatbot to name your new furball. How about "Bark Twain" (if it's a literary hound)? '''}, 
            
            {'pet':'cat', 
             'response':'''Oh, absolutely. Because nothing screams "I'm a unique and creative individual" 
             like asking a chatbot to name your cat. How about "Furry McFurFace", "Sir Meowsalot", or "Catastrophe"? '''}, 
            
            {'pet':'fish', 
             'response':
             '''Oh, absolutely. Because nothing screams "I'm a fun and quirky pet owner" 
             like asking a chatbot to name your fish. How about "Fin Diesel", "Gill Gates", or "Bubbles"?'''}]
few_shot_prompt = FewShotChatMessagePromptTemplate(examples = examples, 
                                                   example_prompt = example_template, 
                                                   input_variables = ['pet'])
chat_template = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([few_shot_prompt, 
                                                  message_template_h])
chat_value = chat_template.invoke({'pet':'rabbit'})  # Execute the graph
chat_value
for i in chat_value.messages:
    print(f'{i.type}: {i.content}\n')
response = chat.invoke(chat_value)  # Execute the graph
response
print(response.content)

from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough  # LangChain framework imports

What are the five most important tools a {job title} needs?

1. Python

'''}))

chain_books = chat_template_books | chat | string_parser

chain_projects = chat_template_projects | chat | string_parser
chain_parallel = RunnableParallel({'books':chain_books, 'projects':chain_projects})
chain_parallel.invoke({'programming language':'Python'})  # Execute the graph
chain_time1 = (RunnableParallel({'books':chain_books, 
                                'projects':chain_projects}) 
              | chat_template_time 
              | chat 
              | string_parser
             )
chain_time2 = ({'books':chain_books, 
                'projects':chain_projects}
              | chat_template_time 
              | chat 
              | string_parser
             )
print(chain_time2.invoke({'programming language':'Python'}))  # Execute the graph
chain_time2.get_graph().print_ascii()

Code Lab The @chain Decorator

The @chain Decorator

# Run the line of code below to check the version of langchain in the current environment.
# Substitute "langchain" with any other package name to check their version.
pip show langchain
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda  # LangChain framework imports
from langchain_core.runnables import chain  # LangChain framework imports
def find_sum(x):
    return sum(x)

def find_square(x):
    return x**2
chain1 = RunnableLambda(find_sum) | RunnableLambda(find_square)
chain1.invoke([1, 2, 5])  # Execute the graph
@chain
def runnable_sum(x):
    return sum(x)

@chain
def runnable_square(x):
    return x**2
type(runnable_sum), type(runnable_square)
chain2 = runnable_sum | runnable_square
chain2.invoke([1, 2, 5])  # Execute the graph

S11: Foundations of Agentic AI

📈
Scaling
Architecture determines if system handles 10 users or 10,000 without redesign
🔒
Reliability

🎛️
