Governance guardrails, cost limits, and oversight hooks must be designed in from the start

Agentic Workflows vs. AI Agents

Workflows follow predefined code paths with LLMs at specific steps; agents let the LLM autonomously decide which tools to use and what steps to take.

A critical distinction exists between agentic workflows and AI agents. Workflows use LLMs within predefined, programmer-designed code paths; the sequence is fixed and repeatable. Agents give the LLM autonomy to decide how to approach tasks and which tools to invoke. Workflows offer predictability and control; agents offer flexibility and adaptability for ambiguous tasks.

  • Workflows: predefined steps, LLM operates within fixed parameters
  • Agents: LLM independently decides approach and tool selection
  • Workflows are predictable and easier to debug
  • Agents handle ambiguous tasks requiring adaptive reasoning
  • Choose based on task structure: defined path vs. open-ended problem
AspectAgentic WorkflowAI Agent
ControlProgrammer-defined stepsLLM decides autonomously
PredictabilityHigh (same path every run)Variable (adapts per input)
Best ForStructured, repeatable tasksAmbiguous, open-ended problems
DebuggingEasy (fixed flow)Harder (dynamic decisions)

Takeaways

  • Default to workflows when the solution path is known; use agents for ambiguous tasks
  • Many production systems combine both: workflows with agent nodes at decision points

Core Building Blocks of an AI agent

Seven building blocks form the foundation of every AI agent: perception, reasoning/planning, memory/retrieval, action/execution, feedback/adaptation, evaluation/monitoring, and governance/safety.

Every AI agent is composed of seven fundamental building blocks. Perception handles input processing. Reasoning and planning enable decision-making. Memory and retrieval provide context. Action and execution interface with the external world. Feedback and adaptation enable learning. Evaluation and monitoring ensure quality. Governance and safety guardrails enforce boundaries.

  • Perception: processing and understanding inputs
  • Reasoning & Planning: decision-making and strategy
  • Memory & Retrieval: storing and accessing context
  • Action & Execution: interfacing with external systems
  • Feedback, evaluation, and governance complete the loop
👁️
Perception
Input processing and understanding
🧠
Reasoning
Planning and decision-making
💾
Memory
Context storage and retrieval
⚡
Action
External system interaction
🔄
Feedback
Learning and adaptation loops
🛡️
Governance
Safety guardrails and boundaries

Takeaways

  • Ensure every agent design addresses all seven building blocks explicitly
  • Weak blocks create system-wide vulnerabilities; audit each independently

When (and when not) to Use AI Agents

Use agentic workflows when steps are clearly defined; use full agents when the problem is ambiguous and requires adaptive decision-making.

Choosing between workflows and agents depends on task structure. Agentic workflows suit well-structured projects with known solution paths. Full agents are appropriate when problems are ambiguous, require dynamic tool selection, or involve reasoning over uncertain inputs. Over-engineering with agents when a simple workflow suffices wastes resources and adds unpredictability.

  • Workflows: steps clearly defined, path to solution known
  • Agents: ambiguous problems requiring adaptive decisions
  • Over-using agents adds unnecessary unpredictability
  • Start with workflows; escalate to agents only when needed
  • Hybrid approaches combine both for optimal results
ScenarioUse WorkflowUse Agent
Known steps✓
Ambiguous problem✓
Predictability needed✓
Dynamic tool selection✓

Takeaways

  • Default to the simplest approach (workflow) unless the task demands autonomy
  • Document why an agent is needed when choosing that pattern

Why Architecture Matters: Scaling, Reliability & Control

Architecture decisions determine whether an agent system can scale, recover from failures, and remain under organizational control as complexity grows.

Early AI interactions were simple chat interfaces, but production agents require deliberate architectural design. Architecture decisions determine three critical properties: scalability (handling 10 or 10,000 users without redesign), reliability (error handling, retries, graceful degradation), and control (governance guardrails, cost limits, oversight hooks). These properties cannot be bolted on after the fact; they must be designed in from the start.

  • Simple chat interfaces do not scale to production agent systems
  • Scalability: handle growing load without architectural rework
  • Reliability: error handling, retries, and graceful degradation
  • Control: governance, cost limits, and human oversight hooks
  • These properties must be designed in from the beginning
📐
Scalability
System handles 10 or 10,000 users without redesign
🔒
Reliability
Error handling, retry logic, and graceful degradation
🎛️
Control
Governance guardrails, cost limits, and oversight hooks

Takeaways

  • Never skip architecture design even for 'simple' agent projects
  • Build scalability, reliability, and control into the foundation, not as afterthoughts

Section Introduction

Prompt engineering is the prerequisite skill for controlling LLMs before building workflows and multi-agent systems.

Before constructing agentic workflows and agents, prompt engineering must be mastered. It provides the fundamental skill for controlling LLM behavior through instructions. Once prompt design is understood, the transition to systems-level thinking (workflows, agents that reason and improve) becomes natural and well-grounded.

  • Prompt engineering is the foundation for all agent design
  • Master single-prompt control before building multi-step systems
  • Prompting skills transfer directly to system prompt design for agents
1

Prompt Engineering

Learn to control individual LLM responses

2

Workflows

Chain prompts into predefined sequences

3

Agents

Design autonomous systems that reason and act

Takeaways

  • Invest time in prompt engineering before attempting agent architecture
  • Every agent's effectiveness ultimately depends on prompt quality

General Principles of Prompt Structuring

The system prompt is the agent's foundational blueprint, defining its personality, role, tone, limitations, and how it interprets all user input.

System prompt design is among the most critical aspects of single-agent systems. The system prompt acts as the agent's instruction set, defining personality, role, tone, and behavioral boundaries. It shapes how the agent interprets input and generates responses. Well-structured system prompts directly improve agent performance, consistency, and reliability.

  • System prompt = agent's foundational instruction set
  • Defines personality, role, tone, and limitations
  • Shapes interpretation of all user input
  • Directly impacts agent performance and consistency
  • Goes far beyond a technical detail; it is the agent's worldview
🎭
Role
Who the agent is and its expertise domain
🗣️
Tone
How the agent communicates (formal, casual, technical)
🚧
Boundaries
What the agent cannot or should not do
📐
Structure
How responses should be formatted

Takeaways

  • Treat system prompt design as a first-class engineering task, not an afterthought
  • Test prompts against edge cases to verify boundaries hold

Prompting Frameworks

Zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting trade off between prompt simplicity and model performance, with more examples yielding better but costlier results.

Three prompting frameworks define how much context the model receives. Zero-shot prompting provides no examples, relying entirely on the model's training. One-shot gives a single example to establish the pattern. Few-shot provides multiple examples for complex or nuanced tasks. The trade-off is between prompt size/cost and output quality; more examples generally improve performance but increase token usage.

  • Zero-shot: no examples, relies on model's inherent capability
  • One-shot: single example establishes the expected pattern
  • Few-shot: multiple examples for complex or nuanced tasks
  • More examples = better performance but higher token cost
  • Choose based on task complexity and required output precision
FrameworkExamples GivenBest ForTrade-off
Zero-shotNoneSimple, well-known tasksCheapest but least reliable
One-shot1Pattern establishmentGood balance for most tasks
Few-shot2-5+Complex/nuanced outputsMost reliable but costly

Takeaways

  • Start with zero-shot; add examples only when output quality is insufficient
  • Few-shot examples should cover edge cases, not just happy paths

Positive and Negative Prompting

Combining 'do this' (positive) and 'don't do this' (negative) instructions gives the model clear behavioral boundaries from both directions.

Beyond examples, explicit do/don't instructions improve model output. Positive prompting tells the model what to do (green lights for desired qualities and structure). Negative prompting tells the model what to avoid (red lights for unwanted behaviors). Combining both creates clear behavioral boundaries that reduce ambiguity and improve response consistency.

  • Positive prompting: instruct what the model SHOULD do
  • Negative prompting: instruct what the model should NOT do
  • Combining both reduces ambiguity significantly
  • Do/don't instructions complement examples (few-shot)
  • Particularly effective for tone, format, and boundary enforcement
TypePurposeExample
PositiveDefine desired behavior"Always cite sources", "Use bullet points"
NegativePrevent unwanted behavior"Never make up facts", "Don't use jargon"
CombinedComplete boundary definition"Be concise (do) but don't omit key details (don't)"

Takeaways

  • Always include both positive and negative instructions in system prompts
  • Negative prompts are especially important for safety-critical agents

Chain-of-Thought (CoT)

Forcing an LLM to show its reasoning steps dramatically improves answer accuracy and transparency.

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is a prompt engineering technique that instructs models to explain their reasoning step by step before delivering a final answer. Without CoT, a model might give a correct but unexplained response. With CoT, it breaks the problem into logical steps, enabling better accuracy on complex queries and giving users visibility into the decision process. This is especially effective for multi-constraint questions where the model must weigh trade-offs.

  • CoT prompts the model to articulate intermediate reasoning steps before concluding
  • Improves accuracy on multi-step or multi-constraint problems
  • Makes model outputs more transparent and debuggable
  • Can be triggered with phrases like "think step by step" or "explain your reasoning"
🧠
Without CoT
Model gives direct answer with no explanation of how it arrived there
🔗
With CoT
Model explains each reasoning step, improving accuracy and interpretability
🎯
Best For
Multi-constraint questions, math, logic puzzles, planning tasks

Takeaways

  • CoT is one of the simplest yet most effective prompt engineering techniques for improving LLM output quality
  • The technique trades token efficiency for accuracy and explainability
  • It forms a foundation for more advanced agentic reasoning patterns

Section Introduction

Agentic workflows are predefined architectural patterns that guide LLMs through structured multi-step processes without full autonomy.

This section covers the architecture patterns of critical agentic workflows, starting from the foundational augmented LLM and progressing through prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker, and evaluator-optimizer patterns. These workflows remain rigid structures where the LLM follows set patterns rather than making entirely independent decisions. They represent the middle ground between simple prompting and fully autonomous agents.

  • Agentic workflows are predefined structures, not fully autonomous agents
  • Progression: augmented LLM, prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker, evaluator-optimizer
  • Each pattern adds complexity and flexibility over the previous one
  • The LLM adheres to set patterns rather than making independent decisions
1

Augmented LLM

Foundation: LLM enhanced with retrieval, tools, and memory

2

Prompt Chaining

Breaking large tasks into sequential smaller steps

3

Advanced Workflows

Routing, parallelization, orchestrator-worker, evaluator-optimizer

Takeaways

  • Agentic workflows bridge the gap between simple prompting and full agent autonomy
  • Start with simpler patterns and increase complexity only when needed

The Augmented LLM

An LLM becomes truly powerful when augmented with retrieval, tools, and memory, forming the fundamental building block of all agentic systems.

The augmented LLM is the foundational building block of agentic systems. A base LLM is powerful alone, but augmenting it with three capabilities transforms it: retrieval (access to external data not in training), tools (APIs for specialized tasks like calculations, translations, or sending messages), and memory (ability to retain and recall information across interactions). This combination enables the LLM to operate beyond its static training data.

  • Retrieval: search and access external data not in the model's training set
  • Tools: invoke external APIs for specialized tasks (calculations, weather, messaging)
  • Memory: retain information across interactions for contextual continuity
  • All three augmentations together form the base unit for agentic architectures
🔍
Retrieval
Access external knowledge bases, documents, and real-time data beyond training cutoff
🔧
Tools
Call external APIs for calculations, translations, web searches, and actions
💾
Memory
Store and recall information across sessions for persistent context

Takeaways

  • The augmented LLM (retrieval + tools + memory) is the atomic unit of all agentic systems
  • Each augmentation addresses a specific LLM limitation: knowledge staleness, inability to act, and lack of persistence

Prompt Chaining

Break large tasks into sequential smaller steps where each step's output feeds into the next, dramatically improving quality on complex problems.

Prompt chaining addresses the limitation that LLMs cannot reliably handle very large tasks in a single pass. Instead of asking for a complete business plan or full textbook summary at once, the task is decomposed into sequential steps. Each step produces output that becomes input for the next. This approach improves quality by keeping each individual prompt focused and manageable, while the chain collectively solves the larger problem.

  • Decomposes large tasks into smaller, sequential LLM calls
  • Each step's output becomes the next step's input
  • Improves quality by keeping individual prompts focused
  • Ideal for business plans, research summaries, multi-part content generation
1

Decompose

Break the large task into logical sequential subtasks

2

Execute

Run each subtask through the LLM in order

3

Chain

Pass each output as context/input to the next step

Takeaways

  • When a task is too complex for one prompt, chaining multiple focused prompts yields far better results
  • The key design decision is how to decompose the task into the right sequence of steps

Routing

A router LLM dispatches queries to the most appropriate model or handler, optimizing for cost, speed, or capability per request.

Routing acknowledges that no single LLM is optimal for every situation. Some queries need cheap and fast models; others require advanced reasoning. A router LLM acts as a dispatcher, analyzing each incoming query and directing it to the most suitable model or specialized handler. This enables systems to balance cost, latency, and quality dynamically based on the specific demands of each request.

  • No single model is optimal for all queries; routing selects the best fit per request
  • A dispatcher LLM classifies queries and routes to specialized models
  • Enables cost optimization by using cheaper models for simple tasks
  • Allows fine-tuned models to handle domain-specific queries
💨
Fast/Cheap Route
Simple queries go to lightweight models for low-latency, low-cost responses
🧠
Reasoning Route
Complex queries go to powerful models with advanced reasoning capabilities
🎯
Specialist Route
Domain-specific queries go to fine-tuned models for that domain

Takeaways

  • Routing optimizes the cost-quality-latency trade-off by matching query complexity to model capability
  • The router itself is typically a lightweight classifier that adds minimal overhead

Parallelization

Split a task into independent subtasks and process them simultaneously to dramatically reduce response latency.

Parallelization addresses the critical user experience factor of response speed. Rather than processing subtasks sequentially, this workflow divides a task into independent components and distributes them across multiple LLM instances running concurrently. The results are then aggregated into a final response. This is effective when subtasks do not depend on each other's outputs and the number of parallel branches is known in advance.

  • Divides tasks into independent subtasks processed concurrently
  • Dramatically reduces total response time compared to sequential processing
  • Works when subtasks are independent and their count is known in advance
  • Results are aggregated after all parallel branches complete
AspectSequentialParallel
LatencySum of all subtask timesMax of any single subtask time
When to useSteps depend on each otherSteps are independent
ComplexitySimple linear flowRequires aggregation logic

Takeaways

  • Parallelization is the go-to pattern when subtasks are independent and latency matters
  • It differs from orchestrator-worker in that the number of subtasks is predetermined

Orchestrator-worker

An orchestrator LLM dynamically decomposes tasks and delegates to worker LLMs when the number of subtasks cannot be predicted in advance.

The orchestrator-worker workflow handles tasks where the required subtasks are not known upfront. An orchestrator LLM receives the user query, dynamically breaks it into subtasks, delegates each to worker LLMs, and then passes their outputs to a synthesizer LLM for final assembly. This differs from parallelization (where subtask count is fixed) by offering flexibility to adapt the decomposition based on the specific query.

  • Orchestrator receives query and dynamically determines required subtasks
  • Worker LLMs execute individual subtasks independently
  • Synthesizer LLM combines worker outputs into a coherent final response
  • Used when subtask count is unpredictable, unlike fixed parallelization
1

Orchestrator

Analyzes query and dynamically decomposes into subtasks

2

Workers

Execute delegated subtasks independently

3

Synthesizer

Combines worker outputs into final coherent response

Takeaways

  • Use orchestrator-worker when the number of subtasks depends on the specific input and cannot be hardcoded
  • The key differentiator from parallelization is dynamic (not predetermined) task decomposition

Evaluator-optimizer

A generator LLM produces solutions while an evaluator LLM critiques them, iterating until quality criteria are met.

The evaluator-optimizer pattern consists of two core components: a generator LLM that produces initial solutions, and an evaluator LLM that assesses the output against quality criteria and provides feedback. If the output does not meet standards, the evaluator sends it back with improvement suggestions, creating an iterative refinement loop. This continues until the evaluator approves the output or a maximum iteration count is reached.

  • Generator LLM produces candidate solutions based on the user query
  • Evaluator LLM assesses output quality and provides actionable feedback
  • Iterative loop continues until quality criteria are satisfied
  • Prevents infinite loops with a maximum iteration threshold
  • Mimics human creative workflows: draft, review, revise
✍️
Generator
Produces initial solution and incorporates evaluator feedback in subsequent iterations
🔍
Evaluator
Assesses output against criteria, provides specific improvement feedback
🔄
Loop
Iterates until quality threshold met or max iterations reached

Takeaways

  • The evaluator-optimizer is ideal for tasks where output quality is critical and iterative refinement improves results
  • Always include a maximum iteration cap to prevent infinite loops
  • This pattern naturally maps to human review workflows

Section Introduction

Single agent architectures give an LLM autonomy to plan, act, and self-correct within a loop, going beyond rigid workflows.

This section transitions from predefined agentic workflows to true single agent architectures. Having established the foundation of workflows and understood when to use agents versus workflows, the focus now shifts to architectures where a single agent operates with planning, action, and self-correction capabilities. These represent a step toward genuine autonomy.

  • Single agents go beyond rigid workflows by incorporating autonomous decision-making
  • Key architectures covered: reflection, ReAct, and Reflexion
  • Single agents typically include planning, tool use, and self-evaluation loops
  • Choosing the right architecture depends on the task requirements
1

Reflection

Self-evaluation of output quality

2

ReAct

Reasoning + acting with external tools

3

Reflexion

Learning from past attempts via episodic memory

Takeaways

  • Single agent architectures represent a meaningful step beyond workflows toward true AI autonomy
  • Each pattern addresses a different aspect: quality assurance, tool interaction, or learning from failures

When to Use a Single Agent Architecture

Use a single agent when the task requires autonomous reasoning and tool use but does not demand collaboration between multiple specialists.

Single agent architectures are appropriate when a task requires autonomous reasoning, planning, and tool use, but does not need multiple specialized agents collaborating. Common patterns include planning loops, tool interaction, and self-evaluation. A single agent excels at focused tasks where one coherent reasoning thread can solve the problem without external coordination overhead.

  • Single agents suit tasks that need autonomy but not multi-specialist collaboration
  • Common patterns: planning, tool use, reflection, and self-correction
  • Lower overhead than multi-agent systems for focused problems
  • Examples: code generation with testing, research with web search, document analysis
FactorSingle AgentMulti-Agent
Task scopeFocused, single-domainBroad, multi-domain
CoordinationNone neededEssential
OverheadLowHigher
Best forAutonomous focused workCollaborative complex tasks

Takeaways

  • Default to single agent architectures unless the task explicitly requires multiple specialists
  • Adding agents adds coordination complexity; justify the overhead with clear benefits

Reflection

A reflection agent generates a response, then critiques its own output to iteratively improve quality before delivering the final answer.

Reflection is a single agent architecture where the agent receives a user request, generates an initial response, and then self-evaluates whether the output meets quality standards. If it identifies shortcomings, it revises the response and re-evaluates, repeating until satisfied. This self-critique loop enables higher quality outputs without external evaluators or tools.

  • Agent generates an initial response then self-critiques it
  • Iterates on its own output until quality criteria are met
  • No external tools needed; purely internal reasoning loop
  • Effective for writing, code generation, and analysis tasks
1

Generate

Produce initial response to user request

2

Reflect

Critique own output against quality criteria

3

Revise

Improve based on self-identified weaknesses, repeat if needed

Takeaways

  • Reflection improves output quality through self-critique without requiring external tools or evaluators
  • It is the simplest single agent architecture and works well for generation tasks where quality is subjective

ReAct (Think-Do)

ReAct interleaves reasoning ("think") with tool actions ("do"), enabling the agent to ground its decisions in real external information.

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) differs from reflection by incorporating external tool use. Where reflection only self-evaluates outputs internally, ReAct allows the agent to reason about what action to take, execute that action (search, calculate, query), observe the result, and continue reasoning. This grounds the agent's decisions in real-world data rather than relying solely on internal knowledge.

  • Interleaves reasoning steps with concrete tool actions
  • Grounds decisions in real external data via observations
  • Differs from reflection: uses external tools, not just self-critique
  • Loop: Think (reason), Act (use tool), Observe (process result), repeat
💭
Think
Reason about current state and decide what action to take next
⚡
Act
Execute an external tool call (search, API, calculation)
👁️
Observe
Process the tool's response and incorporate into reasoning

Takeaways

  • ReAct is the standard pattern for agents that need to interact with external tools and data sources
  • The think-act-observe loop prevents hallucination by grounding reasoning in real observations

Reflexion

Reflexion extends ReAct by adding episodic memory, allowing the agent to learn from past failed attempts within the same task.

Reflexion closely resembles ReAct but adds a critical distinction: episodic memory. The agent reasons and acts like ReAct, but when it fails or produces suboptimal results, it stores a reflection about what went wrong. On subsequent attempts, it retrieves these reflections to avoid repeating mistakes. This creates a learning loop within a single task session, enabling progressive improvement.

  • Builds on ReAct by adding episodic memory of past attempts
  • Stores reflections about failures and mistakes
  • Retrieves past reflections to avoid repeating errors on retry
  • Enables learning within a single task session
PatternCore MechanismMemoryTools
ReflectionSelf-critique loopNoneNo
ReActThink-Act-ObserveNoneYes
ReflexionThink-Act-Observe + LearnEpisodicYes

Takeaways

  • Reflexion is the most capable single agent pattern, combining tool use with learning from mistakes
  • Episodic memory prevents the agent from repeating the same errors across attempts

Section Introduction

Planning patterns enable agents to create and follow structured plans before acting, bridging single agent architectures and multi-agent systems.

Before advancing to multi-agent systems, this section covers planning patterns as a critical capability for complex tasks. Planning allows agents to assess a problem, formulate a structured approach, and execute steps methodically. Topics include task decomposition, the importance of planning, plan-and-solve, ReWOO, and tree-of-thought patterns. These form the cognitive scaffolding that makes agents effective on non-trivial problems.

  • Planning is the bridge between single agent architectures and multi-agent systems
  • Enables structured approaches to complex, multi-step problems
  • Patterns covered: task decomposition, plan-and-solve, ReWOO, tree-of-thought
  • Not all tasks require planning; simple queries benefit from direct execution
1

Task Decomposition

Breaking complex tasks into manageable subtasks

2

Plan and Solve / ReWOO

Planning before execution, separating reasoning from observation

3

Tree of Thought

Exploring multiple reasoning paths with backtracking

Takeaways

  • Planning transforms agents from reactive responders into proactive problem solvers
  • Choose the planning pattern based on task complexity and the need for exploration vs. efficiency

Task Decomposition

Breaking a large task into smaller, manageable subtasks is the most fundamental planning skill for both humans and AI agents.

Task decomposition is the practice of breaking overwhelming tasks into smaller, manageable parts. Just as humans manage complex projects by creating subtask lists, AI agents benefit from decomposing problems before attempting solutions. Effective decomposition requires identifying the right granularity: too coarse and the subtasks remain unmanageable; too fine and coordination overhead dominates.

  • Large tasks become manageable when broken into focused subtasks
  • Granularity matters: balance between too coarse and too fine
  • Foundation skill that underlies all planning patterns
  • Agents can decompose tasks automatically or follow user-provided breakdowns
🎯
Right Granularity
Each subtask should be completable in one focused step without ambiguity
🔗
Dependencies
Identify which subtasks depend on others vs. which can run in parallel
✅
Verification
Each subtask should have clear completion criteria

Takeaways

  • Task decomposition is the prerequisite for all other planning patterns
  • The quality of decomposition directly determines the quality of execution

The Importance of Planning

Planning is essential for complex multi-step tasks but unnecessary overhead for simple, well-defined queries.

Not every task requires planning. Simple, well-defined queries can be answered directly. However, for complex tasks involving multiple steps, unknown constraints, or resource coordination, planning significantly improves outcomes. The analogy is travel: visiting a familiar nearby city needs no plan, but exploring an unfamiliar country benefits enormously from advance planning. Agents should dynamically decide whether a task warrants planning overhead.

  • Planning adds value for complex, multi-step, or unfamiliar tasks
  • Simple queries are better served by direct execution without planning overhead
  • Good agents dynamically assess whether planning is warranted
  • Planning reduces wasted effort and improves resource allocation
Task TypePlanning Needed?Example
Simple lookupNo"What's the capital of France?"
Multi-step researchYes"Compare 5 frameworks for our use case"
Creative generationSometimesShort poem (no) vs. novel chapter (yes)

Takeaways

  • The decision of whether to plan is itself a critical agent capability
  • Over-planning simple tasks wastes tokens and time; under-planning complex tasks produces poor results

Plan and Solve

The agent first creates an explicit plan (assessing task, resources, constraints), then executes it step by step.

Plan-and-solve operates in two distinct stages. First, the agent plans by assessing the task, identifying available resources, and considering constraints. Second, it executes the plan step by step. This separation ensures the agent has a coherent strategy before taking action, reducing wasted effort and improving coherence of the final output. The plan itself can be revised if execution reveals new information.

  • Two-stage approach: explicit planning phase followed by execution phase
  • Planning assesses task scope, available resources, and constraints
  • Execution follows the plan step by step with potential mid-course corrections
  • Separation prevents premature action and improves output coherence
1

Assess

Understand the task, identify resources, note constraints

2

Plan

Create explicit step-by-step strategy

3

Solve

Execute each planned step, adapting if needed

Takeaways

  • Separating planning from execution prevents agents from acting without a coherent strategy
  • Plans should remain flexible enough to adapt when execution reveals new information

ReWOO

ReWOO (Reasoning Without Observation) separates the planning/reasoning phase entirely from tool execution, reducing LLM calls and cost.

ReWOO (Reasoning Without Observation) separates reasoning from tool execution. Unlike ReAct where reasoning and observation interleave, ReWOO has a planner that creates the full plan upfront (including which tools to call and in what order), then a worker executes all tool calls, and finally a solver synthesizes the results. This reduces the number of LLM invocations since the planner does not wait for observations between steps.

  • Planner creates the complete plan before any tool execution begins
  • Worker executes all planned tool calls without LLM reasoning between them
  • Solver synthesizes tool outputs into the final answer
  • Fewer LLM calls than ReAct, reducing cost and latency
AspectReActReWOO
Reasoning/ActionInterleavedSeparated
LLM callsOne per think-act cycleTwo total (plan + solve)
AdaptabilityHigh (reacts to observations)Lower (plan is fixed)
CostHigherLower

Takeaways

  • ReWOO trades adaptability for efficiency by planning all steps before executing any
  • Best for tasks where the required tool calls can be predicted upfront without needing intermediate results

Tree of Thought

Tree of Thought explores multiple reasoning paths simultaneously and backtracks from dead ends, combining planning with exploratory search.

Tree of Thought (ToT) merges planning with exploratory search. Unlike linear chain-of-thought, ToT generates multiple candidate reasoning paths at each step, evaluates them, and pursues the most promising branches while pruning or backtracking from dead ends. This is particularly effective for problems with multiple valid approaches where the best path is not obvious upfront, such as puzzle solving, creative writing, or strategic planning.

  • Generates multiple reasoning paths (branches) at each decision point
  • Evaluates branches and prunes unpromising ones
  • Supports backtracking when a path leads to a dead end
  • Combines planning with search, unlike linear CoT
  • Best for problems with multiple potential solution paths
🌳
Branching
Generate multiple candidate next-steps at each decision point
✂️
Pruning
Evaluate and discard unpromising branches early
↩️
Backtracking
Return to previous decision point when current path fails

Takeaways

  • ToT is the most powerful planning pattern for problems where the optimal path is unclear
  • It is more expensive than linear approaches but excels at complex reasoning tasks
  • Not every problem needs ToT; use it when simpler patterns produce dead ends

Section Introduction

Multi-agent systems enable specialized agents to collaborate on complex tasks that exceed any single agent's capabilities.

This section covers multi-agent system designs, building on the foundation of workflows, single agent architectures, and planning patterns. Multi-agent systems shine when tasks require diverse expertise, parallel workstreams, or collaborative refinement. Topics include when to choose single vs. multi-agent, vertical vs. horizontal architectures, group conversation challenges, and specific patterns like supervisor, hierarchical teams, and dynamic teams.

  • Multi-agent systems enable collaboration among specialized agents
  • Build on all previous concepts: workflows, single agents, planning
  • Key decisions: vertical vs. horizontal, static vs. dynamic composition
  • Introduce coordination overhead that must be justified by task complexity
1

Architecture Choice

Vertical (leader-directed) vs. horizontal (peer collaboration)

2

Patterns

Supervisor, hierarchical teams, dynamic teams

3

Challenges

Group conversations, coordination overhead, resource efficiency

Takeaways

  • Multi-agent systems are the next logical step when single agents hit capability limits
  • The coordination overhead must be justified; do not default to multi-agent when single agent suffices

When to Use Single vs. Multi-agent Systems

Use single agents for focused tasks one specialist can handle; use multi-agent when the task genuinely requires diverse expertise collaborating.

The choice between single and multi-agent systems depends on whether the task requires collaboration among multiple specialists. A social media manager can independently create a post (single agent), but an omnichannel campaign needs a copywriter, designer, ads specialist, and manager working together (multi-agent). The key criterion is whether the task demands diverse expertise that cannot reasonably reside in one agent's context.

  • Single agent: task completable by one focused specialist
  • Multi-agent: task requires diverse expertise and collaboration
  • Multi-agent adds communication and coordination overhead
  • Default to single agent unless collaboration clearly adds value
CriterionSingle AgentMulti-Agent
Expertise neededOne domainMultiple domains
ExampleWrite a blog postLaunch marketing campaign
OverheadMinimalCoordination cost
ScalabilityLimited by contextScales with agent count

Takeaways

  • The litmus test: does this task genuinely require multiple specialists, or can one focused agent handle it?
  • Over-engineering with multi-agent systems when single agent suffices wastes resources and adds failure modes

Vertical vs Horizontal Architectures

Vertical architectures have a clear leader directing agents (faster decisions); horizontal architectures have peer agents collaborating as equals (more creative but slower).

Multi-agent systems split into two structural categories. Vertical architectures feature a single leader that assigns tasks, approves outputs, and coordinates the group. Horizontal architectures have agents operating as peers, collaborating in shared conversations without a designated authority. Vertical offers lower latency for decisions due to clear authority; horizontal enables more creative collaboration but risks inefficiency from unstructured communication.

  • Vertical: single leader assigns tasks, approves outputs, clear chain of command
  • Horizontal: peer agents collaborate without designated authority
  • Vertical has lower decision latency; horizontal enables richer collaboration
  • Vertical suits execution-focused tasks; horizontal suits creative/exploratory ones
📊
Vertical
Leader directs, agents report up. Fast decisions, clear accountability.
🤝
Horizontal
Peers collaborate as equals. Richer ideas, higher coordination cost.

Takeaways

  • Choose vertical when speed and clear task ownership matter; choose horizontal when creative collaboration adds value
  • Many production systems use hybrid approaches with vertical structure and selective horizontal collaboration

Challenges with Group Conversations

Multi-agent group conversations introduce inefficiency through unnecessary chatter, context pollution, and resource waste that single agents avoid entirely.

Single agents maintain focus by working independently without external distractions. Multi-agent systems face group conversation challenges: agents engage in unnecessary pleasantries, waste tokens on casual exchanges, and pollute shared context with irrelevant information. When multiple agents read the same thread, resource use increases and latency grows. These challenges require careful conversation design, message filtering, and structured protocols to mitigate.

  • Agents waste tokens on pleasantries and unnecessary social exchanges
  • Shared conversation threads cause context pollution for all participants
  • Multiple agents reading the same thread increases cost linearly
  • Single agents avoid all these issues by maintaining independent focus
  • Mitigation: structured protocols, message filtering, scoped conversations
💬
Chatter
Agents waste tokens on social exchanges and redundant acknowledgments
🌫️
Context Pollution
Irrelevant messages fill shared context, reducing signal-to-noise ratio
💰
Resource Waste
Every agent reading the full thread multiplies token costs

Takeaways

  • Group conversation overhead is the primary cost of multi-agent systems; design protocols to minimize it
  • Consider whether the collaboration benefit outweighs the coordination cost before choosing multi-agent

Supervisor

A supervisor agent coordinates multiple worker agents by assigning tasks, reviewing outputs, and maintaining overall coherence, similar to the routing workflow but with richer oversight.

The supervisor pattern features a central agent that coordinates subordinate agents. It resembles the routing workflow but with deeper oversight: the supervisor not only routes tasks but also reviews outputs, provides feedback, and ensures coherence across the work of multiple agents. This is a classic top-down vertical architecture where the supervisor maintains the overall vision while workers focus on execution.

  • Central supervisor assigns tasks, reviews outputs, ensures coherence
  • Similar to routing but with richer feedback and quality control
  • Classic top-down vertical architecture
  • Supervisor maintains big-picture vision; workers focus on execution
1

Receive

Supervisor receives user query and decomposes into agent tasks

2

Delegate

Assigns subtasks to appropriate specialist agents

3

Review

Evaluates agent outputs, provides feedback, synthesizes final result

Takeaways

  • The supervisor pattern is the most natural entry point for multi-agent systems due to its clear authority structure
  • It works well for teams of 4-7 agents; beyond that, consider hierarchical teams

Hierarchical Teams

When a single supervisor cannot effectively manage all agents, introduce middle-management layers with team leads supervising sub-groups.

Hierarchical teams extend the supervisor pattern for larger organizations. Just as a growing company needs department managers between the CEO and employees, complex multi-agent systems need intermediate supervisors. Each team lead manages a small group of specialists, and reports to a higher-level supervisor. This enables scaling to many agents while keeping each supervisor's span of control manageable.

  • Extends supervisor pattern with intermediate management layers
  • Each team lead manages a small group and reports upward
  • Enables scaling beyond the 4-7 agent limit of flat supervision
  • Mirrors real organizational structures with departments and team leads
👔
Top Supervisor
Sets overall strategy, delegates to team leads, synthesizes final output
👥
Team Leads
Manage specialist sub-groups, ensure quality within their domain
⚙️
Specialists
Execute focused tasks within their expertise area

Takeaways

  • Hierarchical teams solve the scalability limitation of flat supervisor patterns
  • Each management layer adds latency; use only when scale demands it

Dynamic Teams

Dynamic teams assemble, disassemble, and reconfigure agents on-the-fly based on changing task requirements, combining vertical authority with flexible composition.

Dynamic teams are a flexible pattern where team composition changes based on current needs. Agents are added, removed, or reassigned as workload and requirements shift. Despite this fluidity, an authority layer still assigns tasks, making this a vertical architecture variant. Dynamic teams suit situations where the required expertise changes throughout a task's lifecycle, or where workload fluctuates unpredictably.

  • Team composition changes dynamically based on current needs
  • Agents are added, removed, or reassigned as requirements shift
  • Still maintains an authority layer for task assignment (vertical)
  • Suits tasks where required expertise changes over time
PatternCompositionBest For
SupervisorFixed small teamStable, well-defined tasks
HierarchicalFixed large teamComplex tasks needing many specialists
DynamicFluid, reconfigurableTasks with changing requirements

Takeaways

  • Dynamic teams offer maximum flexibility at the cost of additional orchestration complexity
  • They combine vertical authority with the ability to adapt team composition to evolving task needs

Section Introduction

Once an agent architecture is running, the real challenges are execution management, cost/latency optimization, and error recovery.

This section addresses operational concerns that apply to every agent architecture: asynchronous task execution, performance metrics (cost and latency), and error handling strategies. Regardless of whether you chose a single agent or multi-agent design, these challenges will arise in production. Understanding them early enables building resilient systems that handle failures gracefully and operate within budget constraints.

  • Asynchronous execution enables non-blocking task processing
  • Cost and latency are the primary performance metrics for production agents
  • Error handling and recovery strategies prevent cascading failures
  • These concerns are architecture-agnostic and universally applicable
⚡
Async Execution
Non-blocking task processing for better throughput and responsiveness
📊
Performance
Monitoring and optimizing cost per query and response latency
🛡️
Reliability
Error handling, retries, fallbacks, and graceful degradation

Takeaways

  • Architecture design is only half the battle; operational excellence determines production success
  • Plan for failure from the start: every tool call can fail, every LLM call can timeout

Agents and Asyncronous Task Execution

Parallel task execution through multi-agent systems is the primary lever for reducing end-to-end latency in complex AI workflows.

Sequential task execution bottlenecks AI systems the same way single-worker pipelines bottleneck physical work. Multi-agent architectures split tasks into independent sub-problems executed concurrently by separate agents, dramatically reducing total completion time. The key architectural decision is identifying which sub-tasks have no dependencies and can run in parallel versus those requiring sequential ordering.

  • Sequential execution limits throughput to the speed of a single agent
  • Asynchronous execution splits independent sub-tasks across multiple agents running in parallel
  • The speedup is bounded by the task's inherent sequential dependencies (Amdahl's Law applies)
  • Multi-agent systems introduce coordination overhead that must be managed
⏱️
Sequential
One agent handles all steps in order; simple but slow
⚡
Parallel
Multiple agents execute independent sub-tasks simultaneously
🔗
Dependencies
Tasks with input/output coupling must remain sequential
📊
Speedup
Proportional to ratio of parallelizable vs sequential work

Takeaways

  • Design agent workflows by first mapping task dependencies to identify parallelizable segments
  • Multi-agent parallelism trades coordination complexity for latency reduction
  • Not all tasks benefit equally; highly sequential workflows see diminishing returns

Performance Metrics - Latency and Cost

Agent performance in production is governed by two metrics: latency (speed of response) and cost (token/API expenditure per task).

Once an agent system is validated for correctness, production deployment requires optimizing for latency and cost. Latency decomposes into model inference latency (determined by model size and provider infrastructure) and orchestration overhead (routing, tool calls, retries). Cost scales with token consumption and API call volume. Selecting smaller models where accuracy permits, caching frequent queries, and minimizing unnecessary tool invocations are the primary optimization levers.

  • Latency = model inference time + orchestration overhead
  • Model inference latency depends on model size and provider infrastructure
  • Cost is driven by input/output token volume and per-call API pricing
  • Smaller models reduce both latency and cost when task complexity allows
  • Caching and batching reduce redundant computation
MetricComponentsOptimization Strategy
LatencyInference + OrchestrationSmaller models, parallel tool calls, caching
CostTokens + API callsPrompt compression, model tiering, batch requests
TradeoffSpeed vs AccuracyUse fast models for routing, powerful models for reasoning

Takeaways

  • Profile latency by component (inference vs orchestration) to target the right bottleneck
  • Right-size model selection: use the smallest model that meets accuracy requirements
  • Monitor cost per task, not just per token, to capture orchestration overhead

Error Handling and Recovery

Robust agent systems require explicit error handling at every integration point because failures in LLMs, APIs, and inter-agent communication are inevitable.

Agent systems depend on multiple interconnected components: LLM inference, external tool APIs, and inter-agent messaging. Each connection point is a potential failure source. Error handling strategies include retry with exponential backoff for transient failures, graceful degradation when non-critical tools are unavailable, fallback models when primary inference fails, and circuit breakers to prevent cascade failures across the system.

  • Agents have multiple failure points: LLM, APIs, tools, and inter-agent communication
  • More sophisticated systems have proportionally more failure modes
  • Retry logic with backoff handles transient errors without overwhelming services
  • Graceful degradation allows partial functionality when components fail
  • Circuit breakers prevent cascade failures across interconnected agents
1

Detect

Identify failure type: transient (timeout, rate limit) vs permanent (invalid input, missing resource)

2

Recover

Apply appropriate strategy: retry with backoff, use fallback model, or degrade gracefully

3

Log & Alert

Record failure context for debugging; alert operators if recovery fails

4

Resume

Continue execution from last successful checkpoint or return partial results

Takeaways

  • Design for failure: assume every external call can fail and define recovery behavior
  • Implement layered error handling (retry, fallback, degrade, alert) at each integration point
  • Test failure modes explicitly; reliability engineering is as important as feature development

Section Introduction

Memory transforms stateless AI agents into learning systems that retain and leverage information across interactions.

Without memory, agents treat every interaction as independent, losing all context and learned insights between sessions. Adding memory components enables agents to build on past interactions, recall user preferences, and avoid repeating mistakes. Memory architectures range from simple short-term context buffers to sophisticated vector store retrieval systems, each suited to different retention needs and access patterns.

  • Stateless agents forget everything between interactions, limiting their utility
  • Memory enables learning from past interactions and personalizing responses
  • Different memory types serve different retention horizons and access patterns
  • Memory architecture choice depends on what information must persist and how it will be retrieved
💬
Short-Term
Context buffer within a single conversation session
📚
Vector Store RAG
Long-term retrieval from embedded document collections
👤
Entity Memory
Persistent facts about specific people, products, or concepts
📖
Episodic Memory
Records of past interaction episodes for pattern recognition

Takeaways

  • Memory is what separates simple tools from intelligent assistants
  • Choose memory type based on information lifecycle: ephemeral, session-scoped, or permanent
  • Start with the simplest memory type that solves your use case before adding complexity

Short-term Context Buffer

Short-term context buffers are the simplest memory mechanism: explicitly passing recent conversation history with each API call to maintain conversational continuity.

LLM APIs are stateless by default; each call has no knowledge of previous interactions. A short-term context buffer solves this by appending the last N messages to every request, giving the model conversational context. The tradeoff is between context depth (more messages = better continuity) and token cost/latency (more messages = higher expense and slower inference).

  • LLM APIs are stateless; memory must be explicitly managed by the application
  • Short-term buffer retains the last N messages and passes them with each request
  • Window size is a direct tradeoff between context quality and token cost
  • Simple to implement but limited: oldest messages are lost as the buffer rolls forward
  • Suitable for conversational continuity within a single session
1

Receive

User sends a new message to the agent

2

Prepend

Attach the last N messages from history to the new request

3

Infer

Send combined context + new message to the LLM for response

4

Store

Append both user message and agent response to the rolling buffer, trimming oldest if over limit

Takeaways

  • Always implement at minimum a short-term buffer for any conversational agent
  • Tune buffer size based on task complexity and budget constraints
  • For information that must persist beyond the buffer window, use long-term memory systems

Vector store RAG

Vector store RAG overcomes context window limits by retrieving only the most relevant information from a large knowledge base using semantic similarity search.

Short-term buffers are limited by the context window size. Vector store RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) solves this by embedding documents into a vector database and retrieving only semantically relevant chunks at query time. This gives agents access to arbitrarily large knowledge bases while keeping prompt size manageable. The retrieval step uses embedding similarity to find the most relevant passages, which are then injected into the prompt as context.

  • Short-term buffers cannot scale to large knowledge bases due to context window limits
  • RAG embeds documents into vectors and retrieves relevant chunks via similarity search
  • Only the most relevant information is injected into the prompt, keeping costs low
  • Enables access to unbounded external knowledge without fine-tuning the model
  • Retrieval quality depends on chunking strategy and embedding model choice
1

Embed

Convert documents into vector representations using an embedding model

2

Store

Index vectors in a vector database (Pinecone, Chroma, FAISS, etc.)

3

Query

Convert user query to a vector and find nearest neighbors in the store

4

Augment

Inject retrieved chunks into the LLM prompt as context

5

Generate

LLM produces response grounded in retrieved information

Takeaways

  • Use RAG when agents need access to more information than fits in a context window
  • Invest in chunking and embedding quality; retrieval accuracy determines answer quality
  • RAG is complementary to short-term memory, not a replacement

Entity-level Memory

Entity memory tracks structured facts about specific entities (people, products, concepts) across conversations, enabling personalized and contextually aware interactions.

Entity memory maintains a structured knowledge store of facts about specific entities mentioned in conversations. Unlike buffer memory (which stores raw messages) or RAG (which retrieves document chunks), entity memory extracts and updates discrete facts: 'User prefers dark mode', 'Client X has budget constraint of $50K'. This enables agents to personalize responses and maintain relationship context without re-asking for information already provided.

  • Stores structured facts about named entities (people, organizations, products)
  • Facts are extracted from conversations and updated incrementally
  • Enables personalization without requiring users to repeat preferences
  • More structured than RAG: discrete key-value facts rather than text chunks
  • Useful for CRM-style applications, personal assistants, and support bots
Memory TypeWhat It StoresBest For
Short-Term BufferLast N raw messagesConversational continuity within session
Vector Store RAGDocument chunks (embedded)Large knowledge base access
Entity MemoryStructured facts per entityPersonalization and relationship tracking

Takeaways

  • Use entity memory when your agent needs to track evolving facts about specific subjects
  • Combine with short-term buffer for immediate context and RAG for broad knowledge
  • Design extraction logic carefully to avoid storing incorrect or outdated facts

Section Introduction

Self-reflection and human oversight are the two primary mechanisms for ensuring agent systems remain aligned, safe, and effective in production.

As agent systems grow more autonomous, ensuring they operate correctly and safely becomes critical. This section covers evaluation and governance patterns: self-reflection (agents checking their own work), human-in-the-loop (escalating uncertain decisions to humans), guardrails (hard constraints on behavior), and monitoring (ongoing observation of system health). These patterns form the safety and quality layer above core agent logic.

  • Autonomous agents require explicit governance mechanisms to maintain alignment
  • Self-reflection enables agents to catch and correct their own errors
  • Human-in-the-loop provides a safety net for high-stakes or uncertain decisions
  • Guardrails enforce hard boundaries that agents cannot cross regardless of reasoning
  • Monitoring provides ongoing visibility into system behavior and drift
🪞
Self-Reflection
Agent evaluates its own outputs for quality and correctness
🧑‍💼
Human-in-the-Loop
Escalate uncertain or high-stakes decisions to humans
🚧
Guardrails
Hard constraints preventing dangerous or invalid actions
📡
Monitoring
Continuous observation of behavior, performance, and drift

Takeaways

  • Layer governance mechanisms proportional to the autonomy and risk level of the agent
  • No single governance pattern is sufficient alone; combine multiple approaches
  • Design governance as a first-class system component, not an afterthought

Self-reflection

Self-reflection is an agent's ability to evaluate its own outputs, detect errors, and iteratively improve responses before delivering them.

Self-reflection adds an evaluation loop where the agent critiques its own output against quality criteria before finalizing. The agent generates a response, then applies a separate reasoning pass to check for errors, hallucinations, or logical inconsistencies. If issues are detected, it regenerates or refines the output. This pattern improves quality at the cost of additional inference calls.

  • Self-reflection adds an internal critique step after initial generation
  • The agent checks its own output for errors, consistency, and completeness
  • Failed self-checks trigger regeneration or refinement loops
  • Improves quality but increases latency and cost due to extra inference passes
  • Can be implemented as a separate prompt or a structured evaluation rubric
1

Generate

Agent produces initial response to the task

2

Critique

Separate evaluation pass checks output against quality criteria

3

Decide

If criteria met, deliver output; if not, identify specific issues

4

Refine

Regenerate or edit the response addressing identified issues, then re-evaluate

Takeaways

  • Use self-reflection for high-stakes outputs where correctness matters more than speed
  • Limit reflection iterations (2-3 max) to prevent infinite loops
  • Define explicit evaluation criteria so the reflection step has clear pass/fail conditions

Human-in-the-loop

Human-in-the-loop patterns route uncertain, high-risk, or novel decisions to human reviewers, maintaining safety without sacrificing automation for routine tasks.

Not all agent decisions should be fully autonomous. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) patterns define escalation criteria: when confidence is low, stakes are high, or the situation is novel, the agent pauses and requests human review. This preserves automation benefits for routine tasks while ensuring critical decisions get human judgment. Implementation requires clear escalation triggers, efficient handoff interfaces, and mechanisms to incorporate human feedback.

  • HITL routes uncertain or high-stakes decisions to human reviewers
  • Escalation triggers can be confidence-based, rule-based, or risk-scored
  • Routine low-risk tasks remain fully automated for efficiency
  • Human feedback should be captured and used to improve future agent decisions
  • The handoff interface must provide sufficient context for efficient human review
1

Assess

Agent evaluates task confidence and risk level against escalation thresholds

2

Route

High confidence + low risk = autonomous; low confidence or high risk = escalate

3

Handoff

Present human reviewer with context, proposed action, and uncertainty factors

4

Incorporate

Apply human decision, log the outcome, and update escalation model

Takeaways

  • Define explicit escalation criteria based on confidence thresholds and risk levels
  • Design the human review interface to minimize decision time (show context, not raw data)
  • Use human decisions as training signal to gradually expand autonomous coverage

Governance Patterns

Governance patterns define the organizational rules, permissions, and oversight structures that control how agents operate within enterprise boundaries.

Governance goes beyond individual agent behavior to address systemic concerns: who can deploy agents, what data they can access, how decisions are audited, and how accountability is maintained. Governance patterns include role-based access control for agent capabilities, audit trails for all agent actions, approval workflows for deploying new agent behaviors, and compliance frameworks ensuring agents operate within regulatory requirements.

  • Governance defines organizational boundaries for agent deployment and operation
  • Role-based access controls what data and tools each agent can use
  • Audit trails provide accountability and enable post-hoc review of agent decisions
  • Approval workflows gate deployment of new agent capabilities
  • Compliance frameworks ensure regulatory requirements are met automatically
🔐
Access Control
Role-based permissions limiting agent capabilities and data access
📋
Audit Trails
Complete logging of all agent actions and decisions for review
✅
Approval Workflows
Gated deployment process for new agent behaviors
⚖️
Compliance
Automated enforcement of regulatory and policy requirements

Takeaways

  • Implement governance before scaling agent deployment, not after incidents occur
  • Every agent action should be logged with sufficient context for audit
  • Treat agent permissions like human permissions: principle of least privilege applies

Guardrails and Policy Enforcement

Guardrails are hard-coded constraints that prevent agents from taking specific harmful or invalid actions, regardless of what the LLM reasoning produces.

Unlike soft governance patterns that guide behavior, guardrails are absolute constraints that cannot be overridden by agent reasoning. They operate as filters on agent inputs and outputs: content filters block harmful text, action validators prevent dangerous tool calls, and output sanitizers remove sensitive information. Guardrails are implemented as deterministic code (not LLM-based) to ensure they cannot be bypassed through prompt injection or adversarial inputs.

  • Guardrails are deterministic constraints, not LLM-based suggestions
  • They filter inputs (block harmful prompts) and outputs (sanitize responses)
  • Cannot be bypassed by clever prompting or adversarial attacks
  • Examples: PII redaction, action whitelisting, content safety filters, rate limits
  • Implemented as code layers wrapping the agent, not as prompt instructions
1

Input Filter

Screen incoming requests for policy violations, injection attempts, or harmful content

2

Action Validator

Check proposed tool calls against an allowlist before execution

3

Output Sanitizer

Remove PII, sensitive data, or policy-violating content from responses

4

Rate Limiter

Enforce usage bounds to prevent resource abuse or runaway loops

Takeaways

  • Never rely on prompt-based safety alone; implement guardrails as deterministic code
  • Apply guardrails on both input and output paths for defense in depth
  • Design guardrails to fail closed: if uncertain, block rather than allow

Cost-limiter

Cost limiters cap agent spending by tracking cumulative token/API usage and halting execution when budget thresholds are reached.

Without explicit cost controls, agent systems can incur runaway expenses through infinite loops, excessive retries, or verbose reasoning chains. Cost limiters track cumulative spending (tokens consumed, API calls made, compute time) and enforce hard stops when predefined budgets are exceeded. Implementation involves per-task budgets, per-session caps, and organization-wide spending alerts with automatic shutdown triggers.

  • Agents without cost limits can incur unbounded expenses through loops or verbose reasoning
  • Cost limiters track cumulative token usage and API call counts
  • Budget enforcement operates at multiple levels: per-task, per-session, per-organization
  • Hard stops prevent budget overrun; soft alerts enable early intervention
  • Include cost tracking in logging for post-hoc analysis and optimization
LevelMechanismAction on Breach
Per-TaskToken/call budget per individual taskHalt task, return partial result
Per-SessionCumulative budget across all tasks in sessionEnd session, notify user
Per-OrganizationDaily/monthly spending ceilingAlert admin, throttle all agents

Takeaways

  • Always implement cost limits before deploying agents to production
  • Set per-task budgets based on expected complexity with a reasonable margin
  • Monitor cost patterns over time to identify optimization opportunities and anomalies

A/B Shadow Testing

A/B shadow testing validates new agent versions by running them alongside production and comparing outputs before switching live traffic.

Deploying agent updates directly to production carries risk. A/B shadow testing mitigates this by running the new version in parallel with the current one, comparing outputs without exposing users to the experimental version. Shadow mode processes real requests through both systems, logs differences, and flags regressions. Only after demonstrating equivalent or superior performance does the new version graduate to serve live users.

  • Shadow testing runs new agent versions on real traffic without user exposure
  • Both old and new versions process the same requests; only the old version serves users
  • Output differences are logged and analyzed for regressions
  • Graduation criteria: match or exceed baseline on key metrics over a defined period
  • Catches edge cases that offline benchmarks miss by using real production traffic
1

Deploy Shadow

Run new agent version alongside production, processing same requests

2

Compare

Log output differences between old and new versions on identical inputs

3

Analyze

Evaluate regression patterns, identify failure modes unique to new version

4

Graduate

If metrics meet criteria over sufficient volume, promote to production

Takeaways

  • Never deploy agent updates directly to 100% of traffic; use staged rollout
  • Define clear graduation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, error rate) before starting the test
  • Shadow testing is complementary to offline benchmarks, not a replacement

Bias and Fairness Systems

Bias and fairness systems detect and mitigate systematic disparities in agent outputs across demographic groups or sensitive categories.

AI agents can inherit and amplify biases present in training data or system design. Bias and fairness systems audit agent outputs for systematic disparities across protected categories. Detection methods include statistical parity testing, counterfactual analysis (varying only the sensitive attribute), and outcome distribution audits. Mitigation strategies range from data rebalancing and prompt engineering to post-processing filters that equalize outcomes.

  • Agents can inherit biases from training data, tool outputs, and system design
  • Bias detection uses statistical tests on output distributions across groups
  • Counterfactual testing varies sensitive attributes while holding all else constant
  • Mitigation approaches: data rebalancing, prompt debiasing, output post-processing
  • Fairness metrics must be defined per use case; no single definition fits all contexts
1

Define

Establish fairness criteria and protected categories for your use case

2

Measure

Audit output distributions across groups using statistical parity tests

3

Test

Run counterfactual evaluations varying sensitive attributes

4

Mitigate

Apply corrections (prompt engineering, post-processing, data fixes) and re-measure

Takeaways

  • Proactively audit agent outputs for bias before deployment, not just after complaints
  • Use counterfactual testing: would the output change if only the demographic attribute changed?
  • Document fairness criteria and measurement methodology for accountability

Section Introduction

Agent evaluation requires measuring both task completion accuracy and operational efficiency across standardized benchmarks and real-world metrics.

Evaluating agent systems is more complex than evaluating simple models because agents interact with environments, use tools, and produce multi-step outputs. This section covers offline benchmarks (standardized test suites measuring capability), online metrics (production telemetry measuring real-world performance), and the relationship between them. Effective evaluation combines both approaches.

  • Agent evaluation is harder than model evaluation due to multi-step, tool-using behavior
  • Offline benchmarks test capabilities in controlled, reproducible conditions
  • Online metrics measure real-world performance with actual users and data
  • Benchmarks and production metrics often diverge; both are necessary
  • Evaluation should cover accuracy, efficiency, safety, and user satisfaction
Evaluation TypeEnvironmentStrengthsLimitations
Offline BenchmarksControlled test suiteReproducible, comparableMay not reflect production conditions
Online MetricsLive productionReal-world validityNoisy, harder to attribute causally
Human EvaluationExpert reviewCaptures nuance and qualityExpensive, slow, subjective

Takeaways

  • Never rely solely on benchmarks; production behavior can differ significantly
  • Define evaluation criteria before building, not after deployment
  • Track both capability metrics (can it solve the task?) and efficiency metrics (at what cost?)

How to Measure Agent Performance

Agent performance measurement must capture task success rate, efficiency (steps/tokens), quality of outputs, and alignment with user intent across diverse scenarios.

Measuring agent performance requires metrics across multiple dimensions: did the agent complete the task (success rate), how efficiently (steps taken, tokens consumed, time elapsed), how well (output quality scored by evaluators), and how aligned with user intent (did it solve what the user actually needed). A comprehensive framework combines these dimensions with stratification across task types and difficulty levels.

  • Success rate alone is insufficient; efficiency and quality matter equally
  • Measure steps-to-completion and token usage as efficiency proxies
  • Output quality requires either human evaluation or calibrated automated scorers
  • Intent alignment captures whether the agent solved the real problem vs the literal request
  • Stratify metrics by task type and difficulty to identify specific weaknesses
✅
Success Rate
Percentage of tasks completed correctly end-to-end
⚡
Efficiency
Steps taken, tokens consumed, and wall-clock time per task
⭐
Quality
Output quality scored by evaluators on defined rubrics
🎯
Alignment
Degree to which output matches user's actual intent and needs

Takeaways

  • Build evaluation dashboards that show success, efficiency, and quality together
  • Invest in automated evaluation methods to enable frequent, scalable measurement
  • Use failure analysis (examining wrong answers) to drive targeted improvements

Offline Benchmarks

Offline benchmarks provide controlled, reproducible evaluation of agent capabilities using standardized task suites with known correct answers.

Offline benchmarks evaluate agents against curated test suites where correct answers are predefined. Popular agent benchmarks test tool use, multi-step reasoning, code generation, and instruction following. They enable comparing different architectures under identical conditions. However, benchmark performance does not guarantee production performance due to distribution shift between curated test cases and real-world inputs.

  • Benchmarks use curated test cases with known correct answers for reproducible evaluation
  • Common dimensions: tool use accuracy, multi-step planning, code correctness, instruction following
  • Enable controlled comparison across architectures and configurations
  • Distribution shift means benchmark scores may not predict production performance
  • Benchmarks should be updated regularly to prevent overfitting
Benchmark AspectStrengthLimitation
ReproducibilitySame test, same conditions every runReal world is not reproducible
CoverageTests many capability dimensionsCannot cover all edge cases
ComparabilityFair comparison across systemsMay incentivize benchmark gaming

Takeaways

  • Use benchmarks for development iteration and architecture comparison, not as deployment gates
  • Build custom benchmarks that reflect your specific use case distribution
  • Complement benchmarks with production metrics to validate real-world performance

Online Metrics

Online metrics track real production performance (latency, error rate, user satisfaction, task completion) providing ground truth about how agents behave with actual users.

Once deployed, agents must be monitored through online metrics: real-time telemetry capturing latency distributions, error rates, task completion rates, user satisfaction signals, and cost per interaction. Online metrics reveal issues invisible to benchmarks: edge cases from real user behavior, integration failures, and performance degradation over time. Dashboards and alerting systems enable rapid detection and response.

  • Online metrics capture real production behavior that benchmarks cannot simulate
  • Key metrics: latency P50/P95/P99, error rate, completion rate, user satisfaction, cost
  • Implicit signals (retry rate, session abandonment) supplement explicit feedback
  • Monitoring must detect degradation over time (model drift, data shift)
  • Alerting systems enable rapid response to production issues
📈
Latency
P50/P95/P99 response time distributions
❌
Error Rate
Percentage of requests resulting in failures or exceptions
🎯
Completion
Fraction of tasks successfully completed end-to-end
😊
Satisfaction
User ratings, engagement signals, and retention metrics

Takeaways

  • Instrument every agent interaction for latency, cost, and outcome tracking from day one
  • Set up automated alerts for metric degradation, not just hard failures
  • Use online metrics to identify which offline benchmark improvements actually matter in production

Introduction

LangChain is a framework that simplifies building LLM-powered applications by providing standardized interfaces for models, tools, memory, and orchestration.

LangChain is a Python (and JavaScript) framework designed to streamline the development of applications powered by large language models. It provides modular abstractions for common LLM application patterns: connecting to various model providers, integrating external tools, managing conversation memory, and orchestrating multi-step reasoning chains. By standardizing these components, LangChain reduces boilerplate and enables rapid prototyping.

Tokens

Tokens are the fundamental units LLMs use to process text; all pricing and context limits are measured in tokens, not words.

LLMs do not process raw text directly; they convert text into tokens through tokenization. A token is roughly three-quarters of a word (100 tokens approximates 75 words). This matters because OpenAI prices API usage per token (both input and output), and context windows are measured in tokens. Understanding tokenization helps predict costs and manage context limits effectively.

  • Tokens are subword units; roughly 1 token = 0.75 words (100 tokens = ~75 words)
  • Tokenization converts text into numerical representations the model can process
  • Both input (prompt) and output (completion) tokens are counted and billed
  • Context window limits are defined in tokens, constraining total text per call
  • Different models use different tokenizers, so token counts vary slightly
🔤
Tokenization
Text is split into subword units for model processing
💰
Pricing
Cost is calculated per token for both input and output
📏
Context Window
Maximum tokens the model can process in one call
⚖️

Models and Prices

OpenAI model pricing is token-based and model-dependent; choosing the right model tier for each task is the primary cost optimization lever.

OpenAI offers multiple models at different price points, with costs varying by model capability and token type (input tokens are cheaper than output tokens). More capable models (GPT-4) cost significantly more than smaller models (GPT-3.5-turbo). The optimization strategy is model tiering: route simple tasks to cheaper models and reserve expensive models for complex reasoning, reducing costs by 10-50x on appropriate workloads.

  • Pricing is per-token with separate rates for input and output tokens
  • Output tokens typically cost 2-4x more than input tokens
  • GPT-4 costs roughly 10-30x more per token than GPT-3.5-turbo
  • Model tiering routes tasks to the cheapest model that can handle them
  • Price/performance ratio varies by task; simple tasks don't need expensive models
Model TierCost (Relative)Best For
GPT-3.5-turbo1x (baseline)Classification, extraction, simple Q&A
GPT-410-30xComplex reasoning, code generation, nuanced analysis
GPT-4-turbo5-15xBalance of capability and cost for moderate complexity

Takeaways

  • Default to the cheapest model, upgrade only where quality requires it
  • Implement model routing: classify task complexity, then select appropriate tier
  • Monitor cost per task type to identify where expensive models add no value

System, User, and Assistant Roles

The three message roles (system, user, assistant) give you structured control over how the model behaves and responds.

OpenAI's chat completions API uses three message roles. The system role sets behavioral instructions (persona, format, constraints). The user role contains the end-user's query. The assistant role represents prior model responses, enabling multi-turn conversations. These roles are passed as a list of dictionaries to the messages parameter, each containing 'role' and 'content' keys. Proper role usage gives fine-grained control over model behavior.

  • System role defines model behavior, persona, and output constraints
  • User role carries the end-user's actual question or instruction
  • Assistant role stores previous model responses for multi-turn context
  • Messages are passed as a list of dictionaries with 'role' and 'content' keys
🎯
System
Sets model behavior, persona, and output constraints
👤
User
Contains the end-user query or instruction
🤖
Assistant
Stores prior model responses for conversation context

Takeaways

  • System messages are your primary lever for controlling model behavior
  • Structure conversations as role-tagged message lists for predictable multi-turn interactions
