A system message defines the chatbot's persona, letting you shape tone and behavior with a single instruction.

This lesson implements a chatbot with a sarcastic persona by setting a system message instructing the model to answer sarcastically. The messages list contains a system dictionary defining the persona and a user dictionary with the question. When invoked, the model responds according to the system instruction. This demonstrates how persona engineering through system messages shapes output style without modifying the model itself.

  • System messages shape the chatbot's persona without modifying the model
  • The messages list order matters: system first, then user queries
  • Persona engineering is achieved entirely through prompt design
  • The same model can behave completely differently based on system instructions

Temperature, Max Tokens, and Streaming

Temperature controls randomness, max_tokens caps output length, and streaming delivers responses incrementally.

Three key parameters fine-tune model behavior. Temperature (0-2) controls output randomness: 0 produces deterministic responses, higher values increase creativity. Max completion tokens caps the response length, useful for cost control and concise answers. The stream parameter, when set to True, returns response chunks incrementally rather than waiting for full completion, improving perceived latency in interactive applications.

  • Temperature 0 = deterministic output; temperature 2 = maximum randomness
  • Max tokens limits response length, controlling cost and verbosity
  • Streaming returns chunks incrementally rather than waiting for full completion
  • These parameters are set in the API call alongside the messages list

0 = deterministic, 2 = maximum randomness

Max Tokens

🌊
Streaming
Delivers response chunks incrementally as generated

Takeaways

  • Use temperature 0 for factual/deterministic tasks, higher for creative generation
  • Enable streaming in production to improve user-perceived latency

The LangChain Framework

LangChain abstracts LLM interactions into composable components, enabling complex workflows with minimal code.

LangChain is a framework that simplifies building applications with large language models. It provides modular components (models, prompts, parsers, retrievers) that can be composed into chains. Key sub-packages include langchain-core (base abstractions), langchain-openai (OpenAI integration), and langchain-community (third-party integrations). The framework's value lies in standardizing interfaces so components are interchangeable and pipelines are easy to construct.

  • LangChain provides modular, composable components for LLM application development
  • Key packages: langchain-core, langchain-openai, langchain-community
  • Components include models, prompts, output parsers, and retrievers
  • The framework standardizes interfaces so providers are interchangeable
🧩
langchain-core
Base abstractions: Runnable, messages, prompts
🔌
langchain-openai
OpenAI-specific model wrappers and embeddings
🌐
langchain-community
Third-party integrations and tools

Takeaways

  • LangChain's value is composability: build complex workflows from simple, swappable components
  • Learn the core abstractions (Runnable, Chain, Parser) and the rest follows naturally

ChatOpenAI

ChatOpenAI is LangChain's wrapper around OpenAI chat models, providing a consistent interface for invocation.

ChatOpenAI is LangChain's class for interacting with OpenAI chat models. It accepts parameters like model name, temperature, and API key. Calling its invoke method with a string or message list returns an AIMessage object containing the model's response plus metadata (token usage, model info). This class standardizes the interface so switching between providers requires minimal code changes.

  • invoke() accepts a string or message list and returns an AIMessage object
  • AIMessage contains response content plus metadata (tokens, model info)
  • Parameters like model, temperature, and api_key are set at instantiation

System and Human Messages

SystemMessage and HumanMessage classes give LangChain structured role-based messaging equivalent to OpenAI's API roles.

LangChain provides SystemMessage and HumanMessage classes that mirror OpenAI's system and user roles. You pass a list of these message objects to ChatOpenAI's invoke method. SystemMessage sets instructions, HumanMessage carries the user query. This structured approach makes conversation construction explicit and type-safe compared to raw dictionary manipulation.

  • SystemMessage and HumanMessage are LangChain classes mirroring OpenAI roles
  • Pass a list of message objects to invoke() for structured conversations
  • Type-safe message construction prevents role/content key errors
  • Multiple HumanMessage objects can represent multi-turn user inputs

Prompt Templates and Prompt Values

Prompt templates separate prompt structure from data, enabling reusable and parameterized prompt generation.

PromptTemplate defines a string template with variable placeholders (e.g., {topic}). Calling invoke with variable values produces a PromptValue object, a format-agnostic container that can be converted to a string or message list. This separation of structure from data enables prompt reuse across different inputs and clean composition with other LangChain components.

  • PromptTemplate uses curly-brace placeholders for variable substitution
  • invoke() with variables returns a PromptValue (format-agnostic container)
  • PromptValue can be converted to string or message list as needed
  • Templates enable prompt reuse across different inputs and chains

StringOutputParser extracts raw text from AIMessage objects, simplifying downstream processing of model outputs.

StrOutputParser (StringOutputParser) is a simple component that extracts the text content from an AIMessage object, returning a plain string. CommaSeparatedListOutputParser converts model output into a Python list, enforcing structured data extraction.

CommaSeparatedListOutputParser parses comma-separated model output into a Python list. After the model responds, the parser splits the string on commas and returns a clean list, enabling structured data extraction from free-form model output.

Piping a Prompt, Model, and an Output Parser

Piping prompt, model, and parser with the | operator creates a chain where each component's output feeds the next.

The LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) uses the pipe operator (|) to chain components. A typical chain pipes a prompt template into a model into an output parser: prompt | model | parser. Calling invoke on the chain passes input through each component sequentially. This composability is the core design pattern of LangChain, enabling modular and readable pipeline construction.

  • The pipe operator (|) connects components: prompt | model | parser
  • invoke() on the chain passes input through all components sequentially
  • Each component's output becomes the next component's input
  • LCEL is the core composition pattern in modern LangChain
📋
Prompt
Template formats input into structured prompt
🧠
Model
LLM processes prompt and generates response
🔧
Parser
Extracts structured data from raw model output

Takeaways

  • The pipe syntax (prompt | model | parser) is the idiomatic way to build LangChain chains
  • Each component in the pipe must accept the previous component's output type

Batching

The batch method invokes a chain on multiple inputs concurrently, dramatically reducing total execution time.

The batch method accepts a list of input dictionaries and processes them concurrently. Instead of looping invoke calls sequentially, batch parallelizes requests, reducing total latency. It returns a list of outputs in the same order as inputs. This is especially valuable when processing multiple prompts against the same chain, as API calls run simultaneously.

  • batch() accepts a list of input dictionaries for concurrent processing
  • Parallelizes API calls, reducing total latency vs sequential invoke loops
  • Returns outputs in the same order as inputs
  • Ideal for processing multiple prompts through the same chain
MethodInputExecutionBest For
invoke()Single dictSequentialOne-off calls
batch()List of dictsConcurrentBulk processing

Takeaways

  • Use batch for bulk processing; it parallelizes API calls and reduces wall-clock time
  • Batch is essential for production workloads processing multiple inputs through one chain

Streaming

Streaming delivers tokens as they are generated, improving perceived latency for long responses.

The stream method returns an iterator that yields output chunks as the model generates them. For chains with a StringOutputParser, each chunk is a string fragment. You iterate over the stream and print or process tokens incrementally. This provides a real-time typing effect and reduces time-to-first-token for end-user interfaces.

  • stream() returns an iterator yielding output chunks as generated
  • Provides real-time token delivery for responsive user interfaces
  • Reduces time-to-first-token compared to waiting for full completion
  • Works with any chain ending in a compatible output parser
MethodReturnsLatencyUse Case
invoke()Complete responseWait for full generationBackend processing
stream()Token iteratorFirst token fastChat interfaces

Takeaways

  • Streaming improves UX for chat interfaces by delivering tokens as they generate
  • stream() works on any chain, not just raw model calls

The Runnable and RunnableSequence Classes

Every LangChain component inherits from the Runnable class; piping them creates a RunnableSequence automatically.

All LangChain components (prompts, models, parsers) inherit from the Runnable base class, which defines invoke, batch, and stream methods. When you pipe runnables together with |, LangChain creates a RunnableSequence. This sequence is itself a Runnable, so it also supports invoke/batch/stream. Understanding this inheritance clarifies why all components share a consistent interface.

  • All LangChain components inherit from the Runnable base class
  • Runnable defines invoke, batch, and stream as standard methods
  • Piping runnables with | creates a RunnableSequence automatically
  • RunnableSequence is itself a Runnable, enabling recursive composition
🏗️
Runnable
Base class with invoke, batch, stream methods
🔗
RunnableSequence
Chain created by piping runnables with |
♻️
Recursive Composition
Sequences are Runnables, enabling nesting

Takeaways

  • Understanding the Runnable abstraction unlocks the full power of LCEL composition
  • Every component you pipe is a Runnable; every pipe creates a RunnableSequence

Piping Chains and the RunnablePassthrough Class

RunnablePassthrough forwards its input unchanged, acting as a bridge when piping one chain's output into another.

RunnablePassthrough passes its input directly to its output without modification. This is useful when chaining two chains together: the first chain's output becomes a string, but the second chain expects a dictionary. RunnablePassthrough can be combined with assignment or mapping to restructure data between chain stages, acting as an adapter in complex pipelines.

  • RunnablePassthrough forwards input unchanged to its output
  • Acts as an adapter between chains with incompatible I/O shapes
  • Can be combined with assign() to add keys to passthrough data
  • Enables piping one chain's output as input to another chain

Passthrough
Forwards input unchanged to output
🔀
Adapter
Bridges chains with different I/O shapes
➕
Assign
Adds computed keys to passthrough data

Takeaways

  • RunnablePassthrough is the glue for connecting chains with different I/O expectations
  • Use assign() with passthrough to reshape data between pipeline stages

Graphing runnables with ASCII visualization reveals the execution flow and node order of your chain pipeline.

LangChain provides utilities to visualize chain topology as ASCII graphs. Calling get_graph().print_ascii() on any runnable displays nodes and edges showing data flow. This helps debug complex chains by making the execution order and component connections explicit, especially when parallel branches or multiple stages are involved.

  • Shows nodes (components) and edges (data flow) in the pipeline
  • Helps debug complex chains with multiple branches or stages
  • Available on any Runnable or RunnableSequence object

RunnableParallel

RunnableParallel invokes multiple runnables simultaneously with the same input, returning a dictionary of results.

RunnableParallel accepts multiple runnables (as keyword arguments or a dictionary) and invokes them simultaneously with the same input. It returns a dictionary mapping each key to its runnable's output. Execution time equals the slowest branch rather than the sum of all branches, making it ideal for independent operations that can run concurrently.

  • RunnableParallel invokes multiple runnables simultaneously with the same input
  • Accepts runnables as keyword arguments or a dictionary
  • Returns a dictionary mapping keys to each runnable's output
  • Execution time equals the slowest branch, not the sum of all
AspectSequential (invoke loop)RunnableParallel
ExecutionOne after anotherAll at once
Total TimeSum of all runtimesMax of all runtimes
OutputList of resultsDictionary of results

Takeaways

  • RunnableParallel is ideal for independent operations on the same input (e.g., multiple LLM perspectives)
  • Parallel execution time = max(branch times), not sum(branch times)

Piping a RunnableParallel with Other Runnables

Piping a RunnableParallel into subsequent runnables lets you fan-out then merge parallel results into a single flow.

A RunnableParallel can be piped into subsequent runnables, passing its dictionary output downstream. This pattern enables fan-out/fan-in architectures: split input into parallel branches, process each independently, then merge results in a final step. The downstream runnable receives the combined dictionary and can use all parallel outputs together.

  • RunnableParallel output (dictionary) can be piped to downstream runnables
  • Enables fan-out/fan-in architecture patterns
  • Downstream components receive the merged dictionary of all parallel results
  • Useful for combining multiple LLM perspectives into a final synthesis

Takeaways

  • Fan-out/fan-in with RunnableParallel enables powerful multi-perspective synthesis patterns
  • The output dictionary keys become accessible fields for downstream runnables

RunnableLambda

RunnableLambda wraps any Python function into a Runnable, letting custom logic participate in chain pipelines.

RunnableLambda wraps any Python function (including lambdas) into a Runnable object. The function receives the chain's current value and returns a transformed value. This lets you insert arbitrary Python logic (string manipulation, API calls, data transformation) into a LangChain pipeline alongside prompts, models, and parsers.

  • RunnableLambda wraps any Python function into a Runnable object
  • Function receives current chain value, returns transformed value
  • Enables arbitrary Python logic within LangChain pipelines
  • Works with lambdas, named functions, and async functions

The @chain Decorator

The @chain decorator converts a function into a Runnable without explicitly wrapping it in RunnableLambda.

The @chain decorator from langchain_core.runnables converts a decorated function into a Runnable. Inside the function, you can call other runnables with invoke and perform arbitrary logic. This provides a cleaner syntax than RunnableLambda for complex custom runnables that contain multiple steps or conditional logic.

  • @chain decorator converts a function into a Runnable automatically
  • Cleaner syntax than explicit RunnableLambda wrapping
  • Inside the function, call other runnables with invoke()
  • Supports complex multi-step logic within a single runnable

  • The decorator pattern keeps code readable and explicitly marks functions as chain components

How to Integrate Custom Data into an LLM

LLMs have training cutoff dates and no access to private data; integration strategies bridge this knowledge gap.

LLMs are trained on static datasets with cutoff dates and lack access to proprietary or real-time data. Three strategies integrate custom data: (1) prompt injection for small datasets, (2) fine-tuning for permanent behavioral changes, and (3) retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for large or frequently updated knowledge bases. RAG is the most practical approach for most applications.

  • LLMs have training data cutoff dates and cannot access real-time information
  • Prompt injection works for small, static datasets only
  • Fine-tuning permanently alters model behavior but is expensive
  • RAG is the most practical approach for large or dynamic knowledge bases
💉
Prompt Injection
Paste data directly into prompt; small datasets only
🔬
Fine-Tuning

🔍
RAG

Takeaways

  • RAG is the go-to strategy for integrating custom/private data with LLMs in production
  • Choose integration strategy based on data size, update frequency, and permanence needs

Introduction to RAG

RAG retrieves relevant documents at query time and injects them into the prompt, giving the model access to custom data without retraining.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique where relevant documents are retrieved from a knowledge base at query time and injected into the prompt context. The pipeline involves: loading documents, splitting them into chunks, embedding chunks into vectors, storing in a vector database, retrieving similar chunks for a query, and passing them to the LLM. This gives models access to custom data without expensive retraining.

  • RAG pipeline: load, split, embed, store, retrieve, generate
  • Documents are chunked and converted to vector embeddings
  • Vector databases enable semantic similarity search over custom data
  • Retrieved chunks are injected into the prompt as context for the LLM
  • No model retraining required; knowledge base can be updated independently
1

Load Documents

Ingest raw files (PDF, web, DB) into document objects

2

Chunk and Embed

Split into pieces, convert to vector embeddings

3

Store in Vector DB

Index embeddings for fast similarity search

4

Retrieve and Generate

Find relevant chunks, inject into prompt, LLM generates answer

Takeaways

  • RAG separates knowledge from reasoning: the model reasons, the vector store remembers
  • The RAG pipeline (load, chunk, embed, store, retrieve, generate) is the foundation of most production LLM apps

Introduction to Document Loading and Splitting

RAG indexing starts with loading documents into structured objects and splitting them into semantically meaningful chunks for efficient retrieval.

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) consists of three phases: indexing, retrieval, and generation. The indexing phase itself has four steps: document loading, splitting, embedding, and storing. Document loading ingests raw data from various formats into LangChain Document objects containing text and metadata. Splitting then divides these documents into smaller, semantically coherent chunks that fit within model context windows and enable precise retrieval.

  • RAG has three main parts: indexing, retrieval, and generation
  • Indexing comprises document loading, splitting, embedding, and storing
  • Document loading converts raw files into LangChain Document objects with text and metadata
  • Splitting creates smaller chunks that preserve semantic meaning
  • Chunk size must balance between being small enough for precision and large enough for context

Takeaways

  • The quality of your RAG pipeline depends heavily on how well you split documents into meaningful chunks
  • LangChain standardizes all loaded documents into a common Document object format regardless of source
  • Splitting strategy should be chosen based on document structure and downstream retrieval needs

Introduction to Document Embedding

Embeddings convert text chunks into numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning, enabling fast similarity-based retrieval.

After loading and splitting documents, the next indexing step is embedding. An embedding model converts text into a high-dimensional vector that encodes its semantic meaning. Texts with similar meaning produce vectors that are close together in vector space, measured by cosine similarity or Euclidean distance. This enables retrieval systems to quickly find the most relevant chunks for any given query without keyword matching.

  • Embedding converts text to a numerical vector capturing its semantic content
  • Semantically similar texts produce vectors close together in vector space
  • Cosine similarity and Euclidean distance are common similarity metrics
  • Embeddings enable semantic search rather than keyword-based matching
  • Each chunk is embedded independently and stored for later retrieval
🔢

Text converted to high-dimensional numerical array
📐
Cosine Similarity
Measures angle between vectors; closer = more similar
🔍
Semantic Search
Find relevant content by meaning, not exact keywords
📦
Embedding Model
Neural network that maps text to vector space

Takeaways

  • Embeddings are the bridge between human language and machine-searchable vector space
  • The embedding model choice directly impacts retrieval quality
  • Semantic similarity search outperforms keyword matching for natural language queries

Introduction to Document Storing, Retrieval, and Generation

Vector stores persist embeddings for fast retrieval, and the retrieved context is injected into the LLM prompt to generate grounded answers.

Once documents are loaded, split, and embedded, the vectors are stored in a vector store (e.g., Chroma, FAISS, Pinecone) for persistent, indexed access. During retrieval, a user query is embedded using the same model and compared against stored vectors to find the most relevant chunks. These chunks are then passed as context to the LLM in the generation step, producing answers grounded in the actual source documents rather than relying solely on the model's training data.

  • Vector stores persist embeddings with metadata for efficient similarity lookup
  • The user query is embedded with the same model used for document chunks
  • Retrieval returns the top-k most similar chunks to the query
  • Generation injects retrieved context into the LLM prompt
  • This grounds LLM responses in actual source documents, reducing hallucination

Takeaways

  • The retrieval step bridges the gap between user questions and relevant document content
  • Grounding LLM output in retrieved documents significantly reduces hallucination
  • The full RAG pipeline: load, split, embed, store, retrieve, generate

Indexing: Document Loading with PyPDFLoader

PyPDFLoader loads PDF files into LangChain Document objects, one per page, with text content and page metadata.

LangChain's PyPDFLoader reads PDF files and returns a list of Document objects, each representing one page. Each Document has a page_content attribute (the extracted text) and a metadata dictionary containing source file path and page number. After loading, preprocessing steps like removing extraneous newline characters clean the text for downstream splitting and embedding.

  • PyPDFLoader creates one Document object per PDF page
  • Each Document has page_content (text) and metadata (source, page number)
  • Install pypdf package to use PyPDFLoader
  • Post-loading cleanup (e.g., removing newlines) improves downstream processing
  • LangChain supports many loader types; the pattern is consistent across all

  • Metadata preservation enables source attribution in final RAG answers

Docx2txtLoader extracts text from Word documents into a single Document object, following the same loader pattern as PyPDFLoader.

LangChain's Docx2txtLoader handles .docx files by extracting all text into a single Document object (unlike PyPDFLoader which creates one per page). The usage pattern is identical: instantiate the loader with the file path, call .load(), and receive a list of Document objects. The docx2txt package must be installed. This demonstrates LangChain's consistent loader interface across different file formats.

Indexing: Document Splitting with Character Text Splitter (Theory)

CharacterTextSplitter divides text by a separator character with configurable chunk size and overlap to maintain context across boundaries.

Document splitting is essential for RAG because large documents exceed context windows and reduce retrieval precision. LangChain's CharacterTextSplitter splits text using a specified separator (default: double newline), a maximum chunk_size (in characters), and a chunk_overlap that duplicates text at boundaries to preserve context. The splitter first divides on the separator, then merges pieces until reaching chunk_size, ensuring no chunk exceeds the limit while maintaining semantic coherence.

  • CharacterTextSplitter uses a single separator character to split text
  • chunk_size sets the maximum number of characters per chunk
  • chunk_overlap duplicates text at chunk boundaries to preserve context
  • The splitter first splits on separator, then merges small pieces up to chunk_size
  • Overlap prevents loss of meaning at chunk boundaries
✂️
separator
Character used to split text (default: '\n\n')
📏
chunk_size
Maximum characters per chunk
🔗
chunk_overlap
Characters duplicated between adjacent chunks
🧩
Merge Logic
Small splits are merged until chunk_size is reached

Takeaways

  • Chunk overlap is critical for preserving context that spans chunk boundaries
  • Chunk size should balance retrieval precision (smaller) with context completeness (larger)
  • CharacterTextSplitter is the simplest splitter; more advanced options exist for structured documents

Indexing: Document Splitting with Character Text Splitter (Code Along)

Apply CharacterTextSplitter to real documents by configuring separator, chunk_size, and chunk_overlap, then inspect resulting chunks and metadata.

In practice, apply CharacterTextSplitter to previously loaded documents by instantiating it with chosen parameters and calling .split_documents(). The method returns a list of Document objects, each with page_content (the chunk text) and metadata inherited from the parent document. Inspect chunk count, individual chunk lengths, and content to verify the splitting strategy produces semantically coherent pieces suitable for embedding.

  • Call .split_documents(docs) to split a list of Document objects
  • Resulting chunks inherit metadata from their parent documents
  • Verify chunk count and sizes match expectations for your use case
  • Adjust chunk_size and overlap based on inspection of output quality
  • Each chunk becomes an independent unit for embedding and retrieval

Indexing: Document Splitting with Markdown Header Text Splitter

MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter splits documents along markdown headers, preserving document structure and adding header hierarchy to chunk metadata.

For structured documents with markdown formatting, MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter splits on header levels (H1, H2, H3, etc.) rather than arbitrary character counts. Each resulting chunk corresponds to a section under a specific header, and the header hierarchy is stored in metadata. This produces semantically meaningful chunks that align with the document's logical structure, improving retrieval precision for structured content.

  • Splits on markdown headers (#, ##, ###) rather than character count
  • Header hierarchy is preserved in chunk metadata
  • Produces chunks aligned with document logical structure
  • Specify which header levels to split on via headers_to_split_on parameter
  • Best suited for well-structured documents with consistent header usage

Split basisCharacter count + separatorMarkdown header levels
Chunk boundariesArbitrary text positionsLogical document sections
Metadata addedInherited from parentHeader hierarchy
Best forUnstructured textWell-structured markdown documents

Takeaways

  • Structure-aware splitting produces more semantically coherent chunks than character-based splitting
  • Header metadata enables filtering retrieval results by document section
  • Choose your splitter based on document format: character-based for unstructured, header-based for markdown

Indexing: Text Embedding with OpenAI

OpenAIEmbeddings wraps OpenAI's embedding API to convert text chunks into vectors, using embed_query for single texts and embed_documents for batches.

LangChain's OpenAIEmbeddings class provides a simple interface to OpenAI's embedding models. Use .embed_query() for a single text string (e.g., user queries) and .embed_documents() for a list of texts (e.g., document chunks). Both return numerical vectors. The default model is text-embedding-ada-002. These vectors are then stored in a vector store for similarity-based retrieval.

  • OpenAIEmbeddings requires an OpenAI API key
  • embed_query() embeds a single string, returns one vector
  • embed_documents() embeds a list of strings, returns list of vectors
  • Default model: text-embedding-ada-002 (1536 dimensions)
  • Same embedding model must be used for both documents and queries

  • Batch embedding with embed_documents() is more efficient for multiple chunks
  • The embedding step transforms text into the numerical format required by vector stores

Indexing: Creating a Chroma Vector Store

Chroma.from_documents() creates a vector store by embedding and indexing document chunks in one step, ready for similarity search.

Chroma is an open-source vector database that integrates seamlessly with LangChain. The Chroma.from_documents() class method takes a list of Document objects and an embedding model, embeds all chunks, and stores them in a persistent or in-memory database. Once created, the vector store supports similarity search, MMR search, and can be used as a retriever in RAG chains.

  • Chroma.from_documents() combines embedding and storage in one call
  • Accepts Document objects (with page_content and metadata)
  • Supports persistence to disk for reuse across sessions
  • Integrates directly with LangChain's retriever interface
  • Open-source and suitable for development and small-scale production

Indexing: Inspecting and Managing Documents in a Vector Store

Vector stores support CRUD operations: add new documents, update existing ones by ID, delete specific documents, and inspect stored content.

After creating a vector store, you can manage its content programmatically. Inspect stored documents using .get() to view IDs, content, and metadata. Add new documents with .add_documents(), update existing ones with .update_document() using the document ID, and delete with .delete() by passing document IDs. These operations enable maintaining an up-to-date knowledge base without rebuilding the entire store.

  • Use .get() to inspect stored document IDs, content, and metadata
  • Add documents with .add_documents() (auto-generates IDs or accepts custom ones)
  • Update by ID with .update_document(id, new_document)
  • Delete by ID with .delete(ids=[...])
  • Managing documents avoids costly full re-indexing

Retrieval: Similarity Search

Similarity search embeds the query and returns the k documents whose vectors are closest in embedding space, ranked by relevance.

The most straightforward retrieval method is similarity search. The user query is embedded using the same model as the documents, then the vector store computes distance (cosine similarity or L2) between the query vector and all stored vectors, returning the top-k closest matches. Each result includes the document content, metadata, and optionally a relevance score. This is fast, effective, and the default retrieval strategy in most RAG systems.

  • Query is embedded with the same model used for documents
  • Returns top-k documents with highest cosine similarity to query
  • Call .similarity_search(query, k=N) on the vector store
  • similarity_search_with_score() also returns distance/similarity values
  • Simple and effective for most retrieval use cases
1

Embed Query

Convert user question to vector using same embedding model

2

Compute Distances

Calculate similarity between query vector and all stored vectors

3

Rank & Return

Return top-k documents sorted by similarity score

Takeaways

  • Similarity search is the default and often sufficient retrieval strategy
  • The k parameter controls how many documents are retrieved (trade-off: more context vs. noise)
  • Score inspection helps determine if retrieved documents are actually relevant

Retrieval: Maximal Marginal Relevance Search

MMR balances relevance to the query with diversity among results, reducing redundancy when top-k similar documents overlap heavily.

Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) addresses a limitation of pure similarity search: when top results are very similar to each other, they provide redundant information. MMR iteratively selects documents that are both relevant to the query AND diverse from already-selected documents. The lambda parameter controls this trade-off (1.0 = pure relevance, 0.0 = pure diversity). Use MMR when your document chunks have overlapping content.

  • MMR reduces redundancy in retrieval results
  • Balances relevance (to query) with diversity (among results)
  • Lambda parameter: 1.0 = pure similarity, 0.0 = maximum diversity
  • Call .max_marginal_relevance_search(query, k=N, lambda_mult=0.5)
  • Especially useful when chunks have overlapping content due to chunk_overlap
FeatureSimilarity SearchMMR Search
Ranking criterionRelevance onlyRelevance + diversity
Redundancy handlingNone (may return duplicates)Actively reduces overlap
SpeedFasterSlightly slower
Best forDistinct document chunksOverlapping/redundant chunks

Takeaways

  • Use MMR when similarity search returns near-duplicate chunks
  • Lambda = 0.5 is a good starting point for balanced relevance and diversity
  • MMR is slightly more expensive than pure similarity search but produces better context coverage

Retrieval: Vector Store-Backed Retriever

Converting a vector store to a retriever with .as_retriever() enables seamless integration into LangChain chains and LCEL pipelines.

While vector stores expose search methods directly, LangChain chains expect a Retriever interface. The .as_retriever() method wraps a vector store into a Retriever object that can be plugged into any chain. Configuration options include search_type ('similarity' or 'mmr') and search_kwargs (k, lambda_mult, score_threshold). The retriever's .invoke() method accepts a query string and returns Document objects.

  • as_retriever() converts a vector store into LangChain's Retriever interface
  • search_type parameter: 'similarity' or 'mmr'
  • search_kwargs configures k, lambda_mult, score_threshold, and filters
  • Retriever.invoke(query) returns a list of Document objects
  • Required for integration into LCEL chains and RAG pipelines

Takeaways

  • Always convert to a retriever when building RAG chains with LCEL
  • The retriever abstraction decouples your chain logic from the specific vector store implementation
  • Configure search strategy at retriever creation time for consistent behavior

Generation: Stuffing Documents

The 'stuff' method concatenates all retrieved documents into a single prompt context block, which works well when total retrieved text fits within the model's context window.

The generation step combines retrieved documents with the user query in a prompt sent to the LLM. The simplest approach is 'stuffing': concatenating all retrieved chunks into one context string within the prompt template. An LCEL chain is built by piping a retriever (for context) and a passthrough (for the question) into a prompt template, then to the LLM, and finally to an output parser. This works well when retrieved content is short enough to fit the context window.

  • Stuffing concatenates all retrieved documents into one prompt context
  • Build the chain: retriever | prompt | LLM | output_parser
  • RunnablePassthrough passes the user query through unchanged
  • A dictionary with 'context' and 'question' keys feeds the prompt template
  • Works best when total retrieved text fits within model context limits

Takeaways

  • Stuffing is the simplest and most common document combination strategy for RAG
  • For large document sets exceeding context limits, consider map-reduce or refine strategies
  • The LCEL pipe operator makes RAG chain construction readable and composable

Generation: Generating a Response

Piping the filled prompt through the ChatModel and a StrOutputParser completes the RAG chain, producing a grounded text response from retrieved context.

After constructing the prompt with retrieved context and the user question, the chain pipes it through the ChatModel (e.g., ChatOpenAI) which generates a response grounded in the provided documents. A StrOutputParser extracts the plain text from the model's response object. The complete LCEL chain is: dict(context=retriever, question=passthrough) | prompt | llm | output_parser. Invoking this chain with a query string runs the entire RAG pipeline end-to-end.

  • ChatOpenAI (or other ChatModel) receives the filled prompt and generates a response
  • StrOutputParser converts the AIMessage object to a plain string
  • Full chain: {context: retriever, question: passthrough} | prompt | llm | parser
  • chain.invoke(query) runs the complete RAG pipeline in one call
  • The LLM uses only the retrieved context, reducing hallucination

Takeaways

  • The complete RAG chain is a single invocable object that handles retrieval and generation
  • StrOutputParser is essential for extracting usable text from ChatModel responses
  • End-to-end invocation makes RAG pipelines simple to deploy and test

LangGraph extends LangChain by enabling stateful, graph-based agent workflows with persistent conversational memory.

LangGraph models agent workflows as directed graphs with state management, enabling complex multi-turn conversations where context persists across interactions. It builds on LangChain's foundation while adding the graph abstraction needed for stateful agent architectures.

Setting Up the Environment

Create a dedicated Conda environment, install required packages (langgraph, langchain, openai), and register it as a Jupyter kernel for notebook development.

Environment setup involves creating an isolated Conda environment to avoid dependency conflicts, installing the required packages (langgraph, langchain-openai, python-dotenv, jupyter), and registering the environment as a Jupyter kernel. Store API keys in a .env file and load them with python-dotenv. This isolation ensures reproducible development and prevents package version conflicts with other projects.

  • Register Jupyter kernel: python -m ipykernel install --user --name langgraph_env
  • Store API keys in .env file, load with python-dotenv
  • Activate environment before every session: conda activate langgraph_env

States, Nodes, and Edges

A LangGraph graph consists of a State (shared data schema), Nodes (functions that transform state), and Edges (connections defining execution flow).

In LangGraph, a graph defines an agent workflow through three core components. The State is a TypedDict schema representing all data shared between nodes. Nodes are Python functions that receive the current state, perform operations (e.g., call an LLM), and return state updates. Edges connect nodes and define execution order; they can be unconditional (always follow one path) or conditional (route based on state values). Special START and END nodes mark entry and exit points.

  • State: TypedDict defining the shared data schema passed between nodes
  • Nodes: Python functions that receive state and return state updates
  • Edges: Connections between nodes defining execution flow
  • Conditional edges route to different nodes based on state values
  • START and END are special built-in nodes for graph entry/exit

➡️

🔀

Takeaways

  • Think of state as the shared memory that flows through the entire graph
  • Nodes are pure functions: they read state, do work, return updates
  • Conditional edges enable dynamic routing, making graphs adaptive to runtime conditions

First Graph: Defining a State and a Node

Define state as a TypedDict with typed fields, then create node functions that accept state and return partial state updates.

The state is defined as a class inheriting from TypedDict, with fields representing all data the graph tracks (e.g., messages: list). Node functions accept this state as their argument and return a dictionary containing only the fields they update. For a chatbot node, the function takes the current messages from state, sends them to the LLM, and returns the new message to be appended. The node does not need to return the entire state, only the changed fields.

  • State class inherits from TypedDict with typed fields
  • Node functions accept the full state dict as input
  • Nodes return only the fields they modify (partial update)
  • A chatbot node reads messages, calls LLM, returns new AI message
  • State updates are merged into the existing state automatically
1

Define State

Create TypedDict class with all graph fields (e.g., messages: list)

2

Write Node Function

Function takes state, performs work, returns partial update

3

Return Updates

Only return fields that changed; framework handles merging

Takeaways

  • Partial state returns keep node functions focused and composable
  • TypedDict provides type safety and clear documentation of graph data flow
  • Each node is a self-contained unit of work with a clear input/output contract

First Graph: Building the Graph

Assemble the graph by instantiating StateGraph with your state schema, adding nodes, connecting edges, and calling .compile() to produce a runnable.

With state and nodes defined, assemble the graph: instantiate StateGraph(State), add nodes with .add_node(name, function), connect them with .add_edge(source, target), and call .compile() to produce a runnable graph. The compiled graph exposes .invoke(initial_state) to execute the workflow. For a simple chatbot: START -> chatbot_node -> END, with the chatbot node calling the LLM and updating the messages list in state.

  • Instantiate: graph = StateGraph(State)
  • Add nodes: graph.add_node('chatbot', chatbot_function)
  • Add edges: graph.add_edge(START, 'chatbot') and graph.add_edge('chatbot', END)
  • Compile: app = graph.compile() produces a runnable
  • Invoke: app.invoke({'messages': [user_message]}) runs the full graph
1

Instantiate

StateGraph(State) with your TypedDict schema

2

Add Nodes

.add_node(name, function) for each processing step

3

Add Edges

.add_edge(source, target) to define execution flow

4

Compile

.compile() validates and produces runnable graph

5

Invoke

.invoke(initial_state) executes the workflow end-to-end

Takeaways

  • The compile step validates graph structure and produces an optimized runnable
  • Graph construction follows a consistent pattern: instantiate, add nodes, add edges, compile
  • invoke() accepts an initial state dict and returns the final state after execution

Conditional Edges: Defining Nodes and a Routing Function

Conditional edges use a routing function that inspects state and returns the name of the next node, enabling dynamic workflow branching.

To add branching logic, define a routing function that examines the current state and returns the name of the next node to execute. For example, after a chatbot responds, a router might check if the user wants to continue (route to 'ask_another_question') or stop (route to END). Additional nodes handle the branched paths. The routing function is a pure function: it reads state, applies logic, and returns a string node name.

  • Routing function takes state, returns a node name string
  • Enables dynamic branching based on runtime state values
  • Define separate nodes for each branch path
  • Router can inspect any state field to make decisions
  • Used with add_conditional_edges() on the graph builder
🔀
Routing Function
Inspects state, returns next node name
🛤️
Branch Paths
Different nodes for different conditions
📍
Decision Point
State field determines which path to take
🔄
Loop Capability
Route back to earlier nodes for iteration

Takeaways

  • Routing functions are the decision-makers in LangGraph workflows
  • Keep routing logic simple and testable; complex logic belongs in nodes
  • Conditional edges make graphs adaptive to user input and runtime conditions

Conditional Edges: Building the Graph

Use add_conditional_edges(source_node, routing_function, path_map) to wire dynamic branching into the compiled graph.

After defining nodes and the routing function, wire them together using add_conditional_edges(). This method takes the source node name, the routing function, and optionally a path_map dictionary mapping return values to node names. The graph connects START to the first node with a regular edge, uses conditional edges for branching points, and regular edges for deterministic paths. The compiled graph handles routing automatically at runtime based on state.

  • add_conditional_edges(source, router_fn, path_map) wires dynamic routing
  • path_map: {'continue': 'ask_another', 'stop': END} maps router returns to nodes
  • Mix regular edges (deterministic) with conditional edges (dynamic) in one graph
  • Routing happens automatically at runtime based on current state
  • Multiple conditional edge points can exist in a single graph

Create all processing nodes and branch-specific nodes

Write Router

Function that returns node name based on state inspection

3

Add Regular Edges

Connect deterministic paths with add_edge()

4

Add Conditional Edges

5

Compile & Test

Takeaways

  • Conditional edges are the mechanism for loops and branching in LangGraph
  • path_map provides explicit mapping from routing function returns to node names
  • Combining conditional and regular edges creates flexible, readable workflow graphs

The Annotated Construct and Reducer Functions

Annotated types with reducer functions (e.g., operator.add) define HOW state fields are updated when nodes return values, enabling append vs. overwrite semantics.

By default, when a node returns a state field, it overwrites the existing value. For fields like message lists that should accumulate across nodes, use Annotated[list, operator.add] in the state schema. The second argument is a reducer function that defines how new values merge with existing ones. operator.add concatenates lists, enabling message history to grow as each node appends new messages. Custom reducers can implement any merge logic.

  • Default behavior: node return overwrites the state field value
  • Annotated[type, reducer] changes update behavior for a field
  • operator.add as reducer: appends new list items to existing list
  • Essential for accumulating message history across conversation turns
  • Custom reducer functions enable any merge logic (deduplicate, cap length, etc.)
ApproachState DefinitionUpdate Behavior
Default (overwrite)messages: listNew value replaces old value entirely
Annotated (append)messages: Annotated[list, operator.add]New value appended to existing list
Custom reducermessages: Annotated[list, my_reducer]Custom merge logic applied

Takeaways

  • Annotated with reducer is what makes conversational memory work in LangGraph
  • Without a reducer, each node would overwrite the message history instead of appending
  • Choose reducers carefully: they define the fundamental state evolution semantics of your graph

Reducer Functions in Action

Understanding reducer functions requires seeing state mutations in action through step-by-step execution.

This lesson walks through executing a LangGraph notebook to verify that the add_messages reducer function updates state correctly. By running cells sequentially and inspecting the state after each graph invocation, you confirm that messages accumulate as expected. The key verification is that each new human or AI message appends to the existing list rather than replacing it.

  • Run cells sequentially to observe state changes after each invocation
  • The add_messages reducer appends new messages to the existing state list
  • Verify state updates match expectations by printing intermediate states
  • The annotated construct ties the reducer to the state field declaratively

  • Reducers define HOW state updates happen, not WHAT data the state holds

The MessagesState Class

MessagesState is a pre-built convenience class that eliminates boilerplate for the most common graph state pattern.

Throughout LangGraph, state is typically defined as a TypedDict with a messages key and an add_messages reducer. The MessagesState class packages this exact pattern into a single import, reducing repetitive code. You can still define custom state schemas with different key names, types, or reducers when your use case demands it.

  • MessagesState provides a pre-configured state with a messages key and add_messages reducer
  • Custom state definitions remain available for non-standard patterns
  • The key name, type annotation, and reducer function are all configurable
  • Using MessagesState reduces boilerplate without sacrificing flexibility
AspectCustom TypedDictMessagesState
Setup Code3-5 lines (key + type + reducer)1 import
Key NameAny name you chooseFixed: messages
ReducerAny functionPre-set: add_messages
FlexibilityFull controlStandard pattern only

Takeaways

  • Use MessagesState for standard chatbot patterns to minimize boilerplate
  • Define custom TypedDict state only when you need non-message keys or custom reducers
  • The framework is opinionated about defaults but flexible about overrides

The RemoveMessages Class

RemoveMessages lets you shrink conversation history by ID-based removal, preventing unbounded token growth.

Appending every message to state works for short conversations but causes token and latency bloat over time. The RemoveMessages class provides a mechanism to selectively remove messages from state by their IDs. Despite the counterintuitive API (you 'add' a RemoveMessage object to trigger deletion), this approach integrates cleanly with the existing reducer pattern.

  • Long conversations accumulate tokens, increasing cost and latency
  • RemoveMessages targets specific messages by their unique IDs
  • Deletion is triggered by appending a RemoveMessage object to the state (quirky but consistent)
  • This is a middle-ground solution between keeping everything and aggressive summarization
🗑️
RemoveMessages
Delete specific messages by ID from state
📈
Token Growth
Each message adds tokens; unchecked growth is costly
⚖️
Middle Ground
Between full history and aggressive summarization

Takeaways

  • Unbounded message accumulation is unsustainable for production chatbots
  • RemoveMessages provides surgical control over which messages to drop
  • The add-to-remove pattern preserves reducer consistency across the framework

Trimming Messages

The trim_messages node acts as a preprocessing step that caps conversation length before the LLM processes it.

This lesson implements a trim_messages function as a graph node. The function accepts a MessagesState, identifies messages to remove (keeping only recent ones), constructs RemoveMessage objects for the old entries, and returns the updated state. Placed before the chatbot node in the graph, it ensures the LLM never receives more context than a configured threshold.

  • trim_messages is a standard graph node: takes state in, returns state out
  • It constructs RemoveMessage objects for messages beyond the retention window
  • Position it before the chatbot node so trimming happens before LLM invocation
  • Include a print statement for debugging to confirm the node fires
  • The retention window is configurable (e.g., keep last N messages)

Create trim_messages accepting MessagesState, returning same type

2

Identify Old Messages

3

4

Wire into Graph

  • Message trimming should be a dedicated node placed before LLM calls
  • Trimming is transparent: print statements confirm execution order
  • Configure retention thresholds based on your model's context window

Summarizing Messages

Summarizing past messages into a single condensed message is more token-efficient than trimming while retaining conversational context.

Instead of storing or removing messages verbatim, this approach summarizes prior conversation into a compact representation. A dedicated summarization node invokes the LLM to condense history into a summary message, which replaces the original messages in state. This preserves context for the chatbot while dramatically reducing token consumption for long-running conversations.

  • Summarization replaces N messages with one condensed summary message
  • A separate graph node handles summarization using the LLM itself
  • More context-preserving than simple trimming (retains semantic information)
  • The summary updates incrementally as new messages arrive
  • Token savings compound over long conversations
StrategyToken CostContext PreservedBest For
Full HistoryHigh (grows linearly)100%Short conversations
TrimmingFixed capRecent onlySimple Q&A bots
SummarizationLow (compressed)Semantic gistLong-running sessions

Takeaways

  • Summarization beats trimming when conversational context matters
  • Use the LLM to generate summaries; it understands what to preserve
  • Combine summarization with a threshold trigger to avoid summarizing every turn

Checkpointers and Threads

Checkpointers persist graph state to storage, enabling conversation continuity across sessions via thread IDs.

LangGraph checkpointers save the graph's state at each step to a storage backend. Each conversation is identified by a thread ID, allowing multiple independent sessions. When a graph is invoked with an existing thread ID, it resumes from the last checkpoint rather than starting fresh. This enables true persistence: conversations survive kernel restarts and system reboots.

  • Checkpointers automatically save state after each graph step
  • Thread IDs isolate independent conversations within the same graph
  • Resuming a thread restores full state from the last checkpoint
  • Multiple backend options: in-memory, SQLite, PostgreSQL, etc.
  • No code changes to graph logic required; persistence is infrastructure-level
💾
Checkpointer
Saves state snapshots after each graph step
🧵
Thread ID
Unique identifier isolating each conversation
🔄
Resume
Restore full state from last checkpoint on re-invocation

Takeaways

  • Thread IDs are the key abstraction for multi-session persistence
  • Checkpointers are pluggable: swap backends without changing graph code
  • Persistence transforms a stateless graph into a stateful application

Short-Term Memory with the InMemorySaver Class

InMemorySaver is the simplest checkpointer: fast for development but volatile (lost on restart).

This lesson implements persistence using InMemorySaver, which stores checkpoints in a Python dictionary. The graph is compiled with the checkpointer parameter, and each invocation includes a thread ID in the config. Messages persist across multiple invocations within the same session, demonstrating that the graph truly remembers prior interactions. However, data is lost when the process terminates.

  • InMemorySaver stores checkpoints in a Python dict (RAM only)
  • Pass checkpointer to graph.compile() to enable persistence
  • Include thread_id in the config dict for each invocation
  • Ideal for development and testing; not suitable for production
  • Demonstrates persistence mechanics without external dependencies
1

Import InMemorySaver

from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

2

Compile with Checkpointer

graph.compile(checkpointer=memory_saver)

3

Invoke with Thread ID

graph.invoke(input, config={'configurable': {'thread_id': '1'}})

4

Verify Persistence

Send follow-up message; confirm prior context retained

Takeaways

  • Start with InMemorySaver for rapid prototyping, upgrade later
  • The compile-time checkpointer parameter is the single integration point
  • Thread config is passed at invocation time, not compile time

The StateSnapshot Class

StateSnapshot exposes the full checkpoint history, enabling time-travel debugging of graph execution.

The get_state_history method returns a sequence of StateSnapshot objects representing every checkpoint for a thread. Each snapshot contains the full state at that point, the step number, and metadata. This enables replaying or inspecting any past state, which is invaluable for debugging unexpected behavior or understanding how state evolved over multiple invocations.

  • get_state_history() returns all checkpoints for a given thread
  • Each StateSnapshot contains: state values, step number, config, metadata
  • Snapshots are ordered chronologically (most recent first)
  • Enables time-travel debugging: inspect state at any prior step
  • Useful for auditing conversation flow and diagnosing reducer bugs
📸
StateSnapshot
Frozen state at a specific graph step
⏪
Time Travel
Inspect or replay any historical state
🔍
Debugging
Trace exactly how and when state changed

Takeaways

  • Use StateSnapshot for debugging, not runtime logic
  • Time-travel capability makes state bugs reproducible
  • Checkpoint history grows with invocations; consider cleanup for long-lived threads

Long-Term Memory with SQLite

SQLite checkpointer provides durable persistence that survives process restarts with zero infrastructure overhead.

Replacing InMemorySaver with SqliteSaver gives the graph true long-term memory. State persists to a file on disk, surviving kernel restarts and system reboots. The API remains identical: compile with the checkpointer, invoke with a thread ID. SQLite requires no server setup, making it ideal for single-user or local applications. For multi-user production systems, PostgreSQL is the recommended upgrade path.

  • SqliteSaver writes checkpoints to a local .db file
  • Survives process restarts, kernel restarts, and reboots
  • API identical to InMemorySaver (drop-in replacement)
  • No external server required; perfect for local/single-user apps
  • PostgreSQL recommended for concurrent multi-user production deployments
BackendDurabilitySetupBest For
InMemorySaverVolatile (RAM)ZeroDevelopment/testing
SqliteSaverDurable (file)MinimalLocal/single-user apps
PostgreSQLDurable (server)ModerateMulti-user production

Takeaways

  • SQLite is the sweet spot between volatile memory and full database infrastructure
  • Checkpointer swaps are transparent to graph logic (same API contract)
  • Choose your backend based on deployment context, not application logic

Conclusion

Mastering LangGraph means understanding that graphs, state, reducers, and checkpointers form a composable system for stateful AI applications.

This conclusion recaps the full LangGraph journey: from basic graph construction (states, nodes, edges) through conditional routing, reducer functions, memory management (trimming, summarization), to persistent checkpointers. The key insight is that these components are orthogonal and composable: you can mix any state schema with any persistence backend and any memory strategy.

  • Graphs are built from states, nodes, edges, and conditional logic
  • Reducers control how state updates accumulate (append, replace, custom)
  • Memory management: trimming for simplicity, summarization for context preservation
  • Checkpointers decouple persistence from application logic
  • All components are independently swappable and composable

Agent Development Tools

Choosing the right agent framework depends on your use case: complexity, control needs, and team expertise.

Before building agents, evaluate the available development tools and frameworks. Options range from low-level SDK usage (direct API calls) to high-level frameworks (LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen). Each has tradeoffs in flexibility, abstraction level, community support, and production readiness. The right choice depends on your specific requirements.

  • Direct API calls offer maximum control but require more code
  • LangChain provides composable chains but can be overly abstracted
  • LangGraph adds stateful graph orchestration to LangChain
  • CrewAI and AutoGen target multi-agent collaboration patterns
  • Framework choice impacts maintainability, debugging, and team onboarding
FrameworkAbstractionStrengthBest For
Direct APILowFull controlSimple agents, custom logic
LangChainMediumComposabilityChain-based workflows
LangGraphMediumStateful graphsComplex multi-step agents
CrewAI/AutoGenHighMulti-agentTeam collaboration patterns

Takeaways

  • No single framework fits all use cases; evaluate tradeoffs explicitly
  • Higher abstraction speeds prototyping but can obscure debugging
  • Community size and documentation quality matter for long-term maintenance

Why LangGraph?

LangGraph is chosen for its balance of control, statefulness, and production maturity in the agent framework landscape.

LangGraph stands out because it combines the composability of LangChain with explicit state management and graph-based orchestration. Unlike pure chain abstractions, graphs allow cycles, conditional branching, and persistent memory natively. Its growing adoption and active development make it a pragmatic choice for building agents that need to scale beyond simple linear workflows.

  • Graph-based execution supports cycles and conditional logic natively
  • Built on LangChain ecosystem: access to existing tools and integrations
  • Explicit state management avoids hidden magic and aids debugging
  • Active development with growing community and documentation
  • Production-tested at scale by multiple organizations

  • Explicit state beats implicit state for debugging and reliability

Anatomy of a LangGraph Project

A LangGraph project has four core components: state (memory), nodes (actions), edges (flow), and tools (capabilities).

Visualizing a LangGraph project as a humanoid robot clarifies the architecture. The state is the brain (memory), nodes are limbs (performing actions), edges are the nervous system (routing signals), and tools are hands (interacting with the external world). This mental model helps when designing new agents: define what to remember, what to do, how to route, and what to interact with.

  • State: the data structure holding all information between steps (the brain)
  • Nodes: functions that process state and produce outputs (the limbs)
  • Edges: connections defining execution flow and conditions (the nervous system)
  • Tools: external capabilities the agent can invoke (the hands)
  • Clean separation of concerns enables independent testing of each component
🧠
State
Memory and data persisted between steps
🦾
Nodes
Functions that perform actions on state
🔀
Edges
Routing logic connecting nodes
🖐️
Tools
External integrations the agent can call

Takeaways

  • Design agents by answering: what state, what actions, what routing, what tools?
  • Each component is independently testable and replaceable
  • The robot analogy maps directly to code structure

Prompt Techniques Part 1

Structured prompting (role, context, constraints, output format) transforms unreliable LLM outputs into predictable agent behavior.

Effective agent prompts go beyond simple instructions. Part 1 covers foundational techniques: assigning a clear role, providing relevant context, specifying constraints, and defining the expected output format. These four elements eliminate ambiguity and reduce hallucination by narrowing the model's response space to what your agent actually needs.

  • Role assignment: tell the model WHO it is (e.g., 'You are a senior data analyst')
  • Context provision: supply relevant background the model needs
  • Constraints: explicitly state what NOT to do or boundaries to respect
  • Output format: specify structure (JSON, bullet points, specific fields)
  • Combining all four dramatically improves response consistency
1

Assign Role

Define who the model is and its expertise domain

2

Provide Context

Supply background information relevant to the task

3

Set Constraints

State boundaries, exclusions, and behavioral limits

4

Define Output Format

Specify exact structure for the response

Takeaways

  • Never prompt without a role; it anchors the model's behavior
  • Constraints prevent common failure modes proactively
  • Output format specification is non-negotiable for programmatic consumption

Prompt Techniques Part 2

Few-shot examples and chain-of-thought prompting give agents reliable reasoning patterns to follow.

Part 2 introduces few-shot prompting (providing examples of desired input-output pairs) and chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting (asking the model to reason step-by-step). Few-shot examples establish patterns the model follows by analogy. CoT forces explicit reasoning, reducing errors on complex multi-step problems. Both techniques are especially critical for agent tool-use decisions.

  • Few-shot prompting: include 2-3 examples of desired behavior in the prompt
  • Chain-of-thought: instruct the model to reason step-by-step before answering
  • Few-shot establishes patterns; CoT ensures logical consistency
  • Both reduce hallucination and improve tool-selection accuracy
  • Combine them: examples that show step-by-step reasoning
TechniqueMechanismBest ForCost
Few-shotExamples in promptPattern matching tasksMore tokens per call
Chain-of-thought'Think step by step'Complex reasoningLonger outputs
CombinedExamples with reasoningAgent tool decisionsHighest quality

Takeaways

  • Few-shot examples are the fastest way to align model behavior without fine-tuning
  • Chain-of-thought is essential for any task requiring multi-step reasoning
  • For agents, show examples of when to use (and not use) each tool

Prompting Tips and Tricks

Practical prompting tips (delimiters, temperature, iteration) convert good prompts into production-grade ones.

Beyond core techniques, practical tips make prompts more robust: use delimiters to separate sections, adjust temperature for determinism vs. creativity, iterate prompts based on failure modes, and test with adversarial inputs. These are the difference between a prompt that works in demos and one that works in production.

  • Use delimiters (###, ```, ---) to clearly separate prompt sections
  • Lower temperature (0-0.2) for deterministic tool-use; higher for creative tasks
  • Iterate based on observed failures, not hypothetical ones
  • Test with adversarial and edge-case inputs before deploying
  • Version control your prompts like code
📐
Delimiters
Structural separators for unambiguous sections
🌡️
Temperature
Controls randomness: low=deterministic, high=creative
🔄
Iteration
Refine based on real failure modes, not theory

Takeaways

  • Production prompts require iteration; first drafts always have failure modes
  • Temperature is your primary control lever for output variability
  • Treat prompt engineering as an empirical process, not a one-shot design

System Input vs. User Input

System messages define persistent agent behavior; user messages carry per-turn input. Conflating them causes unpredictable agents.

The system message sets the agent's identity, constraints, and behavioral patterns for the entire conversation. The user message delivers the specific input or question for each turn. Mixing behavioral instructions into user messages (or putting task-specific content in system messages) leads to inconsistent behavior. For agents, the system prompt is your primary control surface.

  • System message: persistent identity, role, constraints, output rules
  • User message: per-turn input, questions, data to process
  • Never put behavioral rules in user messages (they get diluted by context)
  • System prompt is the agent's 'DNA'; user message is the stimulus
  • Most agent failures trace back to poorly structured system prompts
AspectSystem MessageUser Message
PurposeDefine behavior and identityDeliver per-turn input
PersistenceConstant across turnsChanges every turn
ContentRole, constraints, format rulesQuestions, data, requests
Engineering FocusHigh (primary control)Low (variable input)

Takeaways

  • System prompt = agent behavior. User prompt = agent input. Never conflate.
  • Invest most prompt engineering effort in the system message
  • Test system prompts with diverse user inputs to verify behavioral consistency

Project: Job-Helper agent (ReAct)

The Job-Helper agent demonstrates the full ReAct pattern: a chatbot with tools that reasons about when to search and when to read files.

This project builds a Job-Helper agent using LangGraph's ReAct architecture. The agent acts as a career assistant chatbot that can read CV files and search web job postings. It decides on each turn whether to respond directly, invoke the file reader, or search the web. This demonstrates practical tool-use orchestration in a conversational agent.

  • Built on LangGraph with stateful conversation persistence

ReAct Аrchitecture Recap

ReAct (Reason + Act) cycles through thinking, tool execution, and observation until the agent can provide a final answer.

The ReAct architecture alternates between reasoning (the LLM decides what to do next) and acting (executing a tool call). After each action, the agent observes the result and reasons again about whether to act further or respond. This loop continues until the agent determines it has sufficient information. The pattern naturally handles multi-step tasks without explicit step programming.

  • ReAct = Reasoning + Acting in an iterative loop
  • Cycle: Thought (reason) → Action (tool call) → Observation (result) → repeat or answer
  • The LLM decides when to stop the loop (sufficient information gathered)
  • No relation to React.js (the web framework); completely different concept
  • Handles multi-step tasks emergently without hardcoded step sequences
1

Thought

LLM reasons about what information is needed

2

Action

LLM selects and invokes a tool with parameters

3

Observation

Tool result is fed back into context

4

Decision

Reason again: act more or provide final answer

Takeaways

  • ReAct's power is emergent multi-step problem solving without explicit programming

Building the Assistant Node

The assistant node is simply a function that invokes the LLM with the current message state and appends its response back to that state.

In LangGraph, the assistant node is the core reasoning unit. It takes the current conversation state (a list of messages), passes it to the language model (which has tools bound to it), and returns the model's response. The state object uses a MessagesState schema that accumulates messages over time. By defining the assistant as a node function, it becomes a reusable component that the graph can invoke repeatedly in a think-act loop.

  • The assistant node is a Python function that calls the LLM with the current state
  • MessagesState holds the running conversation as a list of messages
  • Tools are bound to the model before being used inside the node
  • The node returns updated state with the model's response appended
  • This pattern separates reasoning logic from graph wiring

Building the Graph

The graph is built by declaring nodes (assistant, tools), connecting them with edges, and using a conditional router to decide whether to loop back or finish.

Wiring the LangGraph graph involves three components: nodes, edges, and conditional edges. StateGraph is the builder object. The START marker defines where execution begins. A ToolNode automatically executes any tool calls the LLM requests. The tools_condition router checks whether the model's last response contains tool calls; if yes, flow routes to the tool node, otherwise to END. After the tool node runs, an unconditional edge loops back to the assistant for further reasoning.

  • StateGraph is the builder that declares nodes and edges
  • START is a marker (not a runnable node) indicating the entry point
  • tools_condition is a built-in router that checks for tool calls in the last message
  • ToolNode wraps tool execution and returns results as messages
  • After tools execute, flow always returns to the assistant node

The output is a state dictionary containing all messages exchanged during execution. Printing each message reveals the full trace: user input, assistant reasoning, tool calls, tool responses, and the final answer.

Adding Memory

A checkpointer gives the agent persistent memory by saving graph state between runs, enabling multi-turn conversations with a thread ID.

Without memory, each graph invocation starts fresh. LangGraph's checkpointer solves this by persisting the state (message history) between runs. A MemorySaver stores state in memory (or a database for production). When compiling the graph, pass the checkpointer. At invocation time, provide a config with a unique thread_id. The agent then resumes from the last saved state for that thread, enabling true multi-turn conversations where context accumulates.

  • Without a checkpointer, the agent has no memory between invocations
  • MemorySaver is LangGraph's built-in in-memory persistence
  • Pass the checkpointer during graph.compile(checkpointer=...)
  • Each conversation thread is identified by a unique thread_id in config
  • The agent resumes from the last checkpoint for the given thread

Persists graph state between invocations

Unique identifier for each conversation session
💾
MemorySaver

🔄
State Resume

Takeaways

  • Thread IDs enable parallel independent conversations with the same graph
  • For production, replace MemorySaver with a database-backed checkpointer
  • Memory transforms a stateless tool-caller into a conversational assistant

ReWOO Architecture Overview

ReWOO separates planning from execution: the LLM creates a full plan upfront, then tools execute in sequence without further LLM calls until the final synthesis.

ReWOO (Reasoning WithOut Observation) is an alternative to ReAct. Instead of interleaving thinking and tool use in a loop, ReWOO has the LLM generate a complete plan first, specifying all tool calls needed. An executor then runs those tools sequentially without returning to the LLM. Finally, a solver node takes all gathered evidence and synthesizes the answer. This reduces LLM calls dramatically, lowering cost and latency while maintaining quality for well-structured tasks.

  • ReWOO uses three phases: Plan, Execute, Solve
  • The planner generates all tool calls upfront in a single LLM invocation
  • The executor runs tools sequentially without LLM involvement
  • The solver synthesizes all evidence into a final answer
  • Fewer LLM calls means lower cost and faster execution
AspectReActReWOO
FlowThink-Act-Observe loopPlan-Execute-Solve sequential
LLM CallsMultiple (one per loop iteration)Two (plan + solve)
AdaptabilityHigh (adjusts based on observations)Lower (plan is fixed)
CostHigher (more tokens)Lower (fewer LLM invocations)
Best ForComplex, unpredictable tasksStructured, predictable tasks

Takeaways

  • ReWOO excels when tasks are predictable and tool calls can be planned ahead
  • ReAct is better for tasks requiring adaptive reasoning based on intermediate results
  • Choose architecture based on task predictability vs. adaptability needs

Building the Planner Node

The planner node uses a structured prompt to make the LLM output a numbered plan with tool calls and variable references that downstream nodes can parse.

The planner node wraps a carefully crafted prompt that instructs the LLM to produce a structured plan. Each step in the plan specifies a tool to call and its arguments, using variable placeholders (like #E1, #E2) to reference outputs from previous steps. The node function takes the state, formats the prompt with the user's query, invokes the LLM, and parses the response into a list of planned steps stored in state. This makes the plan machine-readable for the executor.

  • The planner prompt instructs the LLM to output structured, numbered steps
  • Each step specifies: tool name, arguments, and a variable label (#E1, #E2)
  • Variable references allow later steps to use earlier results
  • The node parses the LLM output into a structured list in state
  • This is a single LLM call that produces the entire execution plan

Create a prompt that instructs structured plan output with tool calls

2

Format with User Query

3

Invoke LLM

Single call produces the complete multi-step plan

4

Parse Plan

5

Store in State

Takeaways

  • Prompt engineering is critical; the plan format must be consistently parseable
  • Variable references (#E1, #E2) create implicit data dependencies between steps
  • Test the planner prompt in isolation before integrating into the graph

Implementing the Executor

The executor iterates through the planner's steps, calls each tool with resolved variable references, and stores results back into state for the solver.

The executor node replaces the ReAct tool loop. It reads the plan from state and iterates through each step. For each step, it resolves variable references (#E1, #E2) by substituting actual results from previously executed steps. Then it calls the specified tool with the resolved arguments. Results are stored in a dictionary keyed by variable label. Once all steps complete, the executor writes all evidence to state. No LLM is involved during execution.

  • The executor reads the plan list from state and processes steps sequentially
  • Variable references are resolved by substituting prior step outputs
  • Each tool is called directly without LLM mediation
  • Results are stored in a dict keyed by variable label (#E1, #E2, etc.)
  • No LLM calls occur during execution, reducing cost
1

2

Iterate Steps
