3

Resolve Variables

Replace #E references with actual prior results

4

Call Tool

Execute the specified tool with resolved arguments

5

Store Result

Save output keyed by the step's variable label

6

Write Evidence to State

Update state with all collected results

Takeaways

  • Variable resolution is string substitution: replace #E1 with its stored result
  • Error handling in the executor should store error messages as evidence for the solver
  • The executor is deterministic given a fixed plan

Implementing the Solver

The solver takes all evidence gathered by the executor and uses a single LLM call to synthesize a coherent final answer for the user.

The solver is the final node in ReWOO. It receives the user's original question and all evidence collected by the executor (stored as key-value pairs in state). A prompt template presents the question alongside the evidence, instructing the LLM to synthesize a clear, comprehensive answer. This is the second and final LLM call in the entire ReWOO pipeline. The solver's output becomes the agent's response to the user.

  • The solver reads the original question and all evidence from state
  • A prompt template formats question + evidence for the LLM
  • This is the second (and final) LLM call in ReWOO
  • The LLM synthesizes evidence into a coherent user-facing answer
  • Output is written to state as the final response
📥
Input
Original question + all executor evidence
📝
Prompt
Template combining question with evidence pairs
🤖
LLM Call
Single invocation to synthesize the final answer
📤
Output
Polished response delivered to the user

Takeaways

  • The solver prompt should instruct concise, evidence-based answers
  • Quality depends on both planner coverage and executor accuracy
  • Two total LLM calls (plan + solve) vs. many in ReAct

Wiring Up the ReWOO Graph

The ReWOO graph wires planner, executor, and solver as sequential nodes with a conditional router that skips execution if the plan is empty.

Wiring the ReWOO graph follows a linear flow: START to planner, planner to router, router to executor or END, executor to solver, solver to END. The router function checks if the planner produced any tool-call steps. If yes, it routes to the executor; if the planner answered directly (no tools needed), it routes to END. This differs from ReAct's loop structure; ReWOO is a single-pass pipeline with one conditional branch.

  • Graph flow is linear: planner -> router -> executor -> solver
  • The router checks if the plan contains tool-call steps
  • If no tools needed, the router short-circuits directly to END
  • No loops exist in ReWOO; it is a single-pass pipeline
  • Compile with the same .compile() pattern used in ReAct

Check if plan has tool steps; return next node name

2

Build Graph

Add planner, executor, solver nodes to StateGraph

3

Wire Edges

START->planner, planner->router(conditional), executor->solver, solver->END

4

Compile

Produce runnable graph

Takeaways

  • ReWOO's graph is simpler than ReAct because there is no loop
  • The router prevents unnecessary executor/solver calls for simple questions
  • Linear graphs are easier to debug and reason about

ReAct vs ReWOO

Side-by-side comparison in LangSmith reveals ReWOO uses fewer LLM calls and tokens than ReAct for the same task, at the cost of less adaptive reasoning.

Running both architectures on identical queries and comparing in LangSmith shows clear tradeoffs. ReAct makes multiple LLM calls (one per loop iteration), consuming more tokens and time, but adapts its approach based on intermediate results. ReWOO completes in two LLM calls (plan + solve), using fewer tokens and finishing faster, but cannot adjust if a tool returns unexpected data. For predictable tasks, ReWOO wins on efficiency; for complex reasoning, ReAct wins on accuracy.

  • LangSmith shows token count, latency, and step count for each architecture
  • ReAct: more LLM calls, higher tokens, adaptive reasoning
  • ReWOO: two LLM calls, fewer tokens, fixed plan execution
  • ReWOO is faster and cheaper for well-defined tasks
  • ReAct handles edge cases better due to observation-based adjustment
MetricReActReWOO
LLM Calls4-8 per query2 per query
Token UsageHigherLower
LatencyHigherLower
AdaptabilityHighLow
Error RecoverySelf-correctsFails if plan is wrong

Takeaways

  • Use LangSmith to make data-driven architecture decisions
  • Default to ReAct for general agents; use ReWOO for cost-sensitive predictable workflows
  • Hybrid approaches can plan with ReWOO and fall back to ReAct on failure

Project Overview

The advanced project combines human-in-the-loop interaction with parallel tool execution to build a multi-advisor business idea evaluator.

This project raises complexity by combining two patterns: human-in-the-loop (HITL) for gathering clarification, and parallelization for running multiple advisor nodes simultaneously. The agent first clarifies the business idea with the user through a conversation loop, then fans out to specialized advisor nodes (market, finance, technical) that run in parallel, and finally collects their outputs into a unified report. This demonstrates production-grade agent architecture.

  • Combines HITL and parallelization in a single graph
  • First phase: clarification loop with the user
  • Second phase: parallel execution of specialized advisor nodes
  • Third phase: collection and report generation
  • Demonstrates composition of multiple agent patterns

Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)

Human-in-the-loop means interrupting agent execution to get human input, approval, or correction before proceeding with consequential actions.

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) encompasses any pattern where a human intervenes during agent execution. Common forms include: approval gates (human confirms before tool execution), input collection (agent asks clarifying questions), correction (human edits agent's plan), and escalation (agent defers to human on low-confidence decisions). In LangGraph, HITL is implemented via interrupt nodes that pause execution, return control to the user, and resume when input is provided.

  • HITL can occur before, during, or after AI decision-making
  • Approval gates prevent risky actions without human consent
  • Input collection ensures the agent has sufficient context
  • LangGraph uses interrupt nodes to pause and resume execution
  • The checkpointer preserves state while waiting for human input
✋
Approval Gate
Human confirms before execution proceeds
❓
Input Collection
Agent asks for missing information
✏️
Correction
Human edits the agent's proposed plan
🚨
Escalation
Agent defers uncertain decisions to human

Takeaways

  • Use HITL for high-stakes decisions where errors are costly
  • The checkpointer is essential for HITL; it saves state during the pause
  • Design the interrupt to clearly communicate what input is needed

Parallelization

Parallelization in LangGraph means fanning out to multiple nodes that execute simultaneously and fanning back in to a collector node.

LangGraph supports parallelization natively through fan-out/fan-in patterns. When multiple nodes share the same upstream edge, they execute concurrently. A downstream collector node waits for all parallel branches to complete before proceeding. This is ideal for tasks where independent analyses can run simultaneously, such as querying multiple APIs or running different evaluation criteria. The state must be designed to accommodate parallel writes without conflicts.

  • Fan-out: multiple edges from one node to several parallel nodes
  • Fan-in: a collector node with edges from all parallel nodes
  • Parallel nodes execute concurrently, reducing total latency
  • State must handle concurrent writes (e.g., using list append reducers)
  • LangGraph handles synchronization automatically at the fan-in point
🔀
Fan-Out
Single node branches to multiple parallel nodes
🔁
Fan-In
Collector waits for all branches to complete
⚡
Concurrency
Parallel nodes run simultaneously
📋
Reducer
State field logic that merges parallel writes

Takeaways

  • Use parallelization whenever tasks are independent of each other
  • Design state fields with reducers that support concurrent appends
  • Total latency equals the slowest parallel branch, not the sum

Initializing the State

The state definition for this project uses typed fields with reducers to hold the conversation, advisor outputs, and final report in a single schema.

The project state extends beyond simple MessagesState. It defines typed fields for: messages (conversation history with list append reducer), business_idea (extracted from clarification), advisor_outputs (list that accumulates parallel results via reducer), and final_report (string set by the collector). Reducers like operator.add ensure parallel nodes can safely append to shared list fields. All imports and environment variables are initialized upfront.

  • State schema has multiple typed fields beyond just messages
  • Reducers (operator.add) enable safe concurrent list appends
  • business_idea stores the clarified concept for advisor consumption
  • advisor_outputs accumulates results from parallel advisor nodes
  • final_report holds the synthesized output from the collector

Building the Human-in-the-loop

The HITL loop uses a clarifier node that asks questions and a router that checks if enough context has been gathered to proceed to the advisors.

The human-in-the-loop implementation uses two components: a clarifier node and a router. The clarifier node prompts the LLM to assess whether it has enough information about the business idea; if not, it generates a follow-up question for the user. The router checks the LLM's assessment: if clarification is complete, it routes to the advisor fan-out; otherwise, it loops back to wait for user input. The interrupt mechanism pauses execution until the user responds.

  • Clarifier node uses LLM to decide if more info is needed
  • If incomplete, the node generates a targeted follow-up question
  • Router checks a flag/signal in state to decide: loop or proceed
  • Interrupt pauses the graph, returning the question to the user
  • On resume, the user's answer is added to messages and the loop continues

Takeaways

  • Let the LLM decide when enough context has been gathered
  • Keep clarification questions specific and actionable
  • Limit loop iterations to prevent infinite clarification cycles

Creating Pre-Made “Advisor” Nodes

Advisor nodes are specialized LLM calls with role-specific prompts that analyze the business idea from distinct perspectives (market, finance, technical).

Each advisor node is a function with a domain-specific system prompt. For example, the market advisor evaluates market size and competition, the finance advisor assesses revenue models and funding needs, and the technical advisor reviews feasibility and tech stack. All advisors receive the same business_idea from state and return their analysis as a string appended to advisor_outputs. Since they are independent, they run in parallel via fan-out edges.

  • Each advisor has a role-specific system prompt defining its perspective
  • All advisors read the same business_idea field from state
  • Outputs are appended to the advisor_outputs list via reducer
  • Advisors are independent and run concurrently
  • Adding new advisors is as simple as creating a new node with a new prompt

  • Parallel execution means adding advisors does not increase latency linearly
  • Keep advisor prompts focused; one perspective per node

Collection Node and Building the Graph

The collection node gathers all advisor outputs from state and uses a single LLM call to synthesize them into a structured final report.

The collect-and-report node is the fan-in point. It reads advisor_outputs from state (a list of analysis strings) and the original business_idea. A prompt template presents all advisor analyses to the LLM, instructing it to synthesize a structured report covering strengths, risks, and recommendations. The LLM output is stored in final_report. The graph wiring connects all advisor nodes to this single collector, which proceeds to END after generating the report.

  • Collection node is the fan-in point after parallel advisors
  • Reads all advisor outputs and the original business idea from state
  • Uses a synthesis prompt to produce a structured report
  • Single LLM call combines multiple perspectives into one document
  • Graph edges: all advisors -> collector -> END

Running the complete graph demonstrates the full flow: clarification loop, parallel advisor execution, and final report generation in one invocation.

The final step is running the assembled graph end-to-end. Invoke it with an initial business idea message. The clarification loop fires first, potentially pausing for user input via interrupt. The output state contains the full message history, individual advisor analyses, and the final report. LangSmith tracing shows the entire execution timeline.

  • Interrupts pause execution for user input during clarification
  • Parallel advisors appear as concurrent branches in LangSmith traces
  • Final state contains messages, advisor_outputs, and final_report
  • Total execution time is dominated by the slowest advisor, not their sum

Bonus lecture

Environment variables protect sensitive API keys from being hardcoded, using OS-level key-value storage accessible by your application at runtime.

Environment variables are OS-level key-value pairs that store configuration and secrets outside your code. For AI agent development, the OpenAI API key must be set as an environment variable to avoid exposing credentials in source files. This is done via the operating system's settings (Windows) or shell profile (Mac/Linux). Python's os.getenv() retrieves the value at runtime. This pattern applies to all API keys, database URLs, and secrets used in agent projects.

  • Environment variables are key-value pairs managed by the operating system
  • API keys should never be hardcoded in source files
  • Set via System Properties (Windows) or .bashrc/.zshrc (Mac/Linux)
  • Python retrieves them with os.getenv('VARIABLE_NAME')
  • Restart your IDE/terminal after setting new environment variables
MethodSecurityUse Case
Hardcoded in codeDangerousNever use for real keys
OS Environment VariableGoodProduction and local dev
.env file + dotenvGood (if .gitignored)Team development
Secret Manager (AWS/GCP)BestProduction cloud deployments

Takeaways

  • Always use environment variables for API keys and secrets
  • Hardcoded credentials risk exposure when sharing code
  • The .env file with python-dotenv is a common development alternative

Additional Code Labs

Code Lab Setting the API Key as an Environment Variable

Setting the API Key as an Environment Variable

In the previous lesson, we logged into OpenAI’s website, generated a personal API key, and saved it locally in a text file. We’ll learn how to set this API key as an environment variable, which will soon be used to communicate with the OpenAI library. First, let’s delve into the concept of environment variables. An environment variable is a key-value pair used by the operating system, with the key corresponding to the name of the variable while the value representing—in our case, the OpenAI API key. The key and the value are typically stored as strings. A classic example is the PATH environment variable, which stores a list of directories where executable programs are located—enabling the operating system to find these programs when needed. Another typical example is the HOME or HOMEPATH environment variable—storing the path to the user’s home directory. Environment variables are essential for protecting such sensitive data as API keys. For example, the OpenAI API key—a required credential for accessing the OpenAI services—should not be exposed within the code. Hardcoding its value risks unintended exposure, such as when you share your code with friends or colleagues. This is a critical security issue because invoking OpenAI’s models through the API corresponds to using tokens, a paid service. By providing your API key to others, you make it possible for them to spend the tokens **you** are paying for. If you notice abnormal behavior that doesn’t match your token usage, revoke the API key immediately and generate a new one. Doing so makes the old API key invalid. Setting the API key as an environment variable and ensuring its confidentiality can prevent this. Moreover, storing the API key as an environment variable enables you to update it and seamlessly propagate that change across all source code files, thereby maintaining a clean code. All right, it's time we get to coding! First, ensure you've selected the **langchain_env** kernel in the Jupyter notebook. You can see the kernel that is currently used in the top-right corner. You can change the kernel by navigating to 'Kernel' in the ribbon menu. Then, select 'Change kernel' from the drop-down menu and choose the appropriate one. Next, ensure the notebook and the text file storing your key are in the same directory, i.e., in the same folder. Open the text file and write the following text: OPENAI_API_KEY="..." In place of the three dots, insert your API key, such that the content of the text file looks as follows: OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..." Save the text file, close it, and rename it ‘.env’ Now, let’s use IPython ’s magic commands to load the environment variable stored in the text file. Use the **%load_ext** command to load an extension. The one we need is **dotenv**.

Use the **dotenv** magic command to read the key-value pair stored in the text file and set it as an environment variable.

You are now prepared to move forward to the exciting bit of the practical part: creating our first chatbot with OpenAI. Can’t wait to see you in the next lesson!
